texto: Sim, eu dou 4 estrelas pra cats. Sim eu sei que é um filme ruim em muitos sentidos. Só que é um músical com alguns músicos muito competentes, atores renomados, um grande orçamento para efeitos especiais, e é impossível compreender como que esse filme foi feito e uma qualidade tão ruim. Há algo lindo e poético na sequência de decisões que fizeram esse filme existir. Tantas coisas incompreensíveis, desde a existência de uma das primeiras versões do filme em que os gatos tinham cús, e quando obviamente se deram conta que isso era bizarro, gastaram milhões para digitalmente tirar os cús dos gatos. A existência de arte para o consumo humano, vinda de forma americanizada e de holllywood raramente nos dará outras sequências de decisões incompreensíveis que resultem em um produto tão absurdo quanto cats. Eu aprecio filmes ruins, esse é um dos melhores dos piores. Ainda assim, por um motivo não posso dar 5 estrelas. Eu achava que única decisão imperdoável que qualquer filme pode tomar é colocar o James Corden na tela, mas há mais uma, colocar o James Corden cantando. Todo o resto consigo perdoar, mas desde a primeira vez que vi, a presença dele por alguns minutos na tela suga a aura camp que era construída e demora pra recuperar. De qualquer forma, vejam cats. É uma experiência única e é um dos filmes que eu mais queria ver pela primeira vez de novo.

texto: After finally watching this I think it might have been a little overhated just due to the creepy-ass cat designs (although, I suppose we have to look at those abominations all through-out the movie so it's a fair reason to hate it). texto: I've seen this three times now, and every experience has just been more transcendent, more gloriously unhinged. I understand that, technically, theoretically, it's bad. But with a full crowd, it's a goddamn party.  The best, most riotously joyous time you'll have in a theatre this side of Gremlins 2. How can you honestly critique that? Other than to say, somehow, through all its flaws, ugly effects, and insane story decisions, Cats emerges as something that, in its own very specific way, is kind of a masterpiece. Alien and weird and awful and beautiful in a way no other film is. Never watch it alone. But never pass up the chance to see it with a packed house. It'll be one of the best theatrical experiences of your life. Long live Jellicle Cats. Long live Skimbleshanks.

texto: Can we actually find value in a film that while yes shows the violence people go through when their material needs aren’t met, but doesn’t actually fully call out the cause of the violence? I don’t think so. Especially when the violence towards the men, women, and children is shown as just a symptom and not actually done tactfully. To not have any discussion about the cause of the violence is because of state and police violence, because of class systems, racism, and sexism is irresponsible. Vague pointing at police is not enough. This film says violence begets violence and that right there is the most violent part of this film. These people deserve more. And if all we do is witness the violence can we say we are any better? I don’t think so.

tema: Retrato explorador e sensacionalista da pobreza
exemplo: O filme é visto como uma exploração da miséria, usando a violência e o sofrimento como espetáculo para o público estrangeiro, sem se aprofundar nas causas sociais ou dar dignidade aos personagens.
texto: I can’t imagine many of the people who live in The City Of God at the time actually saw this theatrically. And I imagine they would find this distasteful. This is all quite gauche and feels exploitative of real poverty and the trap of poverty. The film deals with race quite strangely as well in a way that made me feel a little bit uncomfortable. Im not really a fan of the style of this either, it’s all very flashy but it kind of makes the characters never feel fully realised. They don’t feel like real people because the movie is more interested in being stylised poverty porn exploitation than a story about people. The idea of gazing at disproportionally black poverty and violence and killing is not interesting to me. Especially when it isnt made for or by the community it is depicting the suffering of. The way death and dead bodies are handled in this film intentionally lacks a level of weight i think to alienate people and upset them. But an image  containing only viscera  divorces the humanity of death and turns it into a spectacle to gaze at. If this came out in an English speaking environment i think people would be more critical of this. Most English speaking audiences don’t really watch films in other languages. I think there is an element of this being an incredibly easy to understand narrative and stylistically familiar enough that more people would give this a shot as a “foreign film”. Which i think lends to a level of exoticism to how some people interact with and engage with the film. Of the few negative reviews i have bothered glancing at a lot of them seem to come from Brazil. There are other crime films i share this criticism with. However there are still several crime films that feel connected enough to the communities depicted in them, to where I feel they are less problematic. The gaze and regard in which this film is held in to me reads as somewhat colonial. The Auteurs and audience domination and extraction of respect, life and humanity in exchange for a narrative that allows people to have their “Harrowing” movie where they get to watch vicariously through an audience surrogate. Where is the framework of media analysis with the response to this film? I genuinely think audiences collectively should scrutinise this film so much more. During my film course at uni there have been several films we have seen where we interrogate how we felt about the film we just watched, we process what it was saying, what it meant, and even at times analysed where the point of view of its conception came from. And sometimes this encompassed the ethics of a film’s conception. And oftentimes this inherently led to the concepts of class dynamics and racism. This is a film that is quite frankly begging for this level of interrogation. And the overwhelming majority of people simply don’t care enough to analyse how the film made them feel the way it did or what it has to say about the context in which the film was made in.

texto: Primeira revisão em anos, agora percebo que o Meirelles deve muito do sucesso de “Cidade de Deus” à sua experiência prévia com a publicidade. Ele pesa a mão numa hiperestilização dessensibilizada muito característica desses anos 2000 pós-“Pulp Fiction”, pós-MTV, que se importa sobretudo com estímulos fáceis, e não em manter uma boa unidade dramática. Isso funciona de momentos em momentos, o que realmente me pega e me faz odiar “Cidade de Deus” é o exotismo colonizador com o qual o olhar do Meirelles recai sobre essa realidade, que enxerga de uma perspectiva distanciada interessada em explorar (e, principalmente, vender) o sofrimento dos seus personagens sem nunca dar a dignidade para que eles se tornem seres humanos reais.

tema: Excesso de violência e ritmo exaustivo
exemplo: A violência constante e a edição frenética são criticadas por tornarem a experiência cansativa e por reduzirem o impacto emocional, fazendo com que as mortes pareçam banais e sem peso.
texto: I honestly don’t understand the overwhelming praise for City of God. While the film has impressive camera work and a fast-paced style, I found it exhausting rather than engaging. The constant violence, brutal characters, and endless cycle of crime make it feel more like a long sequence of shocking moments than a meaningful story. The characters are difficult to connect with because so many of them are defined by cruelty and survival, leaving little emotional depth for the audience to hold on to. The movie seems more interested in showing chaos and brutality than exploring the people behind it. The storytelling style, with its rapid editing and nonstop narration, can also feel distracting and overcomplicated. Instead of creating a powerful emotional experience, it sometimes feels like the film is trying too hard to prove how gritty and intense it can be. Although it has technical strengths, City of God was not an enjoyable watch for me. It is violent, overwhelming, and far too focused on misery to be the masterpiece many people claim it is. DONT RECOMMEND WATCHING

tema: Narrativa fragmentada e excesso de narração
exemplo: A estrutura não linear e o uso constante de voz off são apontados como confusos e didáticos, dificultando o envolvimento com a história e entregando informações de forma artificial.
texto: 30 Countries Challenge 2014: Stop 3, Brazil "I smoke, I snort, I've killed and robbed. I'm a man." To be perfectly honest I'm currently unsure how to write this review because I'm still utterly baffled as to how City of God has been elevated to, pardon the joke, a god-like status. I can respect Meirelles for the brutal reality he's shown on screen and I found a few of the performances decent, but for the most part I found the film completely unwatchable for both it's disjointed narrative and obnoxious visuals. To begin I hated the way City of God handled it's multiple story lines. The film opened with a half an hour segment that features the protagonist's brother, a segment of the film that doesn't actually affect the rest of the story besides setting up the Lil' Dice character. Seeing as later in the film Lil' Dice gets reintroduced to us as Li'l Zé, with a whole little montage of Lil' Dice's experience in the hood, that rendered the opening 30 minutes completely pointless from a narrative point of view. The two biggest things I didn't like about the multiple narratives would be the constant narration from Rocket and how abruptly the stories would intertwine. First off, character narration is my biggest gripe about any movie, and it's got all the traits I hate about it in this film. Characters are introduced to us via an impersonal freeze-frame voice over monologue, rather than giving us a natural introduction through dialogue. Narration is used to mask progression in time, rather than simply showing us a montage of events. The narration is delivered in an extremely dry and emotionless manor, which becomes very annoying to listen to. Exposition is frequently delivered to us via voice over, like the character introductions, rather than just giving it to us subtly through dialogue. I feel like I have to write this in every review that features narration. A character's voice over just feels like a cheap way of feeding the audience information without utilizing the language of film. On top of that voice over is a very formal and impersonal way of presenting a story, making us feel disconnected from most characters besides the person consistently talking in our ear. If you're writing a script and it doesn't make sense without having someone literally explain the story to the audience, you have to re-write your script, which is something that should have been done with City of God . The other big thing I didn't like about the narrative was the intertwined stories. Take what was titled the "Knockout Ned story" for instance. In the middle of Ned's story, there were multiple scenes of Rocket working at a newspaper and taking photos in the hood. I don't really understand why the film went through all the effort of even giving us a subtitle for every chapter, when they're just going to freely inter-cut different stories along with it. I actually liked the ambition with the film and I really enjoyed all the character based stories, but I don't feel such a diverse story works if they try to simultaneously split up all the narratives while also editing them together. It made for a film that was inherently difficult to follow because they're attempting to build a kind of formality with the structure while also being very loose about when they told each story. Probably my least favourite thing about the film would be the visuals. I just felt everything was thrown at the camera without any attempts at properly constructing a scene. The camera darting and shaking so frequently that when there was a rare still moment I felt I could finally enjoy watching the film again. I'm not exaggerating when I say I found the film extremely challenging just to watch, which is made even more difficult with the straight-up ugly orange filter everything has. If the visuals were made intentionally unbearable I would understand, maybe the director was attempting to create a film that visually matches the lives of the people on the street, but this doesn't make the film any less disorientating to watch. There was one scene that I felt was impressive visually, and that would be the story of the apartment where we went through all the minor drug dealers that inhabited the same apartment. Not coincidentally that scene was also shot completely still, using cross-fades and overlays to construct the story rather than using multiple camera angles. Unfortunately that scene is an example of my problem with the voice over, because the story could have easily just been shown to us but rather there was a non-stop narration throughout. What the film did have working for it was a handful of decent performances. The lead, Alexandre Rodrigues as Rocket, gave a very enjoyable performance, I especially liked his character during the relationship scenes. I was very disappointed with Rodrigues's vocal performance, to be honest I found his voice very dreary and tiresome to listen to, making him the worst person to choose for the narrator, but my gripe with his voice is probably just because of how much I had to listen to it. I also liked Seu Jorge, who played Knockout Ned. Jorge should have been given a lot more time on screen. I found his character the most understanding and was extremely disappointed when his transformation into a hoodlum was brushed over in a couple of scenes. I also thought Matheus Nachtergaele, who played Carrot, was given far too little time on screen. Especially considering how big a role Carrot played in the story, I don't see why Nachtergaele wasn't given his own segment. The only gang leader that was properly represented was Li'l Zé, who happened to be my favourite character. I liked Lil' Dice's climb to the top, I really liked the child actor who played Lil' Dice, Douglas Silva, I liked his spiritual sub-plot. I liked his relationship with Benny, a character and performance (Phellipe Haagensen) that is given too much credit. I think the best thing this film does is tell the story of Li'l Zé from start to finish, and it shows that if the film wasn't so bogged down with multiple narratives and side-characters that don't amount to anything, it can actually tell a competent story. If a film ends and I don't care what happened to the protagonist, the film has failed. City of God manages to rip all of the character and humanity out of a film based around the lives of people. I wouldn't call it my favourite Paul Thomas Anderson film, but if you want to watch a movie that has as complex a conjoined narrative structure as well as a very emotional story, watch Magnolia . City of God was just obnoxious and difficult for me to watch from start to finish. That doesn't take away the good performances and occasional interesting visual, but those two things are far away from saving this film. I'm in the minority with this film and I'm sure plenty of people will strongly disagree with me, so I recommend you give it a watch yourself, but personally I didn't enjoy it and wouldn't go out of my way to watch it again.

texto: City of God is a glitzy and glamorous Hollywood movie masquerading as a revolutionary foreign language indie. People are so impressed (at least based off my film class) to see the country of Brazil pornographically shot in a Tarantino, MTV-esque fashion that fetishizes violence, drugs and sex with outrageous vigor. No surprise that this was directed by somebody in the advertising field because it is a great looking film that is nonetheless empty of heart and soul. It's Brazil n' tha Hood, a pantomime of popular American films without even a tinge of visual realism or relevance to the real slums of Brazil. Not to say I know a damn thing about how it actually runs but I found very little to find believable among the pretty lighting and eye catching editing. I suppose I understand why this is so highly rated because City of God might be a good movie but it's also one that lies or at least blinds the audience to the non-sensational reality. The movie has many shocking moments but it doesn't earn them because of how it doesn't even bother to make a point out of anything, since again, this is a wildly slick picture interested in the surface and not much else. I can't say I'm a fan, and ignoring the technical merits of it, I feel largely nothing about this shell of "neorealist" cinema.

texto: Primeira revisão em anos, agora percebo que o Meirelles deve muito do sucesso de “Cidade de Deus” à sua experiência prévia com a publicidade. Ele pesa a mão numa hiperestilização dessensibilizada muito característica desses anos 2000 pós-“Pulp Fiction”, pós-MTV, que se importa sobretudo com estímulos fáceis, e não em manter uma boa unidade dramática. Isso funciona de momentos em momentos, o que realmente me pega e me faz odiar “Cidade de Deus” é o exotismo colonizador com o qual o olhar do Meirelles recai sobre essa realidade, que enxerga de uma perspectiva distanciada interessada em explorar (e, principalmente, vender) o sofrimento dos seus personagens sem nunca dar a dignidade para que eles se tornem seres humanos reais.

texto: Assistindo para pesquisa. Acho impressionante o fenômeno de filmes do fim dos anos 90 para início dos anos 2000 nesse ciclo mais mainstream comercial. Claro que hoje tudo é mais padronizado que no passado, mas diria que existe uma forma muito mais explícita na maneira que vários desses filmes se emulavam em suas ideias de linguagem e escolhas narrativas. A ideia do que representava uma encenação de bom gosto tinha uma expressão muito mais clara, até porque existia uma menor quantidade de padrões a ser considerada. E não teria como não entender o grande projeto da retomada neste lugar. Definitivamente existe um primor no que se diz respeito à maneira que o filme se utiliza das personagens. Todos representam em algum lugar uma ideia muito única de si. Mas vejo isso apenas como um embrião que nunca nasce. A virtude se apaga no meio dessa formalização excessivamente programada. Cidade de Deus emula essa montagem ágil dos contemporâneos hollywoodianos. Isso enquanto tenta impor espetacularização em cima de uma banalidade que nunca parece se unir. Enquanto opta por uma narrativa cheia de tropos de outro lugar que não o engloba. Até a metade do filme, essa forma que é uma simbiose meio falha me incomoda menos do que quando decide transformar Leandro Firmino em um adolescente colegial norteamericano com dificuldades em chamar a garota para dançar no baile. Daí em diante a postura dele e do filme assume um caráter falso de infantilização, meio bobo. Eu poderia pensar na voz off didática que impede o filme de acontecer, ou na dramatização meio vazia do filme como um todo. À parte o momento em que Phellipe Haagensen sai de cena, pouco além disso impõe uma intenção dramática. Product of it’s time

texto: There is a relentless, sun-drenched velocity to City of God that tricks you into thinking you’re watching a kinetic crime epic, right up until you realize every scene is quietly mourning. What hits hardest on a rewatch isn't just the breathless editing or the electric, samba infused soundtrack it’s how the film treats youth. Kids in the favela aren't given a grace period to just figure things out; they’re forced into adult archetypes before their voices even break. Rocket’s camera lens becomes his only real shield, a way to witness the chaos without letting it consume him entirely, while Lil Zé treats fear as the only currency that matters You could argue it occasionally risks hyper stylizing real world trauma at times, the late 90s post MTV sheen almost feels too sleek for the gravel and sweat it’s documenting. But underneath all that frantic, kinetic energy is a deeply human pulse. It barely lets you catch your breath, not just to thrill you, but because the kids on screen never got to catch theirs either

texto: I've wanted to watch this for years and years, and yet I never did. Maybe there was a reason for that. City of God brims with flair and technique, and there is nary a moment when the image and sound presented aren't well rendered and constructed. But therein lies the issue with this film. It feels too constructed, too amalgamated. The result of a heap of story material set ablaze specifically to hide from sincerity. Is the story true? To a turn, as many of these kinds of stories are. I think where this one falters is that it never seems to stop to consider that it's got one foot in the door of stylized imaginings of a roughly relatable cinematic narrative, and the other in the door of gritty depiction of the lives of the sub-altern. It tends to choose style more than anything else, and in doing so leaves a lot on the table. The flair and flash of its photography, cutting and acting lose quite a bit of their impact by the time you see the 15th or so callous murder--a weightlessness that it feels like the film encourages after a fashion. Simply put: there isn't enough story behind the pomp and circumstance to keep the style engaging. The narrative feels less like a cohesive tableau and more like a series of loosely connected vignettes that are united by violence and excess and not by character presence or investment. Glad I watched it, but I can't say I'm happy with what I watched.

texto: Not quite for me. This Brazilian film, firmly entrenched in the coveted top-25 highest rated films on IMDB, is the true-story about two boys growing up in the violent "City Of God" neighborhood outside of Rio De Janiero in Brazil - one becomes a photographer, the other a murderous drug-dealer. The 130-minute story feels like a Portuguese version of Scorsese's "Goodefllas" - except with delusional and hopeless children, rather than Ray Liotta and Robert DeNiro. Perhaps it was because of the subtitles, or because all the children looked so similar, or perhaps it was the non-linear and sporadic narrative, but I found myself struggling to follow the complicated plot and character paths for most of the first half of this film. When things finally settled in, and after most of the supporting cast had been killed off - I was pleasantly surprised by "City Of God" - which finally started to come into its own, rather than a string of familiar scenes of people getting murdered. The immensely large cast of local amateurs all did a terrific job, but none of them really stood-out, and I found it difficult to really connect to any of the main characters. I will say this though: the cinematography and editing in this film were absolutely outstanding - keeping things moving at a blistering pace, all while maintaining a very stylized, almost music-video look to some of the shots. The dirty slums of Rio are portrayed with gritty and striking realism that really immerses you in the sounds and sights of this hellish neighborhood. And although this film, and all of its characters are closely based on a true-story, I couldn't help but feel like it was poor-man's version of much better gangster films that had come before. Although beautifully shot, written, and acted - I quite honestly wasn't that impressed with "City Of God", I'd go so far as to say I was even bored at times. Going in with high expectations was probably a mistake, but I really didn't think this movie was anything special. That being said however, I did enjoy the film, especially the last hour - and I can certainly appreciate it for what it was trying to accomplish - so it wins back some points from me there. There were aspects I thoroughly enjoyed, and thought were quite deserving of a higher ratings, while at other times, I found myself disconnected and uninterested with the plot... I thought it was GOOD.

texto: City of God is executed with such technical skill that it almost feels like exhibitionism on the filmmakers’ part. We get split-screens, we get sharply edited montages, we get scenes shown twice from different perspectives, and we get some long, magnificent tracking shots, often through crowds, that must have been almost impossible to pull off. It’s really slick. But what is it? Is it a brutal gangster flick, or a social drama about degradation that carries genuine anthropological weight? The easy answer would be to say it’s both, and the vast swathes of critics and fans who think the movie’s terrific would be sure to express such a sentiment. I’m not so sure. Especially in its second hour, I felt the movie leaned more heavily toward the first description than the second, as its plot became denser and its level of sensationalist violence intensified. Thematically, and often in execution, too, it’s very similar to the TV show The Wire, and I can’t be the first to point that out, though contemporary critics would not have had the luxury of such a comparison. Inevitably, it is not able to say as much in two hours as The Wire was able to say over five seasons and fifty episodes. But, for one thing, The Wire breathed human life into its antagonists, and showed us that their actions are not always motivated by greed or viciousness. This cannot be said for City of God’s principal villain Lil Ze, who laughingly dispatches crying children on-camera and for whom passing jealousy is a perfectly good motive to rape a stranger while making her boyfriend watch. Sympathetic characters- Benny, for example, or Rocket, are conveniently never shown engaging in violent acts at all; we are left in no doubt which characters we are supposed to like and which characters we aren’t. Subsequently, it lacks The Wire’s more complex, incisive dynamics. On a cinema screen in 2002, when here in the UK I was still technically not old enough to watch it, it might have been pretty wild. Oldboy too. But though I did prefer it to Oldboy, ultimately I felt that, with its swathes of characters, its whip-smart edits, its proliferating abundance of death and carnage, the film was using sensory overload in an attempt to steamroller me into exhilaration. As it is, on a small screen 20 years later, I don’t feel the film had the kind of power that it appeared to be striving for. It’s not a bad film- far from it. It’s actually a very good one if the material happens to resonate with you. But what does it have to tell us, really, other than that the slums of Rio are terrible beyond belief, where the police have no power, and where the most amoral of a given generation tend to be the ones that rise up through the ranks and end up essentially running the place? I don’t know, really. That does seem to be the main heft of the piece. And there’s a titillating aspect to City of God that sits uncomfortably with its apparent status as a social document, a ‘message from the front line’. For more of my reviews, why not visit www.wilfullyobtuse.com.

texto: Film #26: Around the World in 30 Days (May 2014 Challenge) Country : Brazil Violence is one big, long, grueling, and—most importantly—circular chain of events. Once you pull a trigger, the bullet eventually ricochets back to you, and unless you never shoot a gun at all, there’ll be no escaping the destruction that violence leaves in its wake. Welcome, my friends, to the world of City of God , a pulsating crime drama that chronicles the rise of organized crime in the titular Brazilian favela since its inception in 1960. Told from the perspective of a young man named Rocket, we see the unrelenting cycle of gangs, guns, drugs, vendettas, victories, defeats, corpses, cops, and cash repeat itself time after time; the scenarios play out differently, but the core elements all remain the same. While there is some mild humor mixed in at times, for the most part Fernando Meirelles keeps things dark and grim, and by the end of it all the body count is so high that it would be pointless to keep track of or tally. Let’s just say that this is A Very Serious Movie, and if you’re not prepared for the level of violence it serves up, you might as well look elsewhere. What’s especially notable about the film is its emphasis on its characters, most of whom are greatly fleshed out with the help of backstories and exposition. I liked this attention to the characters because it really drove the motif of circularity home, as well as gave the amateur actors a real chance to shine as individuals. The cast list is fairly large, but that never becomes an issue due to how to the narrative weaves the disparate character threads together to form an intricately-composed whole. And without this character-driven approach, there’s no way someone like Lil Zé would have been nearly as compelling (and I think it’s pretty much agreed upon that Zé is one hell of a villain). While some films are sorely lacking in believable characters, City of God is teeming with them… and, for me, that may be its saving grace. For, you see, I did not especially enjoy City of God . I won’t deny that it’s an accomplished and no-holds-barred take on the tragic realities of slum life, but I have to admit all the same that I struggled to get through it. I wasn’t big on Meirelles’ shaky camerawork for one, and the use of voiceover for both narration and exposition was a tiresome device after a while. I’m also still trying to work out what I gleaned from the film at the end of the day; aside from its cyclical (not to mention cynical) treatment of violence and retribution, it was all so morbid that not thinking about it too much seems like the best course of action. I know Rocket’s arc ends on a hopeful note, but everything else in the film is so plagued with dire consequences and ill-fated decisions that it never registers as powerfully as it should. Sure, the film is entertaining to a point (anything that gets your adrenaline rushing is), and it’s put together with great skill and flourish, but I’m having trouble seeing why it’s so acclaimed. Am I not its intended audience, or is there something I’m missing? Maybe I’ll just wait for the day when I run into someone who worships this film and they can make their case for it. I don’t think I ever want to sit through it again, but I’m always open to hearing a well-crafted argument. Until then, I’m going to have to side-eye City of God ’s high placement on IMDb’s Top 250 list and wonder what all the fuss is about.

texto: The characters in City of God make the film deeply engaging. Rocket seeks a better life through photography, while Li’l Zé’s ruthless rise to power reflects the effects of violence. Benny adds warmth with his dream of peace, and Knockout Ned’s descent into revenge shows how violence traps people in a cycle. Together, they create a powerful and emotional story about survival and choice.

texto: City of God is executed with such technical skill that it almost feels like exhibitionism on the filmmakers’ part. We get split-screens, we get sharply edited montages, we get scenes shown twice from different perspectives, and we get some long, magnificent tracking shots, often through crowds, that must have been almost impossible to pull off. It’s really slick. But what is it? Is it a brutal gangster flick, or a social drama about degradation that carries genuine anthropological weight? The easy answer would be to say it’s both, and the vast swathes of critics and fans who think the movie’s terrific would be sure to express such a sentiment. I’m not so sure. Especially in its second hour, I felt the movie leaned more heavily toward the first description than the second, as its plot became denser and its level of sensationalist violence intensified. Thematically, and often in execution, too, it’s very similar to the TV show The Wire, and I can’t be the first to point that out, though contemporary critics would not have had the luxury of such a comparison. Inevitably, it is not able to say as much in two hours as The Wire was able to say over five seasons and fifty episodes. But, for one thing, The Wire breathed human life into its antagonists, and showed us that their actions are not always motivated by greed or viciousness. This cannot be said for City of God’s principal villain Lil Ze, who laughingly dispatches crying children on-camera and for whom passing jealousy is a perfectly good motive to rape a stranger while making her boyfriend watch. Sympathetic characters- Benny, for example, or Rocket, are conveniently never shown engaging in violent acts at all; we are left in no doubt which characters we are supposed to like and which characters we aren’t. Subsequently, it lacks The Wire’s more complex, incisive dynamics. On a cinema screen in 2002, when here in the UK I was still technically not old enough to watch it, it might have been pretty wild. Oldboy too. But though I did prefer it to Oldboy, ultimately I felt that, with its swathes of characters, its whip-smart edits, its proliferating abundance of death and carnage, the film was using sensory overload in an attempt to steamroller me into exhilaration. As it is, on a small screen 20 years later, I don’t feel the film had the kind of power that it appeared to be striving for. It’s not a bad film- far from it. It’s actually a very good one if the material happens to resonate with you. But what does it have to tell us, really, other than that the slums of Rio are terrible beyond belief, where the police have no power, and where the most amoral of a given generation tend to be the ones that rise up through the ranks and end up essentially running the place? I don’t know, really. That does seem to be the main heft of the piece. And there’s a titillating aspect to City of God that sits uncomfortably with its apparent status as a social document, a ‘message from the front line’. For more of my reviews, why not visit www.wilfullyobtuse.com.

texto: From its very first scenes, in which our young photographer-protagonist finds himself trapped in the midst of a Mexican (ok, Brazilian) standoff between a street gang and the corrupt cops, City of God makes no bones about its debts to Scorsese and Tarantino. In fact, for much of the film, I was reminded of Guy Ritchie’s Lock, Stock, and Two Smoking Barrels, which brought to London much of the same snappy, experimental camerawork, “funny” gunplay, and street gangster-chic that’s on display here in Rio. But that metaphor only goes so far — this increasingly dark film ultimately feels very different than the breezy Lock Stock. In fact, while Scorsese, Tarantino, and Ritchie gangsters all generally find themselves on the wrong side of the law as a calling, the Brazilian youths here are born into it — crime, violence, and murder are an inescapable part of the Cidade de Deus. Or is it? I know this movie is based on a novel based on real events, but at a certain point, right after the strobelight-marked murder of one of the film’s most likable characters, City of God just gets lost in its own cycle of violence. When L’il Ze, the cruelest hoodlum we meet on our travels, brutally rapes the girlfriend of Knockout Ned (we never see her again — she’s a plot point, not a character), a gang war ensues that drastically escalates the already considerable levels of death and carnage the audience has to deal with. In this final third, the film derails…it’s just too much. (Ken Turan aptly summed it up as “overkill.”) One goes from avidly following the travails of individual characters to watching most or all of them go down in a hail of gunfire. Like I said, I know that much of this tale is based on a real gang war, and that the ridiculously high body count at the end of the film may have a solid grounding in fact. But at times City of God wants to have it both ways. When innocent bystanders are mowed down or child gangsters are forced to make extremely grisly life-and-death choices, we’re shocked sullen by the events depicted here. But when L’il Ze blows away his stooge Tuba in a fit of frustration, it’s a sight gag. In sum, with swooping camerawork, great performances across the board, and a well-crafted narrative, City of God bridges the gap between Tarantino-cool gangsterism and shocking acts of violence reasonably well for its first two-thirds. Alas, it falters in the final act, and I found myself spending the last thirty-five minutes of a movie I’d quite enjoyed up til then keeping my head down and waiting for the last reports of gunfire to die away. Well worth seeing if you’re a fan of the hyperkinetic gangster genre, but ultimately City of God just can’t quite close the deal. texto: Not quite for me. This Brazilian film, firmly entrenched in the coveted top-25 highest rated films on IMDB, is the true-story about two boys growing up in the violent "City Of God" neighborhood outside of Rio De Janiero in Brazil - one becomes a photographer, the other a murderous drug-dealer. The 130-minute story feels like a Portuguese version of Scorsese's "Goodefllas" - except with delusional and hopeless children, rather than Ray Liotta and Robert DeNiro. Perhaps it was because of the subtitles, or because all the children looked so similar, or perhaps it was the non-linear and sporadic narrative, but I found myself struggling to follow the complicated plot and character paths for most of the first half of this film. When things finally settled in, and after most of the supporting cast had been killed off - I was pleasantly surprised by "City Of God" - which finally started to come into its own, rather than a string of familiar scenes of people getting murdered. The immensely large cast of local amateurs all did a terrific job, but none of them really stood-out, and I found it difficult to really connect to any of the main characters. I will say this though: the cinematography and editing in this film were absolutely outstanding - keeping things moving at a blistering pace, all while maintaining a very stylized, almost music-video look to some of the shots. The dirty slums of Rio are portrayed with gritty and striking realism that really immerses you in the sounds and sights of this hellish neighborhood. And although this film, and all of its characters are closely based on a true-story, I couldn't help but feel like it was poor-man's version of much better gangster films that had come before. Although beautifully shot, written, and acted - I quite honestly wasn't that impressed with "City Of God", I'd go so far as to say I was even bored at times. Going in with high expectations was probably a mistake, but I really didn't think this movie was anything special. That being said however, I did enjoy the film, especially the last hour - and I can certainly appreciate it for what it was trying to accomplish - so it wins back some points from me there. There were aspects I thoroughly enjoyed, and thought were quite deserving of a higher ratings, while at other times, I found myself disconnected and uninterested with the plot... I thought it was GOOD.

texto: Proof that the cameraman really never dies… LMAO On a real note, this is an absolute masterpiece. From the cinematography to the acting to the pacing, it is as close to perfection as a film can get. I spent a good 45 minutes after finishing it trying to come up with a single complaint, and not one thing came to mind. From the opening sequence with its incredible 360° transition and beautifully composed still shots to the emotionally devastating ending framed from behind, City of God is one of the best movies I’ve ever seen and, dare I say, the most creatively executed. There are so many things to love about this movie, but after doing my due diligence and learning that roughly 70% of the cast consisted of local children with little or no acting experience, I appreciated it even more. It makes the performances feel that much more authentic. It’s hard to write a review when there are so many aspects deserving of praise, but one thing I have to highlight is how interconnected the story is. There are at least 25 meaningful characters, yet somehow every single one leaves an impression. It doesn’t matter how much screen time they have—their presence is remembered and their role in the story feels important. I’d compare it to The Godfather , another film with an enormous cast, but I actually think City of God handles its ensemble even better. Every storyline feels purposeful, and none of the characters get lost in the chaos. I could easily write four more paragraphs about this film, but to keep it short, if you asked me to describe it in one sentence, I’d simply say it’s as close to a perfect film as I’ve ever seen. “Wanna get shot in the hand or the foot?” 9.9/10

texto: What an amazing watch. This movie perfectly enthralls and immerses you into the setting and time period of 1970s Rio slums. This movie is ambitious as fuck; so many characters and different plot lines being passed back and forth. Lots of moving parts here. It executes it all PERFECTLY. The ensemble cast is flawless with each character leaving an impact and the vibes are HIGH the entire time. Brutal gang violence never seemed so fun! The story sucks you in with characters you love and root for and characters you want to get turned into swiss cheese, stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you wanna look away, but it’s also just lowkey a vibe. It feels like this could be a great movie to hangout to, and because so much is going on at once it could be amazing on a rewatch. This movie literally has it all I can’t recommend it enough. I kept saying it felt like the Brazilian Goodfellas. A stylish crime epic with timeless performances, characters, vibes, and one hell of a score. 5 stars check it out 🇧🇷

O filme é ARTE pura!! As atuações são surreais. Podem até não ter ganhado o Oscar, e sabemos o porquê, mas, no fundo, sabemos que ganhamos. É o tipo de filme que te ensina.

texto: What an amazing watch. This movie perfectly enthralls and immerses you into the setting and time period of 1970s Rio slums. This movie is ambitious as fuck; so many characters and different plot lines being passed back and forth. Lots of moving parts here. It executes it all PERFECTLY. The ensemble cast is flawless with each character leaving an impact and the vibes are HIGH the entire time. Brutal gang violence never seemed so fun! The story sucks you in with characters you love and root for and characters you want to get turned into swiss cheese, stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you wanna look away, but it’s also just lowkey a vibe. It feels like this could be a great movie to hangout to, and because so much is going on at once it could be amazing on a rewatch. This movie literally has it all I can’t recommend it enough. I kept saying it felt like the Brazilian Goodfellas. A stylish crime epic with timeless performances, characters, vibes, and one hell of a score. 5 stars check it out 🇧🇷

texto: C’est définitivement un MOAT ( movie of all time ). J’avais des grandes attentes  envers ce film et il a livré la marchandise sur absolument tout les niveaux. C’était vraiment une belle expérience cinématographique, c’est un film si cru et vrai qui parle de la violence perpétuelle, mais qui trouve quand même le moyen de le faire de façon si belle et artistique. Les personnages sont intéressants les dialogues donne la sensation d’être présent dans une scène de la vrai vie et c’est ce qui fait tout le charme du film. Plusieurs plans magnifiques et une cinématographie incroyable accompagné d’une bande sonore qui agit comme une colle entre les éléments de cette fresque. J’ai adoré la façon dont l’histoire est racontée à travers les différentes perspectives et l’utilisation de la narration tout au long du film est vraiment unique et j’ai adoré. Absolute cinéma / 10

texto: Cujo es una crítica a nuestra sociedad actual. El perro constantemente queda en segundo plano para que nos enfoquemos en las dinámicas familiares que se nos muestran en la película, como lo son las familias de Vic y Joe. Por un lado tenemos la infidelidad de Donna y por el otro el maltrato que Joe ejerce sobre Charity. Con esto claro, puedo ver que la película no quiere enseñarnos la historia de un perro asesino infestado de rabia; quiere mostrarnos cómo este tipo de dinámicas tóxicas afectan a los miembros más vulnerables de la familia; como a los hijos, por ejemplo. Ahora, sinceramente esto me lo saqué del fundillo. Yo sí quería ver una película de un perro asesino infestado de rabia, joder, si quisiera ver una película de drama familiar, pues simplemente miraría una de drama familiar, pero este no es el caso. Joder, yo quería mi película de terror, carajo, odio como dejaron al puto perro en segundo plano solo para enfocarse en las misms problemáticas familiares que mencioné solo para burlarme. La próxima vez, si haces una película que a penas trata sobre un perro asesino, no pongas su nombre como título; algunos nos podemos llevar una gran decepción.

texto: Stephen King’s literary works have birthed some of the most iconic horror masterpieces in cinema history. However, the 1983 film adaptation of Cujo represents a staggering failure in narrative execution, stands as a masterclass in bad screenplaying, and serves as an ultimate waste of audience time. What promises to be a tense, claustrophobic thriller quickly devolves into an exercise in narrative stupidity, structural overkill, and profound boredom. The primary catalyst for the film's failure is the sheer stupidity woven into the fabric of the screenplay. For a horror film to maintain tension, the characters must make choices that feel organic, even if desperate. In Cujo, the characters are driven entirely by contrived ignorance designed solely to force the plot forward. The screenplay relies on a series of absurdly convenient oversights: a breaking car that happens to fail at the worst possible location, characters who refuse to communicate basic information to one another, and a complete lack of survival instincts. Because the script fails to establish intelligent stakes, the audience is left rooting against the human protagonists rather than fearing the antagonist. This structural ineptitude leads directly into the film's most egregious flaw: the central conflict gets boring after exactly five minutes. The novelty of a rabid St. Bernard trapping a mother and child inside a sweltering Ford Pinto wears off almost immediately. Once the physical parameters of the siege are established, the film completely runs out of ideas. The audience is subjected to endless, repetitive cycles of the dog barking at the window, the characters screaming, and the dog retreating, only to repeat the sequence moments later. Stripped of psychological depth or escalating tension, the film ceases to be scary and becomes aggressively monotonous. Compounding this boredom is the screenplay's reliance on overkill. Lacking the nuance required to sustain a feature-length film in a single location, the filmmakers substitute genuine terror with relentless, loud overstimulation. The editing becomes frantic, the score shrieks at every minor movement, and the dog is subjected to an absurd amount of cosmetic gore that feels cartoonish rather than frightening. By dialing every sensory element up to eleven without any narrative progression, the film numbs the audience. The overkill exposes the fundamental emptiness of the script; it is a short story stretched violently beyond its breaking point. Cujo is a monumental waste of time. It takes a terrifying, subtext-rich novel about family fractures and domestic terror and flattens it into a dull, repetitive creature feature. The screenplay lacks the wit to engage the mind, the pacing to hold the attention, or the restraint to build actual dread. Instead of delivering a tight, memorable thriller, Cujo leaves its audience trapped in a stagnant vehicle of poor filmmaking, praying for the credits to roll.

texto: Wenn die Langeweile zur Last wird. Um das direkt zu Beginn klar zu stellen: Ich bin kein großer Fan der Buchvorlage von Stephen King, aber dennoch habe ich versucht dem Film eine faire Chance zu geben. Allerdings ist dieser Film so hochgradig langweilig, dass mir das irgendwann einfach nicht mehr möglich war. Denn die Geschichte zieht sich und zieht sich und es hört nicht auf. Sekunden werden zu Minuten, Minuten zu Stunden. Und dann sitzt da dieser Hund vor dem kaputten Auto, in welchem eine Mutter mit ihrem Kleinkind sitzt und es passiert nichts. Selbst wenn der Hund angreift ist das kaum spannend genug, um die Minuten davor und danach noch zu retten. Ich saß knappe 90 Minuten da und habe mir eine Film angesehen, der sich wie 180 anfühlt und versucht, den Zuschauer durch die Langeweile zu erdrücken. Die Handlung fand ich im Buch schon nicht allzu spannend. Vor allem aber auch, da ein Gefühl aufgebaut wird, welches mir nicht gefällt. Dieser Zeitdruck, der geschaffen wird, da die beiden Festsitzenden langsam einfach nicht mehr durchhalten. Im Film war das auch der Fall, aber es war mir ab einem gewissen Punkt einfach egal. Ich wusste was passieren würde, auch wenn der Film in einem Fall den Schwanz einzieht, und dann war es eben so. Die Handlung hat mich einfach kalt gelassen. Den Punkt, den ich "Cujo" aber geben muss, ist der Look und die Inszenierung. Denn der Look hat mich immer wieder an Horrorfilme aus den 70ern erinnert, die einfach dreckig und räudig aussehen. Genau das schafft der Film auch hin und wieder, was mir ziemlich gut gefallen hat. Die Inszenierung ist ebenfalls nicht übel. Diese beiden Punkt habe ich dann doch noch neutral sehen können. Denn das muss ich einfach sagen. Der Film scheitert an der Prämisse und nicht an der technischen Umsetzung, da ich die Kamera und Inszenierung vollkommen solide fand. Insgesamt ist "Cujo" also ein Film, den ich aufgrund des Pacings ziemlich schwer zu ertragen fand. 2/5 Sternen.

texto: A below average natural horror, with some genuinely horrifying moments but is honestly weighed down by the filler scenes and slow set up in the first half. This story would’ve worked better as a short film. The slow burn elements worked to a small extent only. In the second half when the story actually kicks in, the tight camera angles and strong scripting, accompanied with the lead actress’ devastatingly desperate performance make the film engaging.

texto: "Cujo" ist weniger der Horrorfilm, den man erwartet. Das eigentliche Duell zwischen Mensch und Bestie ist eher in der zweiten Hälfte des Films und hat da schon einige Momente des Ziehens. Am seltsamsten fand ich aber, dass da ein Familiendrama vorangestellt wurde, welches eher den eigentlichen Horror ausbremst bzw. hinauszögert. Das macht das Ganze für Genre-Fans wohl eher enttäuschend und wirkte auch mich unausgegoren. texto: CUJO Kritik Review (1983): Cujo ist ein Horrorfilm, Thriller und Survival-Horror mit Mystery- und Monsterfilm-Elementen und basiert auf Stephen Kings gleichnamigem Roman. Lewis Teagues Verfilmung erzählt von dem zunächst freundlichen Bernhardiner Cujo, der nach einem Fledermausbiss an Tollwut erkrankt und zu einer tödlichen Bedrohung wird. Im Mittelpunkt stehen Donna Trenton und ihr Sohn Tad, die während einer Autopanne auf dem Grundstück der Cambers in ihrem Wagen festsitzen und von Cujo belagert werden. Die größte Stärke des Films ist seine beklemmende Atmosphäre. Cujo braucht erstaunlich wenig klassische Horroreffekte, um Spannung aufzubauen. Besonders die Hitze, die Enge des Autos und das Wissen, dass der Hund jederzeit angreifen könnte, erzeugen ein starkes Gefühl der Ausweglosigkeit. Die scheinbar alltägliche Situation entwickelt sich dadurch langsam zu einem echten Überlebenskampf. Auch Dee Wallace überzeugt als Donna. Sie vermittelt glaubwürdig die zunehmende Panik und Verzweiflung einer Mutter, die nicht nur um ihr eigenes Leben, sondern vor allem um das ihres Kindes kämpfen muss. Danny Pintauro funktioniert ebenfalls gut als Tad, dessen Angst die ohnehin angespannte Situation zusätzlich verstärkt. Besonders interessant ist, dass der Film sich zunächst viel Zeit für das Familiendrama nimmt. Die Eheprobleme zwischen Donna und Vic sowie Donnas Affäre wirken zunächst fast wie eine völlig andere Geschichte. Dadurch entsteht allerdings ein Kontrast zum späteren Horror: Die privaten Probleme werden zunehmend unwichtig, sobald Donna und Tad tatsächlich ums Überleben kämpfen müssen. Cujo selbst ist eine überraschend effektive Horrorfigur. Der Film macht aus ihm kein übernatürliches Monster, sondern einen durch Tollwut gefährlich gewordenen Hund. Gerade diese Bodenständigkeit macht die Bedrohung glaubwürdiger. Der Horror funktioniert dadurch weniger wie Fantasy und stärker wie ein realistischer Survival-Thriller. Auch die Inszenierung von Lewis Teague kann überzeugen. Die Kamera nutzt besonders das Auto als klaustrophobischen Schauplatz und macht aus einem eigentlich kleinen Raum eine zunehmend unerträgliche Falle. Die begrenzte Bewegungsfreiheit der Figuren wird dabei konsequent für die Spannung genutzt. Das größte Problem liegt für mich im langen Aufbau. Der Film braucht relativ viel Zeit, bevor Cujo tatsächlich zur zentralen Bedrohung wird. Das Familiendrama besitzt zwar seine Berechtigung, wirkt aber stellenweise etwas zu ausführlich. Wer hauptsächlich einen Tierhorrorfilm erwartet, muss entsprechend Geduld mitbringen. Auch die Nebenfiguren bleiben teilweise oberflächlich. Einige Handlungsstränge rund um die Familie Camber und Donnas Eheprobleme tragen zwar zur Ausgangssituation bei, erhalten aber nicht immer genügend Tiefe, um wirklich interessant zu werden. Die Horror-Sequenzen selbst sind dafür deutlich stärker. Sobald Donna und Tad im Auto festsitzen, entwickelt Cujo eine wesentlich intensivere Dynamik. Die wiederholten Angriffe könnten leicht eintönig wirken, doch die zunehmende körperliche Erschöpfung und die Hitze sorgen dafür, dass sich die Situation immer weiter zuspitzt. Visuell ist der Film für seine Zeit ordentlich umgesetzt. Die Aufnahmen von Cujo funktionieren vor allem deshalb gut, weil die Inszenierung nicht permanent versucht, ihn spektakulär aussehen zu lassen. Stattdessen reicht häufig schon seine Präsenz vor dem Auto aus, um Spannung zu erzeugen. Auch die vergleichsweise zurückhaltende Darstellung von Gewalt unterstützt den realistischen Ton. Das Erzähltempo ist insgesamt etwas unausgewogen. Die erste Hälfte ist deutlich ruhiger und stärker vom Familiendrama geprägt, während die zweite Hälfte wesentlich konzentrierter auf den Überlebenskampf setzt. Dadurch fühlt sich der Film fast wie zwei unterschiedliche Geschichten an, die erst später vollständig zusammenfinden. Das Finale liefert schließlich einen intensiven Überlebenskampf und funktioniert emotional vor allem durch Donnas Entschlossenheit, ihren Sohn zu retten. Die Auflösung ist wirkungsvoll, auch wenn sie gegenüber Stephen Kings Roman verändert wurde. Fazit: Cujo ist ein atmosphärischer und teilweise sehr spannender Tierhorrorfilm, der besonders durch seine realistische Bedrohung, die klaustrophobische Auto-Situation und Dee Wallaces starke Darstellung überzeugt. Der lange Aufbau, das teilweise ausgedehnte Familiendrama und einige oberflächliche Nebenfiguren verhindern für mich eine höhere Bewertung. Sobald der eigentliche Überlebenskampf beginnt, zeigt der Film jedoch deutlich, warum er zu den bekannten Stephen-King-Verfilmungen der 1980er gehört.

texto: Un thriller de terror bastante simple pero efectivo, que consigue sacar tensión de una situación cotidiana y convertirla en una experiencia claustrofóbica. La película funciona especialmente bien cuando se concentra en la relación entre Donna y su hijo, mientras el peligro permanece constantemente cerca. Dee Wallace hace un buen trabajo y logra transmitir el miedo y la desesperación de su personaje sin exagerarlos. La ambientación y el uso del auto como espacio cerrado ayudan mucho a mantener la tensión, aunque el ritmo tiene algunos altibajos y ciertas decisiones del guion se sienten bastante propias del cine de terror de la época. Tiene una premisa sencilla, pero algunos momentos están muy bien construidos.

texto: This is why I'm a cat person. My wife's been reading through King's entire library and we've been following up each with one of the film adaptations. I vaguely remember watching this as a kid, but didn't remember anything about it so I'm counting this as a first-timer. In all liklihood I turned it off because it takes forEVER to get to the good stuff. I don't give a shit about infidelity and marketing projects - just give me a bloodied up St. Bernard wreaking havoc! Eventually the shit does indeed hit the fan with Dee Wallace and her son (a very convincing & comitted child performance from Danny Pintauro) stuck in a blazing hot Ford Pinto while Cujo repeatedly attacks them. It's a real assault on the senses with constant screaming, barking, yelling, metal crunches, claw scraping, glass shattring, the phone ringing, you name it. There's a couple good jumpscares in there, too. I did prefer the book ending, though. I was also happily surprised to see my guy Jan de Bont as DOP in the opening credits (twice in the same week, too!!). It really is a good-looking film despite the narrative shortcomings. I'll be curious to see how the remake is later this year. 1983 Ranked Stephen King Adaptations Ranked

texto: This adaptation derives its horror from the systematic collapse of domestic security. Rather than presenting evil as an external or supernatural force, the film finds violence within the familiar, transforming the family dog into an agent of biological disorder. Cujo’s descent into rabies is consequently devoid of moral purpose - his violence is pathological, arbitrary and indifferent to human suffering. Dee Wallace gives a notable performance, gradually moving from domestic anxiety towards states of acute psychological and physical distress. Pintauro’s presence intensifies the film’s emphasis on vulnerability and dependence. Teague’s direction is similarly restrained, employing increasingly claustrophobic compositions and restricting movement as the narrative progresses. The automobile becomes both shelter and prison, while heat, dehydration and mechanical failure function as additional instruments of physical deterioration. The film’s fairly austere tone derives from this refusal of melodrama - as Cujo presents terror as a material condition, in which ordinary structures of safety prove temporary, unreliable and ultimately incapable of containing violence. Eureka release viewed.

tema: Fidelidade à obra de Stephen King
exemplo: Alguns comentários comparam o filme ao livro, notando que a adaptação é fiel em vários aspectos, mas perde a profundidade psicológica e o impacto do final original.
texto: When I think of Cujo, one of the first things that comes to mind is what Stephen King once said about the novel: he doesn’t remember writing it. King penned the book while struggling with alcoholism and later admitted that he had no real awareness of the process—he just knew the story came out well and became a huge success. The film adaptation, released in August 1983, didn’t fare as well with critics but was a box office hit. Cujo tells the story of a friendly Saint Bernard who becomes rabid after being bitten by a bat. Donna Trenton (Dee Wallace) has recently separated from her husband following the revelation of an affair. Her five-year-old son, Tad (Danny Pintauro), adores the dog, whose owners—young Brett Camber (Billy Jayne) and his father, a mechanic (Ed Lauter)—don’t mind the visits. One day, Donna and Tad come to see Cujo only to discover that the dog has turned into a violent killing machine and has already attacked one of his owners. When their car dies and they are trapped inside under the summer sun, Cujo’s aggression escalates, and the two must figure out a way to survive with no help in sight. I last watched this film sixteen years ago, and my opinion hasn’t changed. The story is solid, and there are genuinely suspenseful moments, but the pacing drags. The majority of the action takes place in a single location, and the ending is easy to predict. That said, the film is effective in its tension-building, with Cujo appearing suddenly to deliver moments of real terror. The script provides some character development, but the slow progression makes the experience feel longer than it really is. I also read Cujo in high school and, as often happens, the book outshines the film. The novel’s suspense and depth are far superior to the movie, though the adaptation does capture certain frightening moments and presents them in a realistic, well-executed way. Cujo himself is genuinely terrifying at times, and the film does have moments that will make your heart race. Ultimately, while the movie has its merits, it’s a slow burn that doesn’t fully live up to the tension and richness of King’s original story.

texto: In the words of Rachel Greene, “What is wrong with that dog?!?” It’s a very faithful adaptation of the book even with having to slim down on the story and scenes with the wife and son of the mechanic and some of the stuff with the Vic Trenton regarding the Sharpe account that was in the book. But all the elements are there that contribute to Donna and Tad being trapped in the car while being terrorized by Cujo who’s been infected with rabies. Absolutely insane how far they went with certain aspects of that last third to show the slow terror of being trapped in the car by an animal who wants to bite you and kill you. Same with how vicious they let Cujo be and visceral it was to see him bite Donna - same with how gross and bloody he becomes by the end of the film. Another thing I liked with the second to last confrontation between Cujo and Donna was how they used the camera to approach Donna like it was Cujo even moving like the diseased dog to get the effect. Just a good move to get the terror of the situation across without having to show the dog being hit by the baseball bat in the process. One thing I didn’t like about the film was that it chickened out on the ending of the book where Tad dies. Obviously, it’s sad and meant to break you emotionally for what both of the characters went through only to be futile in the end, but it fits with the message of the book that King wrote out in that things can happen beyond your control and that you have to learn to live with it rather than just shove it under the rug. It still could have fit in the movie given that it followed the beats of the plot of the book. Maybe in 1983 it was just too much of a downer or maybe the film didn’t have the budget to have the police and ambulance arrive to a Donna who was trying to resuscitate her son for so long after killing Cujo. I can’t say for certain, but it’s my one disappointment in the movie since it was faithful up until that point.

texto: Un Saint-Bernard amical nommé « Cujo » contracte la rage et fait régner la terreur sur une petite ville américaine. Un autre film de l’époque que l’on disait terrifiant dont j’avais finalement trouvé ennuyant. À cette réécoute, je dois avouer que j’ai trouvé Cujo quand même un peu meilleur que dans le temps. Mais, il faut dire que les deux premiers tiers sont assez lents avec une banale intrigue familiale dont on se fout éperdument des personnages. Heureusement, la dernière partie est plus intéressante alors que le chien, sous l’effet de la rage, garde captif une mère (bonne Dee Wallace, la mère dans E.T.) et son jeune garçon (énervant Danny Pintauro de la futur série Who’s The Bossv?) dans leur voiture. Le scénario du film évacue les éléments surnaturels du roman de Stephen King pour privilégier une approche plus réaliste, ce qui est une bonne chose. Même si les séquences de l’attaque de Cujo sont bien faites, il demeure que le film s’oublie rapidement.

texto: When I think of Cujo, one of the first things that comes to mind is what Stephen King once said about the novel: he doesn’t remember writing it. King penned the book while struggling with alcoholism and later admitted that he had no real awareness of the process—he just knew the story came out well and became a huge success. The film adaptation, released in August 1983, didn’t fare as well with critics but was a box office hit. Cujo tells the story of a friendly Saint Bernard who becomes rabid after being bitten by a bat. Donna Trenton (Dee Wallace) has recently separated from her husband following the revelation of an affair. Her five-year-old son, Tad (Danny Pintauro), adores the dog, whose owners—young Brett Camber (Billy Jayne) and his father, a mechanic (Ed Lauter)—don’t mind the visits. One day, Donna and Tad come to see Cujo only to discover that the dog has turned into a violent killing machine and has already attacked one of his owners. When their car dies and they are trapped inside under the summer sun, Cujo’s aggression escalates, and the two must figure out a way to survive with no help in sight. I last watched this film sixteen years ago, and my opinion hasn’t changed. The story is solid, and there are genuinely suspenseful moments, but the pacing drags. The majority of the action takes place in a single location, and the ending is easy to predict. That said, the film is effective in its tension-building, with Cujo appearing suddenly to deliver moments of real terror. The script provides some character development, but the slow progression makes the experience feel longer than it really is. I also read Cujo in high school and, as often happens, the book outshines the film. The novel’s suspense and depth are far superior to the movie, though the adaptation does capture certain frightening moments and presents them in a realistic, well-executed way. Cujo himself is genuinely terrifying at times, and the film does have moments that will make your heart race. Ultimately, while the movie has its merits, it’s a slow burn that doesn’t fully live up to the tension and richness of King’s original story.

texto: A mother and her young son find themselves ensnared in their immobilized vehicle during a heatwave, threatened by a once-gentle St. Bernard now driven insane by rabies. This taut, surprisingly character-driven adaptation of Stephen King’s novel is anchored by a powerful performance from Dee Wallace, who infuses real emotional depth into the role of a woman already grappling with domestic pressures before the horror unfolds. Danny Pintauro is equally compelling as her terrified son, providing the film with a genuine sense of vulnerability. Director Lewis Teague maintains a tight and grounded focus, prioritizing tension over spectacle. Charles Bernstein contributes an effective, unobtrusive score that subtly heightens the film’s mounting dread without calling attention to itself. The canine effects—a combination of trained animals and practical techniques—are executed with precision, and the film never loses sight of the tragedy underlying the menace. The final act is particularly strong, functioning like a pressure cooker that relies on performance and pacing rather than shock tactics. A lean, earnest thriller that transcends its “killer dog” premise due to dedicated acting and a straightforward, no-nonsense approach. It stands out as one of the more emotionally impactful King adaptations of its time.

texto: Cujo is not really a film about a rabid dog. That is merely the skin it wears. Beneath the blood, the barking, the dust and the suffocating heat is something far more disturbing: the idea that sometimes there is no monster hiding in the darkness because the darkness has already found its way into the ordinary world. Cujo begins as something innocent. A massive, affectionate St. Bernard whose greatest crime is being a dog. Then a single bite changes everything. Rabies becomes the invisible hand reaching inside an innocent creature and turning love into instinct, loyalty into violence, and familiarity into terror. And that is what makes Cujo so fucking bleak. The dog isn't evil. There is no calculated hatred behind those eyes. No supernatural intelligence. No demonic possession. Just a living thing slowly being stripped of itself until instinct is all that remains. In a strange way, Cujo becomes a metaphor for what happens when something innocent is infected by something it never asked for. But the film doesn't stop there. Donna's crumbling marriage, Tad's childhood terror, Vic's absence, the neglected house, the oppressive summer heat everything feels like it is quietly decaying long before Cujo arrives. The dog is almost the physical manifestation of everything that has already gone wrong. And then comes the car. That fucking car becomes a coffin. Trapped inside it with her son, Donna is no longer fighting some cinematic creature that can conveniently be defeated. She's fighting exhaustion, dehydration, heat, panic and the terrifying knowledge that the thing outside only needs one mistake. The car becomes a tiny island of civilisation surrounded by something primitive. Inside: mother and child. Outside: hunger. And between them is nothing but glass. What makes the film particularly cruel is how little control its characters actually possess. There is no heroic cavalry riding over the horizon. No clever escape. No reassuring sense that the universe gives a shit whether these people survive. The world simply keeps moving. That is perhaps the darkest thing about Cujo. The horror isn't that evil exists. It's that sometimes suffering doesn't require evil at all. Sometimes tragedy is just biology, circumstance, bad timing and a series of tiny failures colliding at exactly the wrong moment. Cujo himself becomes almost tragic in the process. Somewhere beneath the blood and madness is the same dog who once wagged his tail and greeted people with affection. The creature attacking Donna is simultaneously the victim and the threat. And that makes him far more disturbing than a conventional monster. Because you can't hate him completely. You can only fear what he has become. The film's atmosphere feels like a fever dream dry, suffocating and increasingly claustrophobic. The heat isn't merely background scenery; it feels like another predator. Everything is baked, exhausted and dying. Even the silence seems to sweat. And Tad's fear gives the film another layer entirely. To a child, the world is already enormous and incomprehensible. A dark closet can become an abyss. A nightmare can become reality. Now imagine being trapped inside a car while something enormous and violent circles outside. The film understands something deeply uncomfortable about childhood: Children don't need to understand death to be terrified of it. They only need to understand that Mum might not be able to protect them. That is where Cujo sinks its teeth into something deeper than animal horror. It's about helplessness. About watching something you love deteriorate and being powerless to stop it. About the thin line separating civilisation from instinct. About how quickly the familiar can become alien. And ultimately, about survival. There is no grand philosophical explanation waiting at the end. No cosmic meaning behind what happens. Just people desperately trying to stay alive while the world closes around them. Cujo isn't frightening because he's a monster. He's frightening because he was never supposed to be one. He was someone's beloved dog. And perhaps that's the cruelest metaphor of all: Sometimes the thing that destroys you isn't born evil. Sometimes it is simply something innocent that has been infected, broken, starved, neglected or pushed beyond the point where it can recognise itself. Cujo leaves you with that uncomfortable thought long after the barking stops. The monster isn't always hiding under the bed. Sometimes it used to sleep beside you.

texto: Mesmo achando a trama familiar competente, é bem questionável a simploriedade na abordagem sobre infidelidade no casamento e a visão que a obra tem sobre a mulher dentro do núcleo familiar. Pelo que sei, isso vem desde o livro do King e, aqui, mesmo nos anos 80, já merecia uma adaptação. Por outro lado, o filme brilha mesmo quando parte para o terror e explorando duas vertentes: o terror de monstro e o de sobrevivência. O cachorro Cujo, apesar de não parecer por se tratar de uma raça costumeiramente dócil, é um dos melhores monstros criados por King e adaptado para o cinema.

texto: Einen verrückt gewordenen Hund, ein Auto, eine Mutter und ihr Kind. Mehr braucht man eigentlich gar nicht, um atemlose Spannung zu erzeugen. CUJO funktioniert auch heutzutage noch bestens, da die Angst vor einem wild gewordenen Tier auch heute noch greifbar ist. Bis auf ein zwei kleinere Ausnahmen wurde für den Film auf echte Hunde zurückgegriffen. Cujo sieht mit seinem Make-up wirklich furchterregend ausnehmen überzeugt darüber hinaus durch seine Masse. Die große Stärke von CUJO liegt in seiner Belagerungssituation, die die komplette zweite Filmhälfte einnimmt und die umso mehr wirkt, weil Cujo eigentlich als gutmütiger Bernhardiner eingeführt wird, der keiner Fliege etwas zuleide tut. Dee Wallace und Danny Pintauro machen ihre Sache sehr gut und bringen die Angstund Verzweiflung, die sie empfinden richtig gut rüber. Eindeutig einer der besten King-Verfilmungen und besten Tierhorrorfilme.

texto: É impressionante que, na época em que escreveu e lançou o livro homônimo, em 1981, Stephen King passava pelo pior momento de sua vida, quando estava viciado em álcool e cocaína. Por causa disso, o autor não se lembrava de ter escrito Cujo. Em sua autobiografia, ele revelou sentir um profundo sentimento de tristeza por não se lembrar de ter trabalhado em uma história da qual gostava muito. A inspiração para criar Cujo veio da vida real. Em 1977, a Harley-Davidson de King quebrou em uma estrada de terra no Maine. Ele levou a motocicleta até o mecânico local, que ficava em uma área isolada. Ao chegar lá, King se surpreendeu ao ver o que considerou o maior cão da raça São Bernardo que já vira na vida. Além de rosnar de maneira agressiva para King, o animal ainda tentou avançar sobre ele. Felizmente, o mecânico apareceu e acalmou o animal, que viria a ser a principal fonte de inspiração para a obra Cujo. A adaptação cinematográfica foi lançada em 1983. Dee Wallace interpreta Donna Trenton, a mãe; Danny Pintauro, Tad Trenton, o filho de cinco anos; e Daniel Hugh Kelly, Vic Trenton, o pai. O maior destaque é a performance visceral de Denise Crosby ao lado do pequeno Danny Pintauro. Destaco também o excelente trabalho com os cães utilizados para interpretar Cujo, o personagem responsável por todo o terror da história, publicada originalmente em 1981. Em "Cujo", o espectador acompanha uma história de drama sobre traição, até que o terror e o suspense tomam conta da trama. O espectador fica apreensivo e imerso no desfecho daquela mãe desesperada, que luta pela própria sobrevivência e, principalmente, pela do filho. A sensação de desespero aumenta com cada aparição do enorme cão raivoso, nojento e implacável, que continua a atacar mesmo em estado de putrefação, devido à raiva transmitida pela mordida de um morcego. Assim, o espectador experimenta um pouco do desespero da mãe e do filho diante de um cenário caótico e isolado, no qual o interior do carro é a única proteção disponível. Acredito que, devido aos seus vícios na época em que escreveu o romance de terror Cujo, King tornou a história mais sombria ao dar um final trágico para a vida do pequeno Tad Trenton. Para "consertar" esse desfecho cruel, o estúdio optou por manter o menino vivo, considerando a morte da criança uma cena muito pesada. Essa mudança foi aprovada pelo próprio King, que admitiu se arrepender de ter matado a criança na história original. Se você está procurando um filme de terror repleto de suspense, que o prenda do início ao fim, o diretor Lewis Teague oferece exatamente isso em uma adaptação cinematográfica que merece ser vista — e até mesmo revisitada. texto: Un thriller psicológico que avanza con mucha calma, pero utiliza ese ritmo para construir una sensación constante de inquietud. Más que resolver un misterio, parece interesado en explorar la fragilidad de la mente humana y lo fácil que una persona puede derribar las inhibiciones de otras cuando encuentra las grietas adecuadas. La violencia no surge de la nada, sino de impulsos que ya estaban ahí, esperando ser liberados. Su final ambiguo me pareció uno de sus mayores aciertos. La idea de que la manipulación y la violencia puedan reproducirse como un ciclo, más que como un hecho aislado, resulta inquietante y deja preguntas abiertas en lugar de respuestas cómodas. En conjunto, me pareció una propuesta muy interesante y bien construida. Su mayor virtud también puede ser su mayor defecto: confía tanto en la ambigüedad que, por momentos, deja demasiado a la interpretación. Para algunos eso será parte de su encanto; para otros, una fuente de frustración.

texto: Though this may controversial, I did not enjoy this film at all. I feel like there’s something i’m missing. I can appreciate its approach in blocking, lighting, and general impact on J-Horror, but it felt like Kurosawa maybe relied too much on abstract storytelling to fully convey his message. Ambiguous endings can be used in very creative ways, but it almost felt like Cure left way too many questions unanswered (to the point where it was hard to interpret every single one). All the intentional “open ended” questions throughout this film almost left a bad impression- and it kind of ruined what could have been an incredibly unique form of storytelling.

La idea de que la manipulación y la violencia puedan reproducirse como un ciclo, más que como un hecho aislado, resulta inquietante y deja preguntas abiertas en lugar de respuestas cómodas. En conjunto, me pareció una propuesta muy interesante y bien construida. Su mayor virtud también puede ser su mayor defecto: confía tanto en la ambigüedad que, por momentos, deja demasiado a la interpretación. Para algunos eso será parte de su encanto; para otros, una fuente de frustración.
