texto: Esse filme foi a segunda decepção do ano, logo depois de "La chimera" e realmente acho, que o grande problema para eu não ter gostado foi, novamente, ter criado muita expectativa. A ideia do filme é genial e as atuações em um geral são muito boas, principalmente do ator que faz o Mamiya, porém a construção dessa ideia e o decorrer da história simplesmente não me agradaram. Tudo é muito monótono, quieto e calmo, quase toda parte do filme. Além disso, é necessário ficar batendo cabeça do início ao fim do filme para entender coisas simples e básicas, que o diretor deixa solto ou apenas disponibiliza migalhas, para que possamos pensar e ligar os pontos, mas certas coisas passam do limite do normal e quando chega ao final do filme você não entendeu grande parte do filme. Não digo que não entendi, mas sim que é um longo caminho até chegar a mensagem que o diretor realmente quer passar. Acredito que o Kurosawa tentou fazer algo tão mirabolante, genial e místico, mas que no final se perdeu um pouco, na minha concepção. Ele quis trazer muitos detalhes e certas coisas que ficam em aberto, ou pistas pequenas, que são de extrema importância para a compreensão de determinados pontos, mas que no final fica difícil ligar tantas informações e tantas pistas para formular uma linha de pensamento. Penso que, talvez, se eu ver esse filme futuramente, posso mudar de ideia, até porque, como falei, a ideia do filme é promissora e bem interessante, mas para mim neste momento, foi mal direcionada e confusa.

A desire - a shameful, unrelenting dark corner of your mind and one you've gotten very good at ignoring, pent up and curled together in an ugly mess that is released through the unassuming, tempting and mesmerising questions of a supposed amnesiac poking and tinkering away at a detectives psyche. Cure starts off surprisingly similar to other words in the genre like memories of murder, but goes in a pretty different mind bending direction. I don't think I've pieced together the entire film just yet but its still an interesting experience.

texto: Cure di Kiyoshi Kurosawa non ha bisogno di alzare la voce per devastare chi guarda: si muove sottotraccia, facendosi largo con un'umiltà apparente che rende la resa finale ancora più sorprendente. Kurosawa lavora di pura sottrazione, appoggiandosi a un montaggio privo di sbavature e a interpretazioni di agghiacciante naturalezza per incollare lo spettatore allo schermo e mutarne radicalmente la prospettiva. Il vero orrore non risiede nell'ostentazione della violenza, ma nello spazio vuoto, in un gioco di luci e ombre gestito con l'autorità dei maestri. È un'opera che scava dritta nelle pulsioni più inconfessabili del nostro inconscio, lasciando un'impronta indelebile nell'immaginario di chiunque si esponga al suo sguardo. Un thriller psicologico ipnotico e viscerale, sconsigliato nelle ore notturne: la certezza che possa insinuarsi nella mente e non lasciarla più è fin troppo reale.

texto: This is filmslop: a terrible movie masked by good production and the illusion of progressivism. Like One Battle After Another (OBAA), this movie takes a very surface-level approach to addressing progressive issues. It uses imagery inspired by the events that took place in District Six, when 60,000 Black South Africans were forcibly removed from their homes and relocated by the Apartheid Government. Furthermore, this movie depicts police brutality, medical torture, xenophobia, segregation, corporate abuse, war profiteering, and more. However, like OBAA, its purpose is to create surface-level sympathy for the aliens and obstacles for our MC, instead of interrogating these issues, their effects, and using them to reflect the ills of our society. This film tries to pull a white-saviour story on us, but utterly fails because of how EVIL our MC is. MC is a horrible person from the get-go; he's a depraved, power-hungry psychopath who only sides with the aliens because he needs to, not because he wants to. He never grows in this story, staying the same miserable human he always was. As for the aliens, how we're meant to see them and how they're depicted are very different. On one hand, they display humanity, with relationships, worries, and feelings, but on the other hand, you can't help but understand the actions of our villains, as the aliens are only depicted as crazed maniacs, and any facts given to us only reinforce these views, instead of debunking them. Its depictions of Nigerians are very racist. This film plays into racist caricatures of Nigerians, viewing them as violent scammers who believe in nonsensical rituals, when this is clearly not the case. The tone is all over the place. I have no idea what I'm supposed to feel in any given moment, and I don't think this movie does either. For example, at the start, it tries to balance its very dark depictions of the beginnings of forced resettlement with humour, but fails miserably as it doesn't know when to stop being comedic or dark. There are also many plot holes apparent in this film, relating to the aliens, the authoritarian company that manages District 9 and more. This adds more layers of confusion to an already confusing mess of a film. In conclusion, this film is SO BAD.

texto: I distinctly remember seeing District 9 in theaters in 2009 and disliking it. Given the overwhelming praise it received, I always wondered whether I had missed something? After finally revisiting it all these years later, I’m convinced that my initial reaction was correct: District 9 isn’t good. The film fails for me in two main areas: story and style. Narratively, it presents itself as an intelligent, original piece of high-concept science fiction, but it’s really anything but. The apartheid allegory is immediately obvious and handled with very little subtlety. Beyond that, the plot becomes repetitive and never develops into anything especially compelling. Wikus is also a weak and passive protagonist, which makes it difficult to invest in his transformation or care about what happens to him. Stylistically, the film combines documentary and found-footage techniques, but neither approach is convincing. The multiple camera angles, conspicuously scripted interviews, and constant shifts in perspective prevent it from ever feeling like an authentic documentary. It also repeatedly uses the “blood on the lens technique” every time someone gets shot, which gets old incredibly quickly. With an unsubtle and unengaging narrative, ugly visuals, unconvincing presentation, and a protagonist I couldn’t root for, I’m left wondering what the film is actually offering? Ultimately, not much.

texto: There are things about the first half of District 9 that I found interesting. The mockumentary format works well, and the film’s depiction of bureaucracy, forced relocation, and casual dehumanization gives it a more interesting foundation than where the movie ultimately finishes. I really struggled with the apartheid allegory at the center of it. I understand the commentary the film is attempting to make, but drawing such an explicit parallel between the victims of South African apartheid and a population of literal aliens feels like a strange and uncomfortable comparison. I understand what the film is reaching for, but I could not get past the feeling that framing such a horrific and very real history through this particular comparison risks delegitimizing some of its horrors rather than meaningfully illuminating them. I also found Wikus difficult to invest in for much of the movie. His eventual empathy feels less like a genuine reckoning with the cruelty he has participated in and more like something forced upon him once he begins experiencing that cruelty himself. There are interesting ideas here, and I understand why the film has endured, but I was much more interested in the movie District 9 seemed to be during its first act. By the time it turns into a fairly conventional action sci-fi movie, a lot of what initially made it interesting gets lost. I kept wishing it would return to the questions it had raised instead of shooting its way through them.

texto: 16/08 – Nota: 2 O começo até achei bom, gostei da tentativa de tom humorado para tratar de temas sérios como direito à moradia, condições de extrema pobreza, controle e burocracia governamental etc. Depois achei que ficou bobo e não entregou o tom sério da história quando precisava. O ator não ajuda. Não gostei da escolha dele pro papel, ele parece ser ótimo pra The Office, mas não conseguiu entregar seriedade. A escolha de tratar a temática alienígena sob uma perspectiva deles virem residir na Terra é bem inusual e curiosa. Há de se pensar que, por ser aliens, eles seriam muito mais avançados que nós (e são), mas caíram em miséria devido a falha de sua nave e vivem aqui em favelas. O lance de ter alguns humanos comendo aliens na crença de ter os “poderes” deles é justificável, mas achei complicadíssimo justo a milícia – todos negros – ficar encarregada desse papel, reforçando uma crença torta de povos africanos serem canibais, perdendo a chance de trabalhar o tema milícia. O final é terrível de ruim. Uma ode aos héteros que amam cenas de tiro. Um filme que poderia ter 1h30 tem quase 2h por conta disso. Insuportável. Os efeitos especiais são muito bons para a época, melhores que o CGI atual. E a gravação feita “amadoramente à mão” também combina muito para a história, para termos uma ideia de proximidade e ponto de vista a partir dos protagonistas.

texto: There’s something fascinating about the movie’s strange sense of realism. Of course, the story itself is completely unrealistic, but the movie is remarkably meticulous in its pursuit of realism. The documentary-style direction is part of it, but so are all the carefully prepared details: the derogatory terms used for the aliens, the justifications put forward by the corporations, the human-rights organizations, and so on. All of these little touches make the world feel much more real. The visual quality is excellent, too. Whether it’s the sight of a gigantic UFO hovering over the city or the scenes inside the alien settlement, everything feels surprisingly natural and never out of place. That’s actually quite an achievement. And although it’s a little grotesque, I also liked the technique of having bits of flesh occasionally splatter against the camera lens. It’s a simple but very effective touch.

texto: There aren't many movies about aliens, and finding this one is rewarding because it shows extraterrestrials occupying spaces on earth in an organized and civilized way as a metaphor for our current society and how it is oppressed, poverty, abuse, repression, etc. It's a very good movie but difficult to digest; there are scenes unsuitable for sensitive people, and the aliens themselves take on a strange appearance to someone who isn't used to it. This doesn't detract from how good it is; on the contrary, it adds realism and authenticity. It's undoubtedly an excellent choice if you want to step away from the usual or everyday cinema.

texto: Sci-fi action movie filmed primarily in a mockumentary/found footage style, but it intermittently breaks from that to a traditional 3rd person narrative and even uses news broadcast blurbs at times. The format switches work very well. The unknown cast adds realism to the mockumentary style. It’s a good story, a fresh take on first contact and a brutally honest portrayal of how humanity would probably react. Heavily themed on Apartheid and racial injustice, while also taking aim at corporate greed and the global military industrial complex. A subplot has a ruthless corporate executive openly plotting against his own son in law. The irony of the main character having to lose his humanity to become humane parallels the viewer’s transformation to rooting for the aliens by the third act. Excellent cgi effects for the aliens and alien technology, and practical body horror. While the sci-fi elements and themes are prevalent, this is first and foremost an action movie. Hardly a dull moment.

texto: Still a very good film after a long time since the first watch. District 9 really performs well by being so different from most Sci-Fi films. It dives much deeper into it's themes and messaging, (Which are all the more relevant today as they were in 2009), Which makes this film come off powerful. Which I can't really say I've felt before with a Sci-Fi film. Blomkamp has very interesting ideas, Which I love! The more originality the better! And while I've heard Elysium was a good step down, And I personally remember not being the biggest fan of Chappie, At least I can appreciate that they feel like passion projects for Blomkamp. District 9 is no different. You can tell he really cared about this film, And just makes the film feel so well directed. Also I gotta mention one of my all time favorite actors Sharlto Copley! Who fuckin aces this film! He is so fuckin good! Also gotta mention the special effects which still for the most part hold up super well, And it's just so mind boggling it was filmed with such a lower budget! Overall, District 9 is a powerful and really well crafted Sci-Fi. Definitely worth a watch if you haven't seen it yet! ................................................................ texto: It’s an action alien movie with crazy weapons and a fair amount of gore, but it’s not your stereotypical action alien movie with crazy weapons and a fair amount of gore. I simultaneously love the story and am pretty pissed off by the story (complimentary). Like I’ve questioned before with movies, including my beloved Arrival , why is mankind so quick to assume the worst intent from those not like us? Why must we always seek self-gain at the expense of others? My main critique is the way in which our main character develops; it’s a fairly common trope that I saw coming from a mile away and didn’t add much substance for me. I have ideas on how I would’ve liked to have seen District 9 end, but we deal with what we’re dealt. Other than that, I love the action, I love the effects, I love the themes and social commentary, and I wish I hadn’t waited years to watch.

texto: I was honestly prepared to give this half a star. Then the Martin Luther King Jr. quotation appeared at the end and, for a moment, I thought the film had managed to redeem itself. Two stars, perhaps. Then came the Malcolm X quotation, and I was back down to one. For me, this is a confused and frustrating film, muddled in its broader argument. The performances are strong, and the actors do what they can with the material, but the dialogue often feels artificial and overly constructed. Rather than emerging organically, the story often feels as if it has been built around a thesis the film itself has not fully worked out. My issue is not with the film’s anger at racism, police brutality or the marginalisation of black communities. Those are urgent and historically entrenched issues. My issue is with the way the film frames its central conflict, particularly around Sal’s pizzeria. Yes, it is an Italian-owned business in a Black neighbourhood, and that context matters. But it is still an Italian-American pizzeria. The demand that Sal place black public figures on his Wall of Fame is presented as a question of representation… but, representation cannot simply mean overriding the cultural identity of a space because it happens to exist within a different community. Yes, in the 1980s, the lack of black representation in American public life is a serious problem. But is the wall of an immigrant-owned pizzeria really the battleground on which that struggle should be fought? The film becomes even more troubling in its final act. Radio Raheem’s death at the hands of the police is unjust and horrifying. The police are clearly responsible for that death. But the escalation that precedes it is not morally simple either. A group enters Sal’s pizzeria aggressively, tensions rise, Sal reacts poorly, violence erupts, and then the police arrive and kill a man. That killing is the central injustice. But does that automatically make Sal responsible for what the police did? Was his business the correct object of retaliation? Spike Lee has said that only white viewers tend to ask whether Mookie “did the right thing”, arguing that the real issue is the difference between property damage and the death of a black man. I understand that distinction, and it is obviously true that a human life is worth infinitely more than a shop window. But that does not, by itself, settle the moral question. Property damage and state violence are not equivalent, but nor does the horror of one automatically justify the other. The question is not whether Sal’s window matters more than Radio Raheem’s life. Of course it does not. The question is whether destroying Sal’s pizzeria was a meaningful act of resistance, an act of misdirected rage, or something more ambiguous. This is where I find the film, and Lee’s later commentary on it, frustrating. There seems to be an almost absolute certainty about what “the right thing” is, yet the film itself ends with two quotations that appear to be in philosophical mismatch with one another. If the answer is supposed to be so obvious, why close the film with both Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X? Why invite that contradiction and then treat the central moral question as if it should not be asked? I would probably have appreciated Do the Right Thing more had I known less about Spike Lee’s own interpretations of it, and less about some of the troubling accounts surrounding his behaviour on set. Taken purely as a film, it has energy, anger and some visual confidence. But as a political statement, I found it far less persuasive than its reputation suggests. The film would be stronger if it allowed more room for doubt, rather than presenting moral certainty as though it were the same thing as moral clarity. The strongest version of this film would have understood that.

texto: From the uncomfortable, unappealing, ugly jig of the film's head-scratching overlong opening to the contradictory and incoherently paired quotations by MLK and Malcolm X at the end, this is an in-your-face obnoxious mess that has no clear idea of what it wants to say but is utterly convinced of its own grand importance. The film consists almost entirely of babbling losers spending the whole day aimlessly wandering back and forth on a small stretch of road. Almost without exception these are not characters but thinly drawn racist stereotypes of purposeless black idiots who are hell-bent on getting themselves into trouble but are too stupid to know how to do even that. What is supposed to pass for acting is way-the-hell over-the-top mugging by everyone except the bland and stilted phoned-in performance of the film's wannabe auteur director/screenwriter/producer Spike Lee as well as two fine performances by two of the film's three major white actors, the always excellent John Turturro and Danny Aiello. Lee loves his grandiloquent soliloquies, which consist either of lists or of outright plagiarism (or "homage," as he would dishonestly put it). There is a short montage of several actors one by one looking directly into the camera and each insulting a particular race; the insults consist of lists of nouns and adjectives; they are predicates without propositions. There is a gratuitously long list of popular black American musicians rattled off by Sam Jackson's radio host; the sole purpose here is to provide evidence that, despite what we see depicted in the film in terms of black people's behavior, many black Americans have been very successful in music; yes, that is as much of a non sequitur as it seems. Also shoehorned into the film is identification by name of to that point (1989) every black American political activist, politician, entertainer, and athlete; it is just a product placement-like in-aggregate information dump intended to serve the same purpose as the radio host's annoying list. The plagiarism is in the form of one mostly mute knuckle dragger's beat-by-beat reiteration of Robert Mitchum's love/hate soliloquy from The Night of the Hunter; it makes no sense that this individual would be familiar, certainly to the extent of memorization, with this cultural reference. This individual's sole mission is to be as irritating as possible by blaring his loud radio at everyone to provoke a response. It is all just back-and-forth yelling until a white character smashes the radio, giving this dude his pretext for attempted murder and Lee his pretext for showing the cops killing the provocateur and the mob its pretext to engage in wanton destruction. At this point the loosely knit mob of miscreants unites in its fulfilling its collective purpose of attempting to murder whitey, burning his business to the ground, and attacking the emergency responders when they arrive. These violent black thugs trying to commit suicide by cop invoke the names of real-life violent black thugs (Michael Stewart and Eleanor Bumpurs, misspelled as "Bumpers" in the end-credits dedication) who in real life did get themselves killed by the fault of their own similar recklessness. Is this hateful, insidious wreck of a movie really positing the perspective that these arsonists and would-be murderers are, or believe themselves to be, oppressed by the genial owner of the one place where they each go multiple times per day to purchase food, namely slices of pizza? What does "fight the power" (a phrase repeated about a million times in this movie) mean if not that? At the same time are we supposed to respond sympathetically when a violent mob of "fucking niggers" (to use Spike Lee's obsessively repeated choice phrase) attempt to murder the white man and then burn the place to the ground before turning on the Korean shop owner across the street and threatening him with the same fate for no reason other than that he is not black? The race riot scene is a sadistic fantasy of a racially inverted recreation of the Howard Beach incident (the mob in the film chants "Howard Beach"), the mythical attack of a black man by a white mob outside of a pizzeria in New York a few years before this movie came out. The myopic libs of 1989 America, and worldwide, were too busy drooling all over themselves and each other in competitive heaping of praise upon this work of fiction to notice or care about the world's largest democracy movement in generations, which was ongoing by the film's May 19 Cannes showing and which was weeks past its bloody finale by the film's June 30 wide release. This film's revolution around interpersonal bickering takes on a sobering context in light of the PLA's massacre of thousands, albeit thousands of miles away. The point is not that the film should be criticized with respect to an unrelated contemporaneous political event, but rather that the inordinately high critical appraisal derives not so much from a considered assessment of the film on its merits as from a conflation of the film's social consciousness with its artistic value, this conflation based in a paucity of perspective of the extent of that consciousness. At one point the graffiti'd phrase "TAWANA TOLD THE TRUTH!" appears very prominently, to put it lightly. Is this a commentary on the credulity of those who were still clinging to their desperate gang-rape fantasy, or is it a statement of sincerity? Just before the end credits why do we have MLK telling us (namely, black Americans) to be non-violent but then Malcolm X exhorting "us" to violence? Is the senseless violence depicted in the film supposed to give its community of perpetrators a sense of accomplishment for having driven out one of the vanishingly small number of businesses operating in their ghetto neighborhood? How does it make any sense that this decent guy would be an oppressor of any sort or part of "the power" to fight? The film has no idea about any of this. Like the rioters leaning in to their true calling of vicious hooliganism, Lee has heard of the names of some high-profile black people, many accomplished, some criminal, and wants to make a movie having something vaguely to do with them, but he got too wrapped up in the aimless wandering to care in the slightest about what his original objective was or where he was going, if he was ever going anywhere at all.

If the answer is supposed to be so obvious, why close the film with both Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X? Why invite that contradiction and then treat the central moral question as if it should not be asked? I would probably have appreciated Do the Right Thing more had I known less about Spike Lee’s own interpretations of it, and less about some of the troubling accounts surrounding his behaviour on set. Taken purely as a film, it has energy, anger and some visual confidence. But as a political statement, I found it far less persuasive than its reputation suggests. The film would be stronger if it allowed more room for doubt, rather than presenting moral certainty as though it were the same thing as moral clarity. The strongest version of this film would have understood that.

texto: Reflecting on the movie Do the Right Thing, the elements that stood out and affected my experience were definitely color, community, and the conflict. Seeing how much color was involved in the film, I feel like I could feel the heat as well. In a way, I would say I felt the heat, and the movie was moving slowly because of how hot it was. I felt the element of community and conflict when the passerby accidentally scuffed up Buggin Out's shoe. Quickly, a group formed behind him, and they were yelling at him and everything. Elements like those made me feel included in a way.  The heat brings out all the tensions that have been brewing day after day. The people of the neighborhood have become irritated and confrontational. We see the neighborhood and its characters change throughout the day; we see this because, in the beginning of the film, it feels somewhat normal. Everyone is going about their business, working and having normal conversations with one another. As the day continues and the heat rises more, the atmosphere becomes more uncomfortable. People try to escape the heat, and one way we see them do this is when they unscrew the fire hydrant and have fun in the water. The afternoon is full of them becoming more hostile. We see many altercations break out in Salś. We see when Buggin' Out talks to Sal about the Wall of Fame and Radio Rahim with the boombox. By night, the whole community has changed; it has become violent and divided. Sals pizza restaurant is now destroyed and on fire, and Radio Rahim died to the cops. In my opinion, the most interesting character in the movie was Da Mayor. To me, he is such an easy character to like. Throughout the movie, he was the most ¨normal/sane¨ person throughout the film. He tries to be nice to Mother Sister and gives her flowers. He also saves the kid from getting run over by the car. Personally, I don't think that the movie ¨didnt¨ have a story; it was a story about a very hot day in the Bronx. But I do think that there was a very loose plot. We jump from person to person and dive into their life. Many of these people's stories don't really mean much for the progress of the story, but for understanding what they are like, and the day I think it works.

texto: Spike Lee wants it both ways where "these are just characters, and this is how they act" and the point is in the discussion of what audiences pick out from their interplay; but he does so while also thinking the movie has an unambiguous clear answer—as the guy who wrote it. I think that description correctly diagnoses the issue holding it back from being good as that thumb-on-the-scale aspect. In that it's said to be a character/ideas-heavy thing where fun stylized characters (more negatively caricatures) exaggerating specific aspects of real world people creates a play space of idea exploration, but it ends up not working out as anything actually explored because its got a message to tell. But then framed that way, as a movie with something to say, it essentially wastes its entire runtime not saying it (and indeed never saying it, as other reviews show people leave the movie having not heard anything at all, talking about how everyone is bad or over-focused on Sal and what he did or did not deserve). And even if it were more openly explicit, it spends no time showing, justifying, or defending the message because of the aforementioned interplay/audience discussion format it wants to be.

texto: Spike Lee's film Do the Right Thing was a very good film that combined many different themes to convey an important message. Personally, I enjoyed watching this film because it shows very unsugarcoated topics that resemble issues that are still going on in the real world. The way Spike Lee directed this movie and the choices he made truly stood out and made this film special to me. Lee chose to film the story on one specific block in New York during one of the hottest days of summer. The way he kept everything in one neighbourhood makes the movie's racial tensions feel very personal. In this movie, I noticed Spike Lee uses a lot of close-ups to show characters raw and true emotions. In some scenes in the film, Lee has the characters break the fourth wall and speak directly to the audience. This makes the audience feel their anger, makes the emotions seem up front and raw, and helps us experience the frustration some of the characters might feel during similar events. I noticed the heat in this film doesn't create every problem on the block, but it does help bring out existing anger, racism, and frustration. As the day gets hotter, these things start to get worse. I also noticed Lee adds louder music to intensify certain situations. Da Mayor definitely stood out to me because he was always very wise and cared about others even when he was judged. Throughout the film, my opinion about him stayed positive because, no matter what, he always tried to fix and solve problems in the neighborhood. He is a bit of a complicated character because he drinks, but he is still always kind, and he always regulated the chaos with his calmness throughout the film.

texto: Fight the power. And by that I mean instigate a local business for not having pictures of my ethnicity on a wall and breaking my radio when I play loud music very loudly when asked not to multiple times. Mookie being an irresponsible arsehole who saw everything that happened and decided to start a violent protest as the protagonist was an interesting decision, even going back to Sal and asking for his goddamn money. The only level headed fella here really was the mayor. All the protest did was make the Italians and Koreans fearful of the local populace, if they got their store destroyed for not having the right images up then what else could happen? The only reason violence was justified is because of the stupid police officersusing too much force. Sal was racist, but he never acted out of line and the violence just served to vindicate him in his feelings as well as his son Pino while Vito trusted the black community, he was let down. Radio Raheem himself talks about hate and love yet he doesn't exactly appear to be loving of very many people except his own. Bugging Out oh my god he's insufferable, I understand Black people aren't represented very much but an Italian pizzeria isn't exactly the place to be causing such incident. If he wants representation, build you own restaurant and support your own community. Ahmad and his crew exist to only instigate tensions further. Spraying down the car, demanding pizzas when they were closed, insulting the mayor and trying to get Bugging to fight the cyclist for making a mistake. None of these characters feel very likeable and they talk about what other ethnicities being in "their neighbourhood", is that not what racism and segregation is? You can't make this up, was this movie meant to be a propaganda piece to not anger the black populace lest they destroy your workplace? As the MLK quote puts it, violence only creates bitterness in the survivors and brutality in the destroyers. This was not a self defense use of violence. Nobody did the right thing this movie and I can't tell if that makes this a good movie or a bad one. I suppose it did make me feel something which makes it good in a sense.

texto: As someone who had never seen a Spike Lee film prior to watching this I think his unique style is super interesting as the viewer! To be occasionally put in the eyes of another character isn’t an experience audience members get very often and it was interesting to see at what points he decided to use that angle. While at times, some scenes were hard to follow, the overall plot and dynamics make for a super interesting story about the relationships and everyday life of an interracial and intercultural community. This film dives into the unity they strive for but shows us the diversion that remains due to the society they lived in in that time.

texto: I can’t remember the last time I had so much fun watching a movie for the first time. Easily an instant top 10. It’s an uptempo one, with a lot of different and colourful characters. The music is great and versatile, not only from the same genre, and it has a lot of symbolism too. Lots of colours and culture too. I love how the movie is set almost entirely on one Brooklyn block, yet it never feels visually limited. It also has to do with the camera work that’s different than usual, especially for an 80s movie, but it worked so well. I also love it when directors break the fourth wall. It’s a little bit of extra experimenting and creativity that makes a movie quickly stand out. What I like most is the ending of the movie, together with the two contradicting quotes from Martin Luther King and Malcolm X. It’s a morally ambiguous ending, my favourite kind.

texto: This is the most alive a film has ever felt. It’s so colorful and energetic. It puts you right into that Brooklyn neighborhood. Each character is so unique and distinct. texto: First time watching this and understood why some call it a classic. It’s definitely Spike Lee’s definitive film in my opinion, especially given his art style. texto: I love everything about this film. The performances, the narrative, the relevance. Spike Lee does an exceptional job of capturing the livelihood of Brooklyn, and contrasts the humour perfectly with some of the most important scenes towards the end. He does an outstanding job at establishing all these characters, introducing us viewers into their world, and even making us love some of them. You can feel the tension building as the film progresses, and it is relentless when the film hits its breaking point. There is not a single aspect of this film that I think is sub par, this is a true achievement in cinema, and to top it off, its message of spreading love rather than hate is beautiful. Always Do The Right Thing . (Notice how Radio Raheem has ‘LOVE’ on his right hand, and ‘HATE’ on his left? Do The Right Thing .)

texto: Dès l’introduction du film c’est brillant avec un montage  percutant. Le jeu entre une caméra très libre entre souplesse et saccades avec un montage qui rappelle la façon dont le mot clé d’un morceau rap tombe dans un  tempo le mettant en relief, confère à la poésie. Et en même temps on sent un film de début de carrière qui expérimente, qui est maladroit car pas encore dans une grande maîtrise. De nombreux personnages, situations qui m’ont dérouté car je n’arrivais pas à deviner la suite (plutôt bon signe quand il ne s’agit pas de faire la peinture de la bourgeoisie qui s’emmerde au pieux). On est vraiment dans les images temps qui ne dépendent pas de la narration linéaire. Le vitalisme fluide est partout mais la vague de chaleur dans laquelle l’intrigue s’insère annonce que les flux vont se heurter  à la nécropolitique raciale. Et La musique « Fight the power » <3 PS:   et Big Up pour les références et pieds de nez à West Side Story

texto: Drive My Car shares its name with a short and fun song by The Beatles , but it’s quite the opposite. Not short, nor fun. A long, quiet, slow-burn trauma bond that never fully clicked for me. Like a melodramatic play, ‘twas grade-A crapola. Critically acclaimed, subtitled snoozefest 😴 I’ll admit, I was already burnt out on slow burns, so seeing the 3-hour runtime didn’t help, but I didn’t realize how much that would be felt. I was confused by the opening; relationship dynamics felt unclear, emotional beats didn’t land cleanly, and by the time the “2 years later” card and intro credits hit (40 minutes in!), I was still trying to piece together that overlong prologue I just saw. After that, it settles into a slow moving, very talky, theatre folk drama with lots of subtlety, themes of infidelity, shared grief, and not ever truly knowing someone. It never felt impactful enough to justify the length. I struggled to stay engaged, and 3hrs of subtitles felt like work rather than immersion. Some foreign films completely absorb me to the point I forget I’m reading; this wasn’t one of them. This one made me feel very outside of everything. Not bad, just not for me. Maybe I’m missing some nuance, but from my POV it feels very overrated. Of course a movie about driving a car will have some nice sweeping shots and cinematography, but it wasn’t incredible, nothing I haven’t seen before, and that plot just wasn’t very captivating. It only finally begins to open up a bit in the last stretch, but by then it’s like… that’s it? A long road to a simple idea. This could’ve been a short film.

texto: i did not like this movie. i do not think it is a very good movie. yes, it's well-crafted, yes, i suppose it is conceptually quite rich (i can see many potential essays about the role of voice in the movie, language, acting and known/unknown selves, etc), but when i watch a movie i'm looking to *feel* something, and drive my car left me feeling nothing. there is a real mismatch between the emotional weight of the experiences the characters have and how we see the character act. obv this is not a problem in and of itself. the problem is that the film sustains this mismatch for far too long, and the characters began, at some point, to feel not hurt/traumatized/in shock but simply flat. the ending scene in the snow, which is meant as a moment of catharsis, produced no real impact on me because i was so alienated from these characters. it was like watching robots have breakdowns. the film also failed, imo, to satisfactorily develop kafuku and misaki's relationship. i really think misaki's actress was robbed of screen time. did we really need all those rehearsal scenes? it was also extremely annoying to find the manic pixie dream girl trope rearing its head in BOTH of the main female characters, who seemed to only exist to accessorize kafuku's character. (i am so damn tired of these 'dead wife' movies. solaris. paris, texas. it's misogyny dressed up in a nice color grade.) i absolutely adore evil does not exist, hamaguchi's most recent film, so i came into this expecting to love it. i still think he's a really talented filmmaker, and there are some scenes in here i loved (the hands out the skylight w/ the cigarettes immediately comes to mind), but it just completely missed the emotional chords it was trying to hit.

texto: Such a pathetic old man bro 😭 This movie really did not need to be almost 3 hours long because this really wasn’t it for me. “Ohhh but he’s supposed to be like that because the movie is about how he deals with his grief.” Yeah, I fucking know that, bro. And because he’s supposed to be like that, I’m also allowed to fucking hate his sorry ass. His character development still made me mad as hell, and the way he handles his grief is giving LOSER ENERGY throughout the entire movie. And holy shit, the scene where he literally sees his wife cheating on him and then just fucking walks away? That was the real embodiment of a loser and a stupid ass man. Bro really stood there, processed the information, and decided, “Yeah, I’m just gonna leave.” I know the whole point is that he’s emotionally repressed and doesn’t know how to confront his feelings, but watching that shit still made me want to punch the screen. But despite how much I fucking hate this type of main character, I have to admit there are so many scenes here that are genuinely beautiful. Especially all those moments when they’re driving around in the car and the camera slowly zooms out, revealing the entire area around them. There’s something so peaceful and almost hypnotic about those shots. The movie can be painfully slow, but visually, I can’t deny that it knows exactly how to create an atmosphere. And the dinner scene with his coworker and his wife who can’t speak? That shit was genuinely moving. It’s one of those scenes where barely anything needs to happen, but the emotion just fucking lands. The way they communicate without being able to communicate normally was probably one of the few moments where I completely understood why people love this movie. My friend actually told me a few years ago that this movie was probably not for me, but I thought, “Nah, I’ve watched enough movies now. I’m ready to step outside my comfort zone.” And to be fair, I’ve actually managed to do that before. I used to hate Linda Linda Linda, and now I fucking love that movie. But this one? Nah man. I can appreciate the aesthetics, the quiet atmosphere, the beautiful cinematography, and some genuinely touching scenes, but spending almost three hours with this fucking loser was still not an experience I enjoyed 😭 I genuinely wanted to laugh in this old man’s face and punch him just because I fucking could. Bro is a loser anyway.

texto: i did not like this movie. i do not think it is a very good movie. yes, it's well-crafted, yes, i suppose it is conceptually quite rich (i can see many potential essays about the role of voice in the movie, language, acting and known/unknown selves, etc), but when i watch a movie i'm looking to *feel* something, and drive my car left me feeling nothing. there is a real mismatch between the emotional weight of the experiences the characters have and how we see the character act. obv this is not a problem in and of itself. the problem is that the film sustains this mismatch for far too long, and the characters began, at some point, to feel not hurt/traumatized/in shock but simply flat. the ending scene in the snow, which is meant as a moment of catharsis, produced no real impact on me because i was so alienated from these characters. it was like watching robots have breakdowns. the film also failed, imo, to satisfactorily develop kafuku and misaki's relationship. i really think misaki's actress was robbed of screen time. did we really need all those rehearsal scenes? it was also extremely annoying to find the manic pixie dream girl trope rearing its head in BOTH of the main female characters, who seemed to only exist to accessorize kafuku's character. (i am so damn tired of these 'dead wife' movies. solaris. paris, texas. it's misogyny dressed up in a nice color grade.) i absolutely adore evil does not exist, hamaguchi's most recent film, so i came into this expecting to love it. i still think he's a really talented filmmaker, and there are some scenes in here i loved (the hands out the skylight w/ the cigarettes immediately comes to mind), but it just completely missed the emotional chords it was trying to hit.

I couldn’t take this movie seriously after i realised that Oto is just another woman written by Murakami - tragic but saved by having sex? I guess i hoped the director made up for the one dimensional and misogynistic elements of Murakami’s writing, well at least the female lead didn’t disappoint. The movie definitely had it’s moments but the 3 hour runtime didn’t justify it.

texto: I like a lot of different parts of this film. But to quickly sum up my feelings, I feel as if “The juice is not worth the squeeze” with this one.. I hate to feel that way as there’s a lot of things to like about this film, it’s just the time it takes to get there. The film has a general slow pace which I don’t mind in films, it’s the execution. There’s a lot of scene developing subtext about characters and their emotions towards one another, not a lot of dialogue and usually if it is it’s not directly saying what is true to the moment. WHICH is the point of the film, but I just never found the dialogue itself and the issues at hand to always be interesting enough to warrant this technique or development to be so prominent throughout the runtime. Then there’s portions where you are getting somewhere and….it’s….getting…there….just….keeeep……waiting……we’re…..THERE. I actually loved those moments for what it’s worth, it’s just that the pacing is already slow as molasses and the better moments in themselves is slow as well. The opening credits rolled around the 45 min mark and that just mentally did something to me, when I realized how that opening portion of the film was meant to actually start the movie. Something that I feel could have been shortened from 45 minutes to about 15-20 with effective dialogue and pacing. It’s hard to really harp on a director on pacing when most of that is intentional in this case. You can feel it’s meant to be a slow grind to the finish line for the pay off to feel that much more emotionally rewarding to see, yet I felt like the finishing beats of the film are something you can read on the characters face the entire time and a lot of the “filler” I experienced was for something I expected the whole time. There’s a few good moments throughout this run time like I said earlier, I enjoy parts. I love most scenes with the driver, this is a character that I think has good interactions with the lead to really break Yūsukes walls down. Her story really came full circle at the end which felt good, yet sometimes in certain emotional moments there’s a point where the dialogue really gets on the nose with things like “AND THIS EMOTIONAL MOMENT IN MY LIFE CAN SERVE AS A LESSON TO YOU BTW….” For a film that’s subtle throughout its entire run, it sort of blows its figurative load randomly throughout the film and seems to have a hard time finding a balance between nuance and convenient dialogue. Something I did like about the film is some of the themes in particular the overhead theme of grief and how you can grieve someone you have complicated feelings about. How hard it may be to let go of certain ideas about this person, that there isn’t going to be a reconciliation. The complexities of human relationships, how one person can never truly be understood 100% even through years and years of a relationship. There are always different sides of us as we grow and change. It’s about adapting, growing, challenging yourself and coming to grips with hard truths. The car scene between Yūsuke & Takatsuki is probably the best directed bit and best written portion of the film. It’s a payoff inside about the last hour of the film. The performances across the board are good, especially the lead, if not a little drab seeing him almost never smile and just look melancholic almost the whole film. Overall I think this just felt like overly long for myself and that could it be cutdown at least half an hour at minimum and have its emotional effectiveness still hit.

texto: Hard one to review. I think when the various source materials are being referenced it’s a very compelling and tasteful and beautiful film. However, the parts that are fully Hamaguchi piecing source material together were very weak, in my opinion. As a viewer, you have to accept some contrived and convoluted circumstances that bring people together. What seemed like obvious character-driven plot existed and was discarded? Specifically around glaucoma. Maybe Murakami and Chekhov are pretty good at what they do. Still, some beautiful imagery.

texto: Three hours were spent watching a film that places itself on an unreachable pedestal. When I tried to search through those popular reviews to understand why it took Cannes Film Festival by storm, I found that none of the reasons were convincing. Everyone in the film walks in the same posture, speaks in the same tone, and faces the camera with the same expression. Several of the major plot developments are driven merely by dense stretches of personal monologues. It is a familiar trope of French cinema, yet the Japanese seem to have given it a new, lifeless interpretation. Cinema is not theatre. Even if you mention theatre within a film, please do not make the film itself feel like a stage play.

texto: Pretty. Nice acting. I like their interpretation of Chekhov and the use of the text for theme. The meat of the movie was moving, but all the emotional depth was lost in long winded driving scenes. Super didn’t need to be 3 hours. Like i get the level of grief the director intended the audience to feel in those moments - but still kept finding myself thinking about other things I would rather be doing. Couldn’t connect with the work like I wanted. But it wasn’t baaaad. It was like if Phantom Thread and Manchester by the Sea had a baby.

texto: Thought this was a beautiful movie. There is so much to pick up on underneath the dialogue. The movie is perfect being surrounded by the play Uncle Vanya, and the story Oto chooses to share with her husband has so much depth and authenticity to it. I don't think I've ever enjoyed a 3 hour long movie as much as this one. It wasn't necessarily sad to me, nor was it happy, it was a movie that took its time trying to convey a complex yet seemingly simple message - sometimes forgiving is hard, but having a painful past and grief shouldn't stop you from living.

texto: A deeply beautiful exploration of regret, loss, and grief. I was truly submerged in the weight of their pain, loneliness, and everything they were carrying. The relationship and dynamic between Yusuke and Misaki was just beautiful. And despite the three-hour runtime, I was completely engaged throughout, to the point where I found myself wishing the film would go on longer as the end approached. texto: Drive My Car no es una película sobre aprender a vivir con una pérdida. Es, quizá, una película sobre descubrir que nunca terminamos de conocer a las personas que amamos. Kafuku pasa buena parte de su vida intentando descifrar a Oto: sus silencios, sus infidelidades, las historias que inventa, aquello que calla. Pero cuando ella muere, descubre una paradoja devastadora: a veces la muerte no nos arrebata solamente a una persona, sino también la posibilidad de hacerle las preguntas que dejamos para después. Quizá amar sea convivir con esa clase de incertidumbre. La película parece decir que escuchar no siempre significa alcanzar al otro. Podemos conocer su voz, sus gestos, sus rutinas y hasta sus heridas, y aun así existir frente a una habitación interior cuya puerta nunca se abre del todo. Por eso el auto funciona como algo más que un escenario: es un espacio de confesión. Dos desconocidos avanzan durante horas sin mirarse directamente, y paradójicamente, en esa ausencia de mirada consiguen verse de verdad. Misaki y Kafuku no se salvan mutuamente; simplemente se reconocen en el lugar donde ambos están rotos. Y quizá ahí está lo más hermoso: no necesitamos resolver el dolor de alguien para acompañarlo. La película también cuestiona esa idea romántica de que amar significa conocer al otro por completo. Tal vez sea exactamente al contrario. Amar es aceptar que el otro siempre conservará una parte de sí mismo que no nos pertenece. Hay algo profundamente humano en nuestra necesidad de encontrar explicaciones: creemos que ponerle palabras a una herida hará que duela menos. Pero algunas heridas no se cierran cuando encontramos una respuesta, sino cuando dejamos de exigirla. Drive My Car me dejó pensando que el duelo no consiste solamente en extrañar a alguien, sino en aprender a vivir con todo lo que nunca sabremos de esa persona. Y quizás amar a alguien sea también hacer las paces con ese misterio. ¿Es posible conocer verdaderamente a alguien a quien amamos, o el amor exige abrazar la imposibilidad de comprenderlo por completo?

texto: Drive My Car follows an actor and theater director, Yusuke Kafuku who get invited to direct a multilingual production of Uncle Vanya in Hiroshima, two years after his wife passed away. There, he meets Misaki, his quiet personal driver. Through long drives and theater rehearsals, he slowly confronts his grief, secrets, and inner healing. It’s a slow film, but it never feels boring to watch. The cinematography is outstanding the views of Hiroshima by the sea feel so fresh and beautiful, also the snowy scenes in Kutsukake’s hometown are stunning. I really liked how the film gives a long 40-minute prologue as background for the character, so there are no flashbacks for the rest of the movie. Even though it’s slow, the pacing feels just right. It’s interesting to follow the characters’ theater rehearsals and preparations, and how the play’s dialogues parallel the characters’ inner conflicts. The use of different languages by the actors is also very unique. The “dialogue” between Sonia and Uncle Vanya in the ending is incredibly powerful.

texto: A film about grief, intimacy, guilt, and how little we can ever truly know another person. Loved how the red saab becomes this private space between solitude and connection, where Yusuke and Misaki slowly recognize the same guilt in each other without ever needing to completely explain themselves. Uncle vanya slowly becomes more than a play within the film. The multilingual rehearsals, repetition, sign language… all blur the line between performing and actually confronting yourself. Acting becomes another language for feelings you can’t say as yourself. Such an impressive way to weave a play through three hours where even the lines we understand seem to quietly serve the film’s message. So subtle. Grief lingers through the slow pacing and endless drives, which somehow gave me a bittersweet sense of peace. And that Hokkaido journey with the red car surrounded by snow finally gives them the space to say what they’ve been carrying. Not forgiveness, not closure, just acceptance. Then misaki inherits the saab. The same car that carried Yusuke through his grief, memories, and loneliness now carries her. Maybe that’s all there is to it sometimes. You carry what you’ve lost, you get behind the wheel and you keep the car moving.

texto: - Sr. Kafuku, me siento vacío. No hay nada dentro de mí. Sobre la conexión con el texto que comentó… creo que la sentí con los guiones que escribía Oto. Por eso vine aquí, porque quería volver a sentir eso. Así que… lo que dijo Ud. de que Oto nos unió… tiene toda la razón. Por fin lo entiendo. - […] Oto no tuvo interés por nada durante años, y un día de repente, empezó a escribir historias. Bueno, a contarlas. […] Existía un fuerte vínculo entre el sexo y todas sus historias, aunque no lo pareciera. […] esas historias nos ayudaron a los dos a sobreponernos […]. Como pareja creo que congeniábamos bien. Nosotros dependíamos el uno del otro. Yo pensaba que nuestra vida estaba totalmente completa, tanto en el día a día como en el plano sexual. Al menos así era para mí. […] jamás puse en duda su amor por mí […], no se me ocurriría. […] Aún así había algo oscuro en su interior, un lugar al que yo nunca conseguí llegar. - ¿Y a Ud. nunca se le ocurrió preguntarle por qué hacía todo eso? - Es que lo que más miedo me daba era que yo pudiera perder a Oto. […] - ¿No es posible que ella quisiera que simplemente Ud. la escuchara? - ¿Alguna vez Oto te contó algo a ti? Sé sincero. - [Procede a contarle la historia de la adolescente que era una lamprea, con el final]. Bueno, solo me contó hasta ahí. No sé si ese es el final del relato o quizá sea mucho más largo. Al contármelo, me dejó con un nudo en el estómago pero incluso así, al escucharlo de sus labios, me di cuenta de que Oto había compartido algo importante conmigo. Sr. Kafuku, por lo poco que sé, Oto era una mujer con un gran corazón, está claro que yo apenas la conocí, y que después de tanto tiempo Ud. la conocía infinitamente mejor. Pero lo que sí tengo es una cosa clara en este momento, compartió su vida con una mujer increíble durante 20 años, y debería sentirse agradecido por ello. Es mi humilde opinión. Aunque uno piense que cree conocer a alguien perfectamente, aun si ama a esa persona, nunca podrá saber lo que guarda en lo más profundo de su corazón. Solo conseguirá sufrir. Pero si pudiéramos esforzarnos un poco, lograríamos conocernos a nosotros mismos mucho mejor. Realmente creo que al final lo único que tenemos que hacer es ser sinceros con nosotros mismos, y seguir los dictados de nuestro corazón con honestidad. Si uno desea conocer el alma de los demás, no le quedará más remedio que conocer la suya primero. Eso es lo que pienso. —————————————————————————— #Por lo que he visto en comentarios, la gente suele destacar otras escenas de la peli. Para mi esta escena y su contexto anterior y posterior, resumen todo. #Nunca quise un Ferrari, mi sueño siempre fue ese Saab. #Cada vez que suena Kafuku me acuerdo de Lucas Vazquez (alias Cafúcas). Aunque entiendo que el director quería que sonara a Kafka (?). PD: Kafuku tiene más aura que cualquier personaje creado con ese fin (véase T. Shelby, Ragnar, Jon Snow… se mea a todos)

texto: Hearing the hype around this movie for a while so i was excited to finally get high and dedicate a deserving 3 hrs to it. Hamaguchi, imo Japan's premiere contemporary voice on dramatic, ‘exploration of self’ movies, does what he normally does in creating a set of characters that are both understated and wholly captivating. We care about these people, the traces they leave behind, and the specters they follow. Hamaguchi’s impressive filmography might really be topped here; distinctly Japanese yet subtly critical of 21st century Japan, DMC just does so much to underline a ghostly collective Japanese consciousness, creating a deeply personal, heartfelt and beautiful sense of isolation. As an American person watching DMC it definitely aches; i get a sense of looking inward from the outside at a culture that I think I understand, but do not truly know. Its like touching something through a pane of glass. Then theres the monumental, and perfectly executed attempt at adapting and reimagining a Murakami novel. To take this legendary written voice and put it to screen such that it FEELS like we are truly being transported to several of his multi-realmed kami worlds is significant. Murakami has such fun with the concept of overlay and Hamaguchi doesnt disappoint in his exploration of it; who is Kafka? Who is Misaki? Who is Oto? Where are we? Are we here, or did we lose ourselves somewhere else, searching for answers that shouldnt have questions. How do we express the existence of others in the projections of ourselves and do we move on, or is a part of ourselves never actually with us, but left behind in a place beneath or above us, through a tunnel, unseen.

texto: Asks the essential human question on how do we continue to choose to live in spite of everything. Drive My Car is a film of reserved stillness that rewards the patient, really fell into this one. Ambient, slow and steady yet full of humanistic integrity, Hamaguchi’s rendition lifts Murakami's 20 or so page short story about an isolated man dialoging through his past and turns it into an incredibly ambitious project concerning art, personhood, grief, transference through creation, and acceptance. The creative liberties it takes with the initial story turns it from a compelling piece about two people conversing into an incisive and engaging treatise on the anatomy of melancholy and complex yet essential human truths. The words we leave unsaid end up corroding us from the inside out; sometimes all we need is someone not to fix anything for us, but simply to hear us out. Life changes when we move away from drifting inaction and decide to choose every second. To be heard is to feel connected, to be connected is to feel alive, and to feel alive is to save ourselves. Visually gorgeous and the soundtrack had me floating… sometimes films come to you at the right time when you need them, and this one did just that. Can feel myself returning to this one a lot in years to come.

texto: I think this is the greatest example of a “good” movie vs. an “enjoyable/favorite” movie I’ve ever seen. I say that because this movie is GREAT from nearly all technical standpoints. Great actors doing some great acting, absolutely beautiful cinematography and special effects, insanely impressive sets, and just a sheer feeling of grandness that, I feel, is only topped by a handful of movies. All around, just a beautifully made film. Still, I didn’t enjoy myself AT ALL. I don’t think the story is nearly as impressive as the first one, or impressive at all for that matter. I find it boring, confusing, and just honestly dull. I find that they waste unreasonable amounts of time on storylines that don’t matter and/or just aren’t entertaining, and rush the very few things I actually enjoyed. I mean, and this is obviously the card they were dealt, seeing as this was based on a book, it’s all just talking and politics, but they do it so different in this land, “Arakkis,” that half the film is spent explaining all of that through boring exposition and whatnot, and the other half is not very interesting at all, as someone who enjoys stories similar to this, like Game of Thrones. The action scenes, though VERY far and few were, again, gorgeously and impressively shot, but I feel lack stakes, substance, and, again, enjoyment. Half of the scenes just felt like Neo and Agent Smith going at it, even though Neo already knows all of the moves Agent Smith will make. This was a dumb comparison, in hindsight, but what I mean to say is that they’re un-compelling and boring for the most part, besides that gladiator-type fight in the middle and the fight scene with the big tank thing near the 40-minute mark. The characters- don’t get me started on the characters. I’m guessing this is something most people actually LIKE about Dune- seeing as they are able as realistic of characters you can write given their positions, but I sincerely couldn’t name you one that I care about/ like. I mean, in the first one, I cared about Paul because he actually had a personality, I liked Jason Momoa’s character a lot, and I thought the Baron was a very intriguing villain, but this time around, there was none of that charm. Everyone was just this boring, dull, character with seemingly the same personality, unless you’re Paul or his mother, because then you have NO personality, making the finale and all of the stuff with Chani pretty uninteresting and unrewarding to be quite honest. Again; the fact that this movie even got to be made is a wonder within itself- with all of those spacecrafts, settings, character designs, buildings, etc, that they had to create, shoot, and put to film is such a tasteful way, but I just didn’t enjoy it at all. I found it to be INSANELY long, like, blood-curdlingly long in my opinion, to the point where I was just actually started to breathe heavier (coming from someone who likes longer movies) and (with zero exaggeration whatsoever) probably checked how much longer it was roughly 15-20 times, very boring and dull, lifeless if you will, and everything I “liked” about it wasn’t done any better than what I’ve seen a gazillion times before. My rating: 3.4/10

texto: Somehow Dune: Part Two managed to be even longer, louder, and somehow still feel like nothing was happening. In the first film, Paul Atreides was treated like a legendary figure before I ever understood why I should care about him. Unfortunately, Part Two doubles down on that. Everyone keeps looking at Paul like he’s the greatest thing to ever walk across the desert, but the movie never really earns that feeling. We’re constantly told he’s a messiah or the chosen one but I’m still waiting for the part where I understand why. Instead of watching a character become extraordinary, it feels like watching everyone else convince themselves that he already is. The Fremen’s devotion to Paul also made the story harder to take seriously. It feels less like a believable movement and more like an entire population suddenly joining a religion because the script told them to. And the final was strangely underwhelming. A story that spends so much time preparing for greatness somehow ends on a very ordinary note. Two movies, almost five hours, and my main takeaway is still: more sand, more silence, more people telling me Paul is special.

texto: 3 stars only because I love the book so much and enjoy watching it come to screen. Too many things have been squeezed into this film, it covers such a large period of time as well as squeezing in the details about the Harkonens that happen in the first part of the story in the book that aren't included in the first film. Consequently, this film feels like a series of events strung together with little impact when major items happen. Many of the character motivations and personalities are also changed, some for the better (like Chani who frankly has no personality in the books) and some for the worse (Stilgar and Lady Jessica). Because of all of this, I also don't really believe in Chani and Paul's romance in this film, we're given no time to see an actual relationship blossom, we're just told through a montage and time jump that they're together. And Timothee Chalamet and Zendaya have no chemistry. Highlights of the film include Austin Butler's Feyd-Rauther, which he plays brilliantly, and the amazing cinematography (which at times feels a little excessively self-indulgent and doesn't necessarily blend with the rest of the film (Geidi Primes)).

exemplo: A direção de Denis Villeneuve e a fotografia são frequentemente elogiadas, com destaque para as sequências em preto e branco do planeta Giedi Prime e a magnitude das paisagens de Arrakis.
texto: Denis Villeneuve en su máximo esplendor. La película es una obra maestra. Realmente magistral. Es de esas películas en las que cuesta encontrar algo que no esté a la altura: el guion, la dirección, la fotografía, los efectos visuales, las actuaciones y, por supuesto, la apoteósica banda sonora de Hans Zimmer. Absolutamente todo funciona. La primera vez que la vi en el cine, en IMAX, salí completamente alucinado. La amé de principio a fin. Pero después de haber leído Dune, la experiencia fue todavía mejor. Amé el libro de Frank Herbert y, precisamente por eso, una de las cosas que más me impresionó de la primera película fue su enorme fidelidad a la obra original. Sin embargo, al leer el libro y volver a Dune: Part Two, entendí que Denis Villeneuve tomó muchas más libertades para llevar la historia hacia una dirección diferente. Y, lejos de molestarme, me pareció maravilloso. Porque eso demuestra que Villeneuve no buscó simplemente trasladar el libro página por página a la pantalla. Entendió su esencia, tomó decisiones propias y construyó su propia visión de Dune. Y eso, para mí, es precisamente lo que hacen los grandes directores. Volver a ver esta película una y otra vez es un verdadero lujo. Cada visionado permite apreciar algo nuevo: la composición de cada plano, los colores, la fotografía, los detalles de los escenarios, la magnitud de Arrakis y el nivel técnico de una producción que visualmente es simplemente impresionante. Y si hablamos de sus grandes virtudes, es imposible no detenerse en la banda sonora de Hans Zimmer. Personalmente, es mi compositor favorito de música para cine y aquí vuelve a entregar un trabajo extraordinario, completamente diferente al de la primera película. Hay momentos en los que basta con cerrar los ojos para sentir el desierto de Arrakis, la inmensidad del planeta y, sobre todo, cómo la tensión va aumentando poco a poco hasta convertir la historia en la promesa de una guerra santa. Las actuaciones también están a un nivel extraordinario. Era algo que podía esperarse después de una primera película con un elenco tan sólido, pero las nuevas incorporaciones elevan todavía más el conjunto. Austin Butler como Feyd-Rautha y Florence Pugh como Irulan son excelentes, pero para mí hay dos que se roban absolutamente la película: Javier Bardem como Stilgar y Timothée Chalamet como Paul Atreides. Chalamet, especialmente, entrega una de las mejores actuaciones de su carrera. Se puede ver en su rostro el tormento, el miedo y el dolor de un hombre que sabe perfectamente hacia dónde lo está llevando el camino que ha elegido, pero que también entiende que cada paso que da puede acercarlo cada vez más al caos que intentaba evitar. Dune: Part Two es una película maravillosa, épica y técnicamente impresionante. Una obra que consiguió conquistar tanto al público como a la crítica y que, en mi opinión, tiene absolutamente merecidos todos los elogios que recibió. Denis Villeneuve tomó una de las obras más importantes de la ciencia ficción, la llevó a la pantalla grande con una visión propia y consiguió convertirla en una experiencia cinematográfica monumental. Una verdadera obra de arte moderna.

texto: I recognise your footsteps, old man. Absolutely monumental. Outstanding in every way. My favourite film of the decade and maybe all time. I love every second of it. Somehow it was just as good in my living room as it was in the cinema. The Harkonnens haunt the screen. The big three, Baron , Rabban and Feyd-Rauth motivate the picture with their spotless greed and pure soulessness. They will be missed in Part Three . The progression of the story in Part Two had me so concentrated in absorbing every detail that I felt like I was the Emperor himself receiving updates on Arrakis . The moments of Chani in Part One , lead so well into her role as Paul’s reality anchor in Part Two she is the life of the story and the heart of the Fremen. Zendaya’s best. The revelation of Paul’s family history is still a shock. I knew he was a genetic sight to be hold but being the heir to the Atreides thrown, the Son of a Bene Gesserit with Harkonnen blood leaves no room for surprise at what he accomplishes as a leader. This film being so much better visually than Part One is sooooo pleasing. There is spice in every frame and crack in Hans Zimmers score. I can’t wait for the third of the trilogy and WILL be seated the day of release, and WILL be rewatching the first two before we get blessed by Denis. I will always remember my first watch and will always love the story of Dune. Modern Masterpiece, timeless story. Thank you Frank Herbert , Thank you Denis Villeneuve. Long Live the Fighters.

texto: Vou começar pelo o que digo ser a melhor experiência cinematográfica da minha vida. E não havia forma melhor de começar, duna 2 é para mim o suprassumo do épico de ação e politica, a trama messiânica traz um ar atemporal e muito verídico quanto a situação geopolítica internacional, pode ser vista como uma perfeita analogia à opressão americana em cima dos povos árabes ou até mesmo associado a figura messiânica de jesus de Nazaré aos povos judeus. Sem duvidas uma obra prima

texto: Dune 2; Harkonnen Boogaloo The production on these movies continues to blow me away.  It feels like watching something from Moebius or Druillet in live action.  The costumes, the music, the differences in the worlds, heck even the language is all so well done that it feels both alien and completely natural all at the same time. I also really loved the looks of all of the Harkonnen machines.  One of the things that Villeneuve and the crew here have done very well across both films is give a sense of the weight and physics of these things.  The giant worms, the miners, the crashed ornithopters.  They all have very believable weight to them.  I've seen several bad sci-fi films where they forget about that in the fx.  They'll have these giant machines that look like they are walking across rice paper without damaging it. Watching these movies gives me the same sort of feeling that I got when I was watching The Lord of the Rings for the first time.

texto: Vou começar pelo o que digo ser a melhor experiência cinematográfica da minha vida. E não havia forma melhor de começar, duna 2 é para mim o suprassumo do épico de ação e politica, a trama messiânica traz um ar atemporal e muito verídico quanto a situação geopolítica internacional, pode ser vista como uma perfeita analogia à opressão americana em cima dos povos árabes ou até mesmo associado a figura messiânica de jesus de Nazaré aos povos judeus. Duna 2 estabelece um padrão a ser seguido na industria, a trilha sonora de hans zimmer está perfeita (como de costume) e a cinematografia de Denis Villenueve traz ousadia e sofisticação típica do diretor e que se destaca muito dentro da indústria, todos os atores estão de parabéns principalmente para a atuação de Timothée Chalamet que flutua sobre todas as camadas de Paul Atreides. Sem duvidas uma obra prima

texto: Dune 2; Harkonnen Boogaloo The production on these movies continues to blow me away.  It feels like watching something from Moebius or Druillet in live action.  The costumes, the music, the differences in the worlds, heck even the language is all so well done that it feels both alien and completely natural all at the same time. I also really loved the looks of all of the Harkonnen machines.  One of the things that Villeneuve and the crew here have done very well across both films is give a sense of the weight and physics of these things.  The giant worms, the miners, the crashed ornithopters.  They all have very believable weight to them.  I've seen several bad sci-fi films where they forget about that in the fx.  They'll have these giant machines that look like they are walking across rice paper without damaging it. Watching these movies gives me the same sort of feeling that I got when I was watching The Lord of the Rings for the first time.

Quiero destacar la parte técnica de la película, porque la fotografía es espectacular, las secuencias de Giedi Prime son magníficas, a pesar de ser monocromático tiene un look y composición fascinante, y no sólo ahí, a lo largo de toda la película se notó un salto de calidad enorme, la primera entrega estuvo bien, pero esta es sorprendente. Hablando de la pista de audio en Dolby Atmos es mejor que la Parte Uno mismamente, el soundtrack es muy bueno, la mezcla y el rango dinámico es muy bueno, en esta entrega noté mas actividad en los canales de altura y eso me encantó. Sin duda alguna me quedo con muchísimas ansias de ver la Parte Tres en unos meses

texto: this was the film that really helped me out a ton when I first started doing production design- watching interviews with Sam Lisenco (the p.d) introduced me to a new world of film production, and I'm forever thankful for it. finally, after some years, I've come around to see the film that had a huge impact on my aspiring career and deepened my understanding and appreciation of film as a whole. it's a given that what makes this film feel very special is the world and setting of this middle school, the use of intertextuality, and fantastic direction from the character acting, the specific style of cinematography, and the outstanding art direction. This is a very charming coming-of-age story that feels very magical for its modern and internet-age depiction of middle school. I was going into my senior year of high school when this came out, but youth-hood is a timeless experience all the same. In all honesty it would be unfair to compare this to a show like PEN15 because of its lack of social commentary, yes obviously they are both coming of age stories with awkward and anxious preteens, but both pieces of media are accomplishing two different goals. PEN15 has its two female leads, Maya and Anna, who bring a lot of interesting dialogue to be said about race and class in television. Usually I would label a film like this as “white people: the movie” but it would rub me the wrong way doing so as such, so I’ll make a one time exception for this film.

texto: First off, I loved that Bo Burnham cast actual eighth graders. It made everything feel so much more believable. Honestly this was a hard for me to get through purely because of how accurate it was in portraying social anxiety and those painfully embarrassing moments in middle school. It made me think about a lot of not great memories I have. Even as a 27 year old, there were scenes with Kayla that I could still relate to. Elsie Fisher, given how young she was at the time, gave a great authentic performance. Captured all of the awkward, cringey moments in a way that felt incredibly real. The film also addressed the nuances of social media really well. Another thing of note was the awkward but genuinely loving relationship between Kayla and her dad, added a lot to the movie. An excellent coming of age movie that I probably will never watch again!

texto: Penso sia uno dei film più realistici che io abbia mai visto. Di solito al cinema quando cercano di rappresentare un certo tipo di ragazza, lo fanno sempre attraverso il classico bullismo, quando in realtà in molti casi il vero problema è semplicemente il sentirsi invisibili. Mi sono rivista tantissimo in lei in molti momenti della mia vita. La difficoltà a farsi nuovi amici, ad entrare nei discorsi, il sentirsi sempre la persona fuori posto che non c’entra niente. È una cosa che mi è successa alle medie, al liceo e persino all'università, anche se fortunatamente non ai livelli di Kayla. Guardare alcune scene di questo film mi ha fatto venire dei flashback del Vietnam e sono felicissima che quel periodo sia ormai passato. Queste storie di solito si soffermano sempre e solo sul dramma o sulla tragedia, mentre molto spesso la verità dei fatti è esattamente quella raccontata qui. Mi è piaciuto davvero tanto come tutto questo non distrugga mai del tutto la protagonista, ma anzi lei cerchi sempre di uscire dalla propria comfort zone mantenendo un'attitudine positiva.

An excellent coming of age movie that I probably will never watch again!

Spending hours trying to engineer the perfect Instagram post like it might somehow engineer a better version of yourself. Every Snapchat story felt like evidence in the case for whether or not you of all people were worth noticing. Eighth Grade understands that before you know who you are, you're already performing as someone else. Every hallway feels like an audience. The boys are impossibly dreamy, the girls impossibly cruel, your parents impossibly embarrassing, and adulthood seems like the cure for it, a glimmer of hope through it all. What a beautiful tragedy it is to be thirteen; how special it is that a movie can almost let us do it all over again.
