exemplo: O filme apresenta uma sucessão de elementos desconexos e sobrepostos, que mais cansam do que envolvem, e a tentativa de justificar essa bagunça como parte da proposta estética não convence; a falta de uma narrativa clara e a quantidade de estímulos visuais deixam a experiência exaustiva e prejudicam a compreensão.
texto: Quando comecei o filme, a primeira sensação que tive foi a de estar assistindo a uma versão alternativa de algum filme da Marvel, principalmente uma espécie de Doutor Estranho no Multiverso da Loucura com uma abordagem diferente. Talvez por eu não estar tão acostumado a ver o conceito de multiverso sendo explorado fora do universo dos super-heróis, Tudo em Todo Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo parecia uma ótima oportunidade de enxergar essa ideia por uma perspectiva mais autoral e menos limitada pelas regras de uma franquia. E é curioso porque o conceito de multiverso aqui é muito mais amplo do que simplesmente mostrar versões alternativas dos personagens ou brincar com realidades diferentes. O filme usa essa ideia quase como uma representação das infinitas possibilidades da vida, das escolhas que fazemos e de todos os caminhos que poderiam ter sido seguidos. Essa é uma proposta interessante, e eu gostei da forma como o filme tenta enxergar o multiverso por um lado mais humano e existencial. O problema, para mim, está na forma como essa ideia é apresentada. Em muitos momentos, o filme parece querer ser mais inteligente do que realmente é, como se precisasse constantemente provar sua própria genialidade. A mistura de estilos, o exagero visual e a quantidade absurda de ideias fazem parte da identidade da obra, mas às vezes a sensação é de que o filme força tanto a sua criatividade que acaba perdendo um pouco da naturalidade. Ele quer ser caótico, profundo, engraçado e emocionante ao mesmo tempo, mas em alguns momentos parece mais preocupado em mostrar o quanto consegue ser diferente do que realmente desenvolver tudo aquilo que propõe. Eu gostei mais do ato final justamente porque é o momento em que o filme finalmente parece entender a própria força. Depois de passar boa parte da duração mergulhado em um caos constante, entre cortes frenéticos, exageros visuais e uma tentativa quase desesperada de ser irreverente, ele finalmente desacelera e permite que seus personagens existam de verdade. É quando Tudo em Todo Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo deixa de tentar provar o tempo todo o quanto é criativo e começa a explorar aquilo que realmente tinha de mais interessante: as relações humanas por trás de todo aquele espetáculo. Antes disso, porém, eu tive muita dificuldade de me conectar com a proposta. Não é pelo fato de o filme ser absurdo ou querer ser engraçado, porque essa é claramente a identidade dele, mas pela forma como ele constantemente interrompe os próprios momentos de profundidade. Sempre que surge uma oportunidade de desenvolver melhor suas ideias sobre arrependimentos, escolhas e a sensação de insignificância diante de infinitas possibilidades, o filme parece escolher quebrar a atmosfera com uma piada que muitas vezes não funciona e acaba tirando todo o peso daquilo que estava sendo construído. E isso acaba prejudicando justamente a profundidade que ele tenta alcançar. Algumas cenas são tão forçadas e constrangedoras que, ao invés de aproximarem o espectador dos personagens, criam uma distância. O filme quer ser caótico, divertido e emocionante, mas em muitos momentos o caos domina tanto que a parte humana fica escondida. Só quando ele finalmente abandona um pouco essa necessidade de transformar tudo em uma grande piada é que a mensagem começa a encontrar espaço para respirar. Eu realmente acredito que a campanha desse filme no Oscar foi um delírio coletivo. Sinceramente, não consigo enxergar uma obra digna de sete estatuetas aqui. Para mim, o único prêmio realmente justificável é o de Melhor Montagem. Todo o restante parece premiar mais a ideia do filme do que a sua execução. É uma obra que força a própria genialidade, insiste em uma profundidade que raramente alcança e, justamente quando parece prestes a dizer algo verdadeiramente significativo, escolhe sabotar o momento com um humor que, para mim, soa artificial e deslocado. E no fim, eu continuo com a sensação de que assistir a Tudo em Todo Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo não foi uma experiência tão distante de assistir a um filme da fase 4 da Marvel. Talvez exista mais criatividade na forma, uma identidade visual mais autoral e uma ambição maior nas ideias, mas a essência ainda me parece muito semelhante. O multiverso continua sendo tratado como um grande espetáculo, onde tudo precisa ser maior, mais caótico e mais excêntrico do que o anterior. Se a Academia decidiu premiar justamente esse tipo de proposta com o maior prêmio da noite, então talvez fosse mais coerente ter reconhecido um dos próprios filmes da Marvel, que, gostando ou não, sempre assumiram esse espetáculo sem a necessidade de revesti-lo com uma profundidade que, para mim, aqui nunca se concretiza.

texto: Went in with zero expectations. Didn't need logic, didn't need deep character work — just wanted something genuinely fun and entertaining. And honestly, I just ended up bored. The whole “genre-blending” thing isn't as wild as people say. Sure, it jumps between worlds and tosses in sci-fi, action, and some emotional moments, but none of it ever actually blends into something fresh or mind-blowing. It's just a movie that changes costumes without ever becoming genuinely entertaining. The multiverse stuff, which is supposed to be the big selling point, got repetitive fast. They create a couple of cool, weird worlds early on, but then keep revisiting the same handful over and over. “Everything Everywhere All at Once” quickly shrinks into “a few things, a few places”. That killed the sense of endless possibility and just made it feel small and monotonous. Also, people praise the relentless pace, but I honestly didn't feel it. The editing is busy, not fast — there's a difference. Especially the last hour dragged like crazy. So many slow-motion moments that didn't earn their weight, stretching out scenes that already felt emotionally repetitive. And the humor? The problem isn't that the jokes are random or dumb — it's that the movie never commits to real chaos. It gives you a couple of weird ideas, then just keeps circling back to them until they're completely worn out. A truly random, limitless multiverse should be throwing something new at you constantly, but instead the jokes become predictable, cliché, and as limited as the worlds themselves. That's really the core issue here: the movie runs out of ideas and then just stretches everything thin, repeating itself because it doesn't know what else to do. If you're going to be this narratively limited, you'd better have deep characters, sharp logic, or some real emotional weight to fall back on — and it has none of that. The emotional beats are so forced, practically holding up cue cards that say “care now” and “cry here”. Given how wild and limitless the premise is, the ending lands as preachy, cliché, and a total drag — exactly the kind of safe landing a film like this should have avoided. Honestly, it's not that different from plenty of other weak films that start with a decent premise and then fumble it. The only difference is this one got a sky-high rating and a pile of Oscars.

texto: Quando comecei o filme, a primeira sensação que tive foi a de estar assistindo a uma versão alternativa de algum filme da Marvel, principalmente uma espécie de Doutor Estranho no Multiverso da Loucura com uma abordagem diferente. Talvez por eu não estar tão acostumado a ver o conceito de multiverso sendo explorado fora do universo dos super-heróis, Tudo em Todo Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo parecia uma ótima oportunidade de enxergar essa ideia por uma perspectiva mais autoral e menos limitada pelas regras de uma franquia. E é curioso porque o conceito de multiverso aqui é muito mais amplo do que simplesmente mostrar versões alternativas dos personagens ou brincar com realidades diferentes. O filme usa essa ideia quase como uma representação das infinitas possibilidades da vida, das escolhas que fazemos e de todos os caminhos que poderiam ter sido seguidos. Essa é uma proposta interessante, e eu gostei da forma como o filme tenta enxergar o multiverso por um lado mais humano e existencial. O problema, para mim, está na forma como essa ideia é apresentada. Em muitos momentos, o filme parece querer ser mais inteligente do que realmente é, como se precisasse constantemente provar sua própria genialidade. A mistura de estilos, o exagero visual e a quantidade absurda de ideias fazem parte da identidade da obra, mas às vezes a sensação é de que o filme força tanto a sua criatividade que acaba perdendo um pouco da naturalidade. Ele quer ser caótico, profundo, engraçado e emocionante ao mesmo tempo, mas em alguns momentos parece mais preocupado em mostrar o quanto consegue ser diferente do que realmente desenvolver tudo aquilo que propõe. Eu gostei mais do ato final justamente porque é o momento em que o filme finalmente parece entender a própria força. Depois de passar boa parte da duração mergulhado em um caos constante, entre cortes frenéticos, exageros visuais e uma tentativa quase desesperada de ser irreverente, ele finalmente desacelera e permite que seus personagens existam de verdade. É quando Tudo em Todo Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo deixa de tentar provar o tempo todo o quanto é criativo e começa a explorar aquilo que realmente tinha de mais interessante: as relações humanas por trás de todo aquele espetáculo. Antes disso, porém, eu tive muita dificuldade de me conectar com a proposta. Não é pelo fato de o filme ser absurdo ou querer ser engraçado, porque essa é claramente a identidade dele, mas pela forma como ele constantemente interrompe os próprios momentos de profundidade. Sempre que surge uma oportunidade de desenvolver melhor suas ideias sobre arrependimentos, escolhas e a sensação de insignificância diante de infinitas possibilidades, o filme parece escolher quebrar a atmosfera com uma piada que muitas vezes não funciona e acaba tirando todo o peso daquilo que estava sendo construído. E isso acaba prejudicando justamente a profundidade que ele tenta alcançar. Algumas cenas são tão forçadas e constrangedoras que, ao invés de aproximarem o espectador dos personagens, criam uma distância. O filme quer ser caótico, divertido e emocionante, mas em muitos momentos o caos domina tanto que a parte humana fica escondida. Só quando ele finalmente abandona um pouco essa necessidade de transformar tudo em uma grande piada é que a mensagem começa a encontrar espaço para respirar. Eu realmente acredito que a campanha desse filme no Oscar foi um delírio coletivo. Sinceramente, não consigo enxergar uma obra digna de sete estatuetas aqui. Para mim, o único prêmio realmente justificável é o de Melhor Montagem. Todo o restante parece premiar mais a ideia do filme do que a sua execução. É uma obra que força a própria genialidade, insiste em uma profundidade que raramente alcança e, justamente quando parece prestes a dizer algo verdadeiramente significativo, escolhe sabotar o momento com um humor que, para mim, soa artificial e deslocado. E no fim, eu continuo com a sensação de que assistir a Tudo em Todo Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo não foi uma experiência tão distante de assistir a um filme da fase 4 da Marvel. Talvez exista mais criatividade na forma, uma identidade visual mais autoral e uma ambição maior nas ideias, mas a essência ainda me parece muito semelhante. O multiverso continua sendo tratado como um grande espetáculo, onde tudo precisa ser maior, mais caótico e mais excêntrico do que o anterior. Se a Academia decidiu premiar justamente esse tipo de proposta com o maior prêmio da noite, então talvez fosse mais coerente ter reconhecido um dos próprios filmes da Marvel, que, gostando ou não, sempre assumiram esse espetáculo sem a necessidade de revesti-lo com uma profundidade que, para mim, aqui nunca se concretiza.

texto: Wild and warm and chock-full of just about everything you’d expect from cinema that isn’t bound to IP or convention of any sort. Swiss Army Man is one of my very favorite films, so it was a real joy to see the Daniels go sicko mode once again, yet I couldn’t help but feel that this didn’t quite come together the way it intends. There is a lot - and I mean A LOT - going on here: Hot dog fingers, rocks, a butt-plug brawl, the ultimate everything bagel, a frumpy Jamie Lee Curtis, chewing glue, and so much more, all branching from a multiverse guided by every possible scientific outcome and human decision ever dreamed of. Despite the film’s wholly original extravagance, the sheer scope of its visual and thematic ambitions prove to be a bit exhausting. The climax in particular becomes increasingly winded as the film sounds off on all its grand declarations about the messy contradictions life has in store for us. A flawed, but no less admirable marriage of the sacred and the profane as only the Daniels could conceive.

texto: Charlie Kaufman’s multiverse- Tree of Life , if made for Adult Swim -or- The feminine urge to eat a bagel. Whatever it is it comes out like Scott Pilgrim vs. the World - an alive diversion that doesn’t hit the emotional notes and gets repetitive on the rest. I was absolutely giddy for the first hour, something I’d like to bottle for an energy drink. Everything Everywhere is overlong and reaching for some pathos that doesn’t feel genuine but more like an attempt to ground the insanity with spelled out motives (practice patience and kindness and everything shall pass). Everything Everywhere All at Once works best as a multiverse marriage of expansions and retractions - shared memories, disappointments, parallel lives - and then it becomes about mother-daughter bridges. In fact, the mother-daughter arc isn't too far removed from something like Inside Out — even though the daughter beats some people to death with huge, floppy dildos. But it is constantly inventive, ridiculous, and the sheer number of inserts/locations/costumes to pull off the concept are beyond commendable. Michelle Yeoh is great. TikTok is gonna eat this up with out-of-context usage. -so- See it on the big screen with a crowd. -because- There's a lot in this blender and it has lots of nutrients — even if they’re liquified by the end.

texto: I was so excited for this film ever since its trailer debuted at the end of 2020. Remember how cool that trailer was, especially when it did quick cuts between different variations of Michelle Yeoh’s character? I guess there is such a thing as having too much of a good thing, because the actual film leaned too much into that editing technique, eventually to the point where it felt gimmicky. Everything Everywhere All at Once tries to do and be too many things all at once, resulting in an uneven, exhausting, underwhelming, and overbearing assault on the senses that would have benefitted from someone behind the scenes reining The Daniels in on their ambitions in order to tell a coherent story. Read my full review here.

texto: На одной чаше весов занятная концепция (пусть историей о мультивселенной в 2022 году никого не удивишь, но некоторые решения здесь выглядят крайне нетривиально), харизматичная главная героиня (от Мишель Йео глаз не оторвать), безудержно-кринжовый экшн (чего только стоят люди с сосисками между пальцев). На другой чаше весов диалоги, украденные из условной методички «Как разговаривают персонажи (для чайников)», нагромождение героев второго плана без должного раскрытия и абсурд ради абсурда. В общем, красивую и яркую историю свели к глупости и банальности под конец.

texto: Wild and warm and chock-full of just about everything you’d expect from cinema that isn’t bound to IP or convention of any sort. Swiss Army Man is one of my very favorite films, so it was a real joy to see the Daniels go sicko mode once again, yet I couldn’t help but feel that this didn’t quite come together the way it intends. There is a lot - and I mean A LOT - going on here: Hot dog fingers, rocks, a butt-plug brawl, the ultimate everything bagel, a frumpy Jamie Lee Curtis, chewing glue, and so much more, all branching from a multiverse guided by every possible scientific outcome and human decision ever dreamed of. Despite the film’s wholly original extravagance, the sheer scope of its visual and thematic ambitions prove to be a bit exhausting. The climax in particular becomes increasingly winded as the film sounds off on all its grand declarations about the messy contradictions life has in store for us. A flawed, but no less admirable marriage of the sacred and the profane as only the Daniels could conceive.

texto: Charlie Kaufman’s multiverse- Tree of Life , if made for Adult Swim -or- The feminine urge to eat a bagel. Whatever it is it comes out like Scott Pilgrim vs. the World - an alive diversion that doesn’t hit the emotional notes and gets repetitive on the rest. I was absolutely giddy for the first hour, something I’d like to bottle for an energy drink. Everything Everywhere is overlong and reaching for some pathos that doesn’t feel genuine but more like an attempt to ground the insanity with spelled out motives (practice patience and kindness and everything shall pass). Everything Everywhere All at Once works best as a multiverse marriage of expansions and retractions - shared memories, disappointments, parallel lives - and then it becomes about mother-daughter bridges. In fact, the mother-daughter arc isn't too far removed from something like Inside Out — even though the daughter beats some people to death with huge, floppy dildos. But it is constantly inventive, ridiculous, and the sheer number of inserts/locations/costumes to pull off the concept are beyond commendable. Michelle Yeoh is great. TikTok is gonna eat this up with out-of-context usage. -so- See it on the big screen with a crowd. -because- There's a lot in this blender and it has lots of nutrients — even if they’re liquified by the end.

texto: I was so excited for this film ever since its trailer debuted at the end of 2020. Remember how cool that trailer was, especially when it did quick cuts between different variations of Michelle Yeoh’s character? I guess there is such a thing as having too much of a good thing, because the actual film leaned too much into that editing technique, eventually to the point where it felt gimmicky. Everything Everywhere All at Once tries to do and be too many things all at once, resulting in an uneven, exhausting, underwhelming, and overbearing assault on the senses that would have benefitted from someone behind the scenes reining The Daniels in on their ambitions in order to tell a coherent story. Read my full review here.

texto: By balancing destructive nihilism with joyful absurdism, the film captures how small human connections can heal the deep wounds of generational trauma. This movie perfectly showcases the complexities of Asian cultural dynamics, as parental love is often masked as strict criticism and heavy expectations to protect the family’s future. This creates a painful cycle of conditional love, leaving a feeling unseen and burdened by the pressure to be perfect. Seeing this with my Asian mother was the cherry on top of this already deeply resonating experience.

texto: THE MULTIVERSE WILL NEVER BE THE SAME www.youtube.com/watch?v=deS4dxRv_ZU Everything Everywhere All at Once changes the game for what cinematic multiverses can be, with thrilling action, excellent performances, and a world of possibilities. Michelle Yeoh in particular gives a powerhouse performance in a story that puts a fresh, welcome spin on the idea of the multiverse. Read full written review by Rafael Motamayor

texto: (SXSW 2022 Festival: Opening Film) - Day 1 The REAL Multiverse of Madness!! Update #2: Just like their previous venture (The Swiss Army Man) , The Daniels have once again successfully pulled off an absurd film that would make you ask, "How the F did they think of this!? And more importantly, how the hell did they get the funding for this, and turn it into such an uniquely outlandish film!?!!" Just like 'The Swiss Army Man', I believe even this one deserves to be applauded for its sheer originality and zaniness. Also, one can't talk about this movie without talking about the brilliance of its four main leads, Michelle Yeoh, Ke Huy Quan, Jamie Lee Curtis and Stephanie Hsu. A Multiverse of Madness that's filled with crazy martial arts, over-the-top production designs, chef raccoons, slick editing, talking rocks, colorful cinematography, hotdog fingers, great acting, dildos that give superhuman strength, and most importantly, two very well written superstrong female leads. In short, it's Everything Everywhere All At Once.

texto: SXSW 2022 , World Premiere:    That was…fucking phenomenal. Watching this film made me feel like I was on a rollercoaster, not really sure what was coming next. It’s not predictable, there’s no static narrative structure, and it is jam-packed with bizarre ideas. It’s an experience that completely engages all of your senses, and like the directors stated, “will keep you at the edge of your seats”. You’ll wince, burst out laughing, and maybe shed a few tears (especially if you’ve experienced your own generational trauma). If you particularly like action, comedy, drama, or sci-fi, I guarantee you that all of these genres will be covered. There is something for everyone, but there is also nothing out there quite like it. The editing/effects were INCREDIBLE. The fight sequences were extremely well-choreographed. There was a lovely score and superb performances from Michelle, Ke Huy, Jamie, and Stephanie. Don’t think too hard about it. Just sit back, relax, and enjoy the ride as you go through everything, everywhere, all at once .

A triumph of a sophomore effort from the Daniels who prove they are two of the most brilliant filmmakers currently working today.

texto: é um daqueles filmes que parecem ter conquistado um status quase intocável na cultura pop, mas pra mim, essa fama é muito maior do que seus méritos. o filme é frequentemente tratado como uma obra profunda e revolucionária, porém acho uma narrativa que, apesar de começar com uma proposta interessante, termina se rendendo a um espetáculo vazio. nos primeiros atos, a história parece caminhar para uma crítica ao capitalismo, ao consumismo e à alienação da vida moderna. até há espaço para imaginar uma discussão mais complexa sobre o sistema e sobre como ele molda a identidade masculina. mo entanto, essa possibilidade logo é abandonada e em vez de aprofundar suas críticas, o filme transforma esse discurso em um pretexto para cenas de violência, caos e ação, esvaziando boa parte do potencial que havia construído. outro aspecto que me incomodou foi a forma como os personagens são apresentados. Achei todos profundamente antipáticos e difíceis de acompanhar. a impressão é de que o filme espera que o espectador admire figuras que, na prática, são dominadas pelo ego, pela agressividade e por uma visão bastante limitada das relações humanas. me parece um filme pensado prioritariamente para um público masculino. sua reflexão sobre masculinidade é quase inteiramente construída a partir da violência, da destruição e da necessidade de reafirmação do homem. falta sensibilidade para explorar outras dimensões dos personagens ou das pessoas afetadas por suas ações, o que torna a experiência emocionalmente distante. sei bem que o filme possui uma direção marcante, um ritmo envolvente e um desfecho que surpreendeu muitos espectadores. ainda assim, esses elementos não foram suficientes para me convencer. Para mim, trata-se de um filme superestimado: começa sugerindo uma crítica social promissora, mas termina reduzindo suas ideias a um espetáculo de violência que parece muito menos inteligente do que acredita ser.

exemplo: A crítica ao capitalismo e ao consumismo é percebida como superficial ou mal desenvolvida, perdendo-se em cenas de violência.
texto: Fight Club (1999) Fight Club: Violence in Place of Understanding Human Alienation On its surface, Fight Club is a film about the alienation of modern man: alienation from work, from the body, from objects, from the crowd, from the self. My thesis is that instead of building a machine for understanding this alienation, the film builds a machine for discharging it, and that this discharge is substituted for analysis through an aestheticization of violence. Contrary to the common reading that treats the film as a critique of late-twentieth-century consumerism (a reading I'll address below and show to be insufficient), my argument is that the film's formal structure, at a level deeper than the characters' explicit dialogue, presents violence not as an object of examination but as the very telos of liberation. The choice of an unreliable narrator is, at first glance, a classic device for representing the subject's internal rupture, a tradition running from The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari to Taxi Driver . The key difference, however, lies in how the camera positions itself relative to that rupture. In the scene introducing Tyler on the airplane, Fincher uses a low-angle medium shot that places Tyler in a position of visual authority from the very first moment, before the narrator himself even understands his relationship to this man. This choice, unlike Scorsese's treatment of Travis Bickle, where the camera deliberately maintains a cold, alienated distance from the subject, invites the viewer into identification from the outset. The film's form makes the audience fall in love with Tyler before the narrative ever discloses that he is a hallucination. This formal-narrative contradiction is where the problem begins: the final revelation (that Tyler and the narrator are one) is shocking at the level of story, but at the level of form it has already been neutralized. The camera has been complicit with Tyler from the start, not with the narrator. Comparing two key fight scenes, the narrator's first brawl with Tyler in the parking lot and the narrator's fight with "Angel Face," reveals the film's editing pattern. In both scenes, the cutting rate accelerates as the fight continues, and the sound design shifts from realistic effects toward exaggerated sonic design (heartbeat, echo), a pattern nearly identical to the escalation used in genre action sequences. The contrast with something like the fight scenes in Scorsese's Raging Bull is instructive: there, slow, repetitive editing turns violence into an experience of attrition and meaninglessness; the blows repeat until pleasure is drained away. In Fight Club, by contrast, the editing builds toward a rhythmic climax that completes pleasure rather than dissolving it. This formal choice is not incidental; it is meaning-making. At the sensory level, the audience experiences violence not as crisis but as resolution, precisely reproducing the same psychological pattern the film claims to be exposing. The most significant objection to this reading is the common argument, made by critics such as actor Edward Norton and in academic readings including those of Ruben Austin and Henry Giroux, that the film is a self-aware critique of toxic masculine ideology: the final scene, in which the narrator shoots Tyler and stands beside Marla, is read as a symbolic rejection of the fantasy of violence. This reading is defensible at the level of plot, but it fails at the level of form. Visually, the closing scene is accompanied by a triumphant score (the song "Where Is My Mind," with its melodic swell) synchronized with images of the towers collapsing, a combination that evokes liberation and grandeur, not warning or catastrophe. If the film truly intended to reject violence, its final sound design and editing should have conveyed a sense of emptiness or horror, not an inspirational musical crescendo. In other words, the explicit language of the plot (the rejection of Tyler) contradicts the implicit language of form (the celebration of destruction). In cinema, form always has the last word. In the film's framing system, Marla is almost always shown in tight shots, from angles that place her at the margins or behind the narrator. For example, in the support-group scenes, the camera focuses on the narrator's reaction to Marla's presence rather than on Marla herself as a subject with an independent crisis. This consistent framing choice reveals that within the film's formal apparatus, alienation is understood not as a universal human problem but as a specifically masculine crisis, whose resolution is sought through the reclamation of the male body via pain. This can be contrasted with a film like Kieślowski's Three Colors: Blue , which builds a crisis of identity through a woman whose relationship to loss is tied not to the body and violence but to silence and quiet reconstruction. The absence of such a possibility in Fight Club is not accidental; it reflects the limits of the film's formal imagination. Fight Club is a film of considerable technical skill, but that skill, rather than serving an understanding of alienation, serves to aestheticize a violent solution. The contradiction between the explicit language of the plot (which claims to critique violence) and the implicit language of form (which celebrates it) is exactly what turns the film not into an analysis but into an unconscious complicity with its own subject matter. For this reason, I give half a star to a film that has put formalist craft in the service of a dangerous thesis: the replacement of understanding with violence.

texto: Antykonsumpcjonizm drugiego roku studiów, nastoletni nihilizm i diagnoza męskości wychowanej przez kobiety - Fincher wie, że to bełkot, ale nie umie tego dobrze pokazać. Krytyka siedzi w dialogach, egzaltacja w kadrze, a kadr zawsze wygrywa. Po demontażu Tylera zostaje tylko trzymanie się za ręce przy walącym się mieście. Twist czytelny co najmniej od końca pierwszego aktu, wyjaśniany jak rewelacja, więc kotara opada w ciszy zamiast w zdumieniu. Pewnie lepiej rezonuje z samotnymi facetami - to nie był zamysł Finchera i najlepiej dowodzi, że bardziej od satyry wybrzmiewa pozorna egzaltacja. Przy okazji - animacje fatalnie się zestarzały. Zostaje parę trafionych satyrycznych obserwacji, niezłe kreacje i czarny humor, który czasem gra. Warsztatowo ładnie: brudne zielonkawe zdjęcia, montaż na bit Dust Brothers, meblowanie mieszkania. Ale dwie godziny mielenia tego bigosu bardziej męczą, niż ekscytują. Muszę złamać pierwszą zasadę Fight Clubu w sieci: nie oceniamy nisko Fight Clubu.

texto: No quiero ser mala porque se que al 99% de los usuarios de acá les encanta esta película, pero a mi parecer esta sobrevaloradisima, acabo de verla y honestamente no le conseguí ese punto que a todos les fascinaaaa. ⊹ ㅤׅㅤReseña ㅤׅㅤ⊹ El plot me parece bastante predecible la verdad, igual no lo voy a acusar tanto porque siento que realmente no me logró impactar más que todo porque ya lo sabía, sin embargo, si no lo hubiera sabido probablemente no fuera tan difícil de adivinar. Admito que no me quedé mirándola fijamente la verdad, pero si la deje de fondo y la ví gran parte del tiempo, no me salte escenas, pero si le quite atención a varias porque honestamente los diálogos eran bastante incómodos y desagradables, aunque también entiendo que está hecho mayormente para provocar y tambien como una visión a toda esa vida callejera, a las adiciones de Marla y a la dinámica que llevaban entre ellos, las peleas y demás, pero no significa que a mi personalmente me haya gustado, entiendo el mensaje, pero fue un disgusto tanto las escenas como varios diálogos. El mensaje de la película como tal no me parece malo, es un buen concepto utilizar a un alter ego para simular la libertad que anhela el protagonista, también es buena la crítica y esa visión a como es la dinámica de los hombres, siempre luchar por quien es mejor y vivir demostrando cosas que no son por simple aprobación, aunque es una lástima que la sátira no haya llegado del mejor modo y los hombres lejos de reflejarse y buscar cambiar esos patrones de la sociedad o dejar de reprimir ciertas cosas solo por querer aparentar hombría, terminaron tomándose la película como un ejemplo, viendo a Tyler como un idolo, admirando las peleas, cuando el verdadero objetivo que busca la pelicula es criticar eso y no tomarlo como referencia, pero buenooo cada quien. A mi perspectiva la escena que más vale es la del final, el soundtrack es buenísimo y hace buena referencia, la escena es memorable por todo lo que significa y representa, si soy honesta ya estaba a nada de ponerme a ver otra cosa, pero me quedé ahí solo para ver ese final. Y en cierta parte eso le quitó emoción a lo que pudo ser mi experiencia viendo la película porque solo estaba esperando el final por una escena, la historia ya me parecía bastante corriente y no se, nunca le ví ese punto fascinante. Con esto no quiero hacerme la más cinéfila ni insinuar que son películas comunes y corrientes, solo que personalmente no la disfruté como la mayoría, pero no quita que sea una película de culto y con un mensaje bastante fuerte y significativo Por cierto, esta buenísimo el coso que aparece cuando reseñas la película JAJJAKAKAKAK ya me dio culpa porque voy a romper las reglas

texto: J'avais détesté ce film quand je l'avais vu ado. Le revoir maintenant n'a pas fondamentalement changé mon opinion. Formellement c'est très bien exécuté, c'est du Fincher à son prime (quoique cette surabondance de numérique verse un peu parfois dans le too much). Quoiqu'un peu trop verbeux. Cornélius ne nous laisse aucun répit avec ses pensées, ça aurait été bien de suggérer plutôt que de réciter. Avec le recul c'est un peu le point faible de Fincher, c'est un très bon illustrateur, mais tous ses films sont d'une froideur clinique - bien que, d'une certaine façon, ce soit assez adapté au sujet, un peu de subtilité sur l'exposition aurait été bienvenue. En revoyant le film en connaissant le twist, on décèle en effet les quelques indices qui sont disséminés ici et là passé la moitié. Mais ça ne me réconcilie pour autant pas avec cette fin qui reste à mes yeux une fin de petit malin. Pour moi le film tient difficilement avec ce twist - je comprends l'allégorie, le message, mais j'ai du mal à accepter tout ce qui se précède. La névrose est trop forte notamment dès qu'il est en public. Ça fait partie de ces films où l'allégorie, l'exercice de style, prime sur la narration ("qu'importe la cohérence, c'est la manière qui importe"). Je ne crois pas une seconde à l'histoire de Cornélius, et c'est trop pratique de tout mettre sous le fait que de toute façon, c'est dans sa tête. Et puis bon, même le message profond, c'est digne d'un adolescent en pleine rébellion : "fuck le capitalisme, faut tout faire péter, vive l'anarchie". Ok, cool, ça a le mérite d'être original d'arriver à être aussi jusqu'au boutiste à Hollywood. Maintenant, il serait temps de grandir. Et allez consulter si vous êtes mal dans votre peau.

texto: ce film m’a vraiment fait réfléchir sur l’identité et sur cette envie de devenir quelqu’un qu’on pense être incapable d’être. le narrateur vivait presque comme une machine : une routine, un travail, des objets, et très peu d’émotions qu’il arrivait réellement à exprimer. puis Tyler apparaît comme tout ce qu’il n’osait pas être : libre, impulsif, en colère, sans peur des règles. mais au fond, Tyler n’est peut-être pas seulement une autre personne. il représente tout ce que le narrateur avait enfermé en lui. et c’est justement ce que j’ai trouvé intéressant dans la fin. quand il comprend enfin ce qui se passe, j’ai l’impression qu’il retrouve une partie de lui-même qu’il avait complètement perdue. pour la première fois, il ressent vraiment : la peur, la colère, l’amour, la douleur. même si tout ce qu’il a vécu était destructeur, il n’est plus cette personne vide et programmée qu’il était au début. j’ai beaucoup aimé cette idée que parfois, on peut tellement vouloir devenir quelqu’un d’autre qu’on finit par créer une version de nous-mêmes qui semble plus vivante que notre vraie vie. et puis cette fin… impossible de ne pas rester devant l’écran à essayer de tout remettre en place dans sa tête.

texto: Brilliant adaptation of the book, however honestly I think the book ending left you more to think about and had more effect than the one from the movie. I was surprised by the choice to change the ending given that so much of the movie was scene for scene and word for word from the book. The details were incredible. If you pay really close attention, you can see single frame splicings of Tyler in the first minutes of the film that are meant to be barely noticeable and the same thing Tyler was doing splicing in shots as a film projectionist (there is also a split second showing of a penis at the end). *Spoiler for Primal Fear ahead if you haven’t seen it* It’s wild to me that Ed Norton played such a niche role twice with Fight Club and Primal Fear- like two homicidal people with an evil alter ego/split personality!?

texto: Yes I gave this movie 5 stars. Yes I understand the underlying themes and criticisms of toxic masculinity and consumerism portrayed in the film. Yes, I understand that Tyler Durden is not supposed to be some kind of role model, and that the entire point is to criticise the exact people who idolise him. Yes, I understand that Fight Club fans who completely miss the point are basically the living embodiment of the film’s criticism. Yes, I know that liking a movie does not mean I agree with every single thing it portrays. Yes, I am aware that the film has been discussed in approximately 47 million video essays explaining why its fans are stupid. And yes, I am still allowed to enjoy the cinematography, performances, screenplay, editing and overall filmmaking without having to submit a 3,000-word essay proving that I understand the movie before rating it. But thank you for assuming that giving a movie five stars means I have spent the last six months punching holes in my drywall and calling everyone a sheep. I genuinely appreciate the concern.

texto: “ It’s only after we’ve lost everything that we’re free to do anything ” Wow. Rewatching fight club after 2 months of letting it marinate and it again reminds me why Fight Club is my favourite movie. To me, Fight Club was about a false sense of what freedom is to the Narrator. We spend 2 hours to see the Narrator in a life he hated, trapped in an endless cycle of insomnia and emptiness. We then see him introduced to a character that embodies his dream of what freedom looks like, Tyler Durden. He offers the narrator a  completely different perspective on what life truly is about, however slowly taking over his life and his sense of control and freedom. Rewatching it, I genuinely felt as if I was watching an intertwined masterpiece unfold where dots were connecting from two ends of the movie and I’ve never felt that way with another movie before. The hidden meanings, subtle themes and a raging philosophy of what life actually means, represented by two very opposing personas is just so beautiful. I also adore the unstable narration where follow the Narrators perspective throughout the movie so we don’t seem to question whether the things that are happening should be happening. However during the final act, where the big plot twist is dropped on us, the rest of the movie, the narration shifts in a way where we view his actions from a third party perspective and there we realise how mentally ill the narrator actually is. On the second watch, expecting the plot twist, I was able to see so much more and the subtle clues that they hinted throughout the movie. Conversations and dialogues that involved the two main characters were SO much more fascinating to follow. Also, I find Tyler Durden to be just a piece of art and his ideology and perspective on certain things is truly fascinating, especially compared to the society we live in today. For example, he states that “ the things you own end up owning you ” and when I really sat down and thought about that, it was just so refreshing to see things like that in a completely different perspective. Another example was when he had tortured and threatened an innocent man, all so that the next day onwards, that innocent man will never try harder in his life to achieve his goals of becoming a veterinarian. All in all, Fight club somehow gets better on the second watch, David Fincher IS the goat and @danyaalkhalid just doesn’t understand peak yet but maybe 1 day 😌

texto: ce film m’a vraiment fait réfléchir sur l’identité et sur cette envie de devenir quelqu’un qu’on pense être incapable d’être. le narrateur vivait presque comme une machine : une routine, un travail, des objets, et très peu d’émotions qu’il arrivait réellement à exprimer. puis Tyler apparaît comme tout ce qu’il n’osait pas être : libre, impulsif, en colère, sans peur des règles. mais au fond, Tyler n’est peut-être pas seulement une autre personne. il représente tout ce que le narrateur avait enfermé en lui. et c’est justement ce que j’ai trouvé intéressant dans la fin. quand il comprend enfin ce qui se passe, j’ai l’impression qu’il retrouve une partie de lui-même qu’il avait complètement perdue. pour la première fois, il ressent vraiment : la peur, la colère, l’amour, la douleur. même si tout ce qu’il a vécu était destructeur, il n’est plus cette personne vide et programmée qu’il était au début. j’ai beaucoup aimé cette idée que parfois, on peut tellement vouloir devenir quelqu’un d’autre qu’on finit par créer une version de nous-mêmes qui semble plus vivante que notre vraie vie. et puis cette fin… impossible de ne pas rester devant l’écran à essayer de tout remettre en place dans sa tête.

texto: I am entirely convinced that Jordan Peele's movies just aren't for me. First Nope, and now Get Out. Both times I got completely invested in the first half, only to be incredibly let down by where the story goes after the reveal. I won't get into spoilers, but everything that followed just felt unbelievably stupid to me. I still have Us left to watch, but I feel that I'm in no hurry anymore. I know these movies get praised for their satire, social commentary, and all the deeper themes, and yes, I get what they're going for. My problem is that none of that matters if the movie loses me as a story. In my opinion, Get Out fails as a horror movie, fails as a satire, and even fails at delivering its message in an interesting way. I genuinely don't understand the level of praise these movies get.

texto: Honestly, this film wasn't very enjoyable to watch; it wasn't the kind of film I wanted to finish quickly, eager to see what would happen next. The flow was a bit lacking. While watching, especially the dialogues in the final scenes kept me engaged, otherwise it was very boring, or maybe my expectations were too high based on social media. I was thinking, "Why didn't I like this film, which is so popular?", but then I did some research and when I read the full version of the story, I understood the system the film was criticizing much better, and my interest in the film increased. The first aspect criticized in the film is: The Commodification and Exploitation of the Black Body: The Armitage family auction scene is a modern representation of the historical slave trade. Black people's genetics, physical strength, agility, or artistic talents (like Chris's photography skills) are admired by whites; however, this admiration stems not from respect, but from a desire to steal and possess those qualities. The dark and desperate void into which Chris is hypnotized represents the suppression of Black individuals' voices in society, their loss of control even over their own bodies, and their marginalization and passivization by the system. Micro-Attacks and Alienation: The questions Chris encounters at the garden party (genetic advantages, athletic ability, etc.) are examples of the racist stereotypes disguised as praise that Black people are subjected to in daily life. The film shows that racism is not just about hate speech; consuming a culture, body, or talent for one's own benefit and ignoring its true owner is one of the most dangerous dimensions of racism. Honestly, the sarcastic questions directed at Chris felt good, but they could have filmed it differently, making it both more enjoyable and engaging to watch, while also conveying the message effectively as it is. It's a good film, just a little boring.

texto: Lots of stuff that works and lots of stuff that doesn’t. Nice social commentary, some really sharp symbolism, and creative metaphors. Some scenes use tension really well, along with some inspired cinematography. But the tonal mess that this movie is can sometimes be simply too much. None of the comedic scenes worked for me, not even a little bit. I would cut out the TSA guy entirely. I don’t believe comedic relief is really necessary in horror movies (especially when it lacks comedy), but most importantly, the job of comedic relief is to relieve tension. Why the hell would you want to relieve tension in a horror film? It seems as though Peele’s background in comedy is hindering his potential as a serious horror director. To clarify, I don’t think you can’t mix genres; I don’t believe in limitations in art. But here, the genre-breaking doesn’t seem to serve any purpose other than wasting my time. Aside from all that, the movie was also uneven in a plethora of ways: some scenes are brilliantly written and directed (helped a lot by some exceptional performances), while others are laughably cliché and interfere with the movie’s strengths. I think a great screenplay is hidden in here but is in dire need of a rewrite. As for Mr. Peele, I can see his obvious talent and potential, and I’m interested to see whether he manages to live up to it in his later projects, which I’m intending to watch.

texto: Extremamente desconfortável Corra! foi um filme que me marcou bastante, principalmente pela forma como aborda o racismo de um jeito tão desconfortável e assustador. Não é apenas sobre o preconceito mais explícito, mas também sobre aquele racismo disfarçado de elogios, educação e falsa aceitação. Assistir ao filme tendo um namorado negro fez a experiência ser ainda mais difícil para mim,me doeu muito ver certas situações e pensar que, infelizmente, algumas formas de preconceito mostradas no filme existem na vida real. Em vários momentos fiquei incomodada e angustiada, justamente porque não consegui assistir apenas como uma história de terror: algumas situações me fizeram pensar em pessoas que amo e nas experiências que elas podem enfrentar. Acho que esse é um dos maiores méritos de Corra!,ele consegue causar medo não só pelo suspense, mas pelo que representa fora da ficção. É um filme que incomoda, faz pensar e mostra como o racismo pode ser muito mais profundo e cruel do que parece. GET OUT..now Absolut cinema!!!!⭐️⭐️⭐️

texto: Jordan Peele isn’t all misses at least. One thing that’s rarely weak in a Jordan Peele movie is the acting, and this movie is no exception. Allison Williams Absolutely kills it with the unsettling vibes and switch towards the end of the movie, outstanding work. Same goes for Daniel Kaluuya who bring easily my favorite performance of his career specially with his eyes truly disappearing into the terror and unforgettableness of the situation. Also like most Jordan Peele work it’s very well shot, very pleasant to look at in terms of quality and color and the score is perfection. The reason this movie hit for me though is cause the story was actually captivating and believable and the characters all take actions that make total sense. Chris isn’t just gonna sit there and be freaked out he actively is on alert the whole time even before visiting the house and he keeps a keen eye on everything, plus he fights his own way out of the situation in an extremely believable way without having to rely on any conveniences. Ro  being worried about him and finding a way to get to him also made total sense, and the cops not believing him yet him still pressing forward was great. Part of me did worry at the end that they were gonna pull a mega twist when Chris asked how he found him and reveal that Rob had the procedure or something but I’m glad they didn’t and just played it as a joke. The motivations also made total sense. These people are clearly racist but not in a way that is the overtly obvious kind that can get a bit much and can demean the core message, no they do view black people as superior in a way but more in the sense of jealousy and wanting what they have and viewing them simply as a vessel for themselves. Still inherently  very racist way of looking at things but done in a way at that I haven’t seen many stories tackle cause instead of the down your throat distracting kind, it more challenges the subtle ways we might think about or approach certain people in a way that clearly alienates them whether purposeful or accidental/negligent. Overall I was very pleased with this movie and now having completed the Peele trilogy I’m at least happy I liked one of them.

Personally, I am a huge fan of Daniel Kaluuya’s emotional acting all throughout the film; he managed to perfectly capture grief, anger, and fear.

texto: Jordan Peele isn’t all misses at least. One thing that’s rarely weak in a Jordan Peele movie is the acting, and this movie is no exception. Allison Williams Absolutely kills it with the unsettling vibes and switch towards the end of the movie, outstanding work. Same goes for Daniel Kaluuya who bring easily my favorite performance of his career specially with his eyes truly disappearing into the terror and unforgettableness of the situation. Also like most Jordan Peele work it’s very well shot, very pleasant to look at in terms of quality and color and the score is perfection. The reason this movie hit for me though is cause the story was actually captivating and believable and the characters all take actions that make total sense. Chris isn’t just gonna sit there and be freaked out he actively is on alert the whole time even before visiting the house and he keeps a keen eye on everything, plus he fights his own way out of the situation in an extremely believable way without having to rely on any conveniences. Ro  being worried about him and finding a way to get to him also made total sense, and the cops not believing him yet him still pressing forward was great. Part of me did worry at the end that they were gonna pull a mega twist when Chris asked how he found him and reveal that Rob had the procedure or something but I’m glad they didn’t and just played it as a joke. The motivations also made total sense. These people are clearly racist but not in a way that is the overtly obvious kind that can get a bit much and can demean the core message, no they do view black people as superior in a way but more in the sense of jealousy and wanting what they have and viewing them simply as a vessel for themselves. Still inherently  very racist way of looking at things but done in a way at that I haven’t seen many stories tackle cause instead of the down your throat distracting kind, it more challenges the subtle ways we might think about or approach certain people in a way that clearly alienates them whether purposeful or accidental/negligent. Overall I was very pleased with this movie and now having completed the Peele trilogy I’m at least happy I liked one of them.

texto: Four thirty-something friends navigate love, marriage and personal growth while supporting each other through life's challenges. Unlike the previous films I've seen from this director, this film does have a sense of authenticity with characters, and chemistry, that feel genuine. However, the characters themselves are relatively uninteresting and the film fails to highlight anything meaningful about them. It often feels like a series of mundane small moments of their lives played out in real time--like a long workshop in trust exercises or an hour long reading of a dull book. As I'm generally not into slice of life type of stories, this may have been somewhat enjoyable had the characters been more layered or the film been more dynamic but as it is it's dull, lacks spark and is way too long for what little it has. texto: The biggest scam of recent years in french cinemas: to cut a 5 hours film in five parts over three (increasingly short) showings, under the guise of some nonsensical theme (the five senses, with some cardboards forcefully inserted into the film). Nevermind, this is a very delicate portrait of modern Japan, especially its women, without big artifice. Some stand out sequences: the beginning, the workshop scene, the reading scene. But after an overall disappointing last fifth stretching an already quite stretched movie, the pretend ending seems tacked on a chronicle that was made without one in mind. texto: I enjoyed this dialogue-driven flick in bursts and flashes -- more than I can say Hamaguchi's other big hit, Drive My Car -- whenever it really productively explored the ways we do or don't communicate with one another. I just wish it wasn't five-plus bloody hours. I know, I know: the entire movie is fundamentally about the ways we do or don't communicate, so my statement above can seem silly. The kick is that it does so with varying degrees of clarity or focus throughout its painful runtime, and I found myself rapt in those stretches where it really was tackling the concepts head-on. So yes, then this thing gets into the meaning of what it is to be in a relationship, and how we center ourselves while also supporting other people? Brilliant. I wasn't sold on its tactics at first, but the way Hamaguchi puts you through these trust exercises, seemingly without purpose, and then has a participant criticize the instructor with the same thoughts as I had, only to have the purpose hinted at a bit more firmly -- well, let's just say it helped crystallize the point of the film. It's not that I'm an idiot; I understand and appreciate some artistic metaphor and allusion. It's when people are staring in silence for five minutes, or moving into much less direct tangents that I find myself being pulled into areas of the film that work for me much less well, and that I think is where the majority of this thing spends its time. I don't need to be spoonfed, as I love when movies trust the viewer; but this also means the movie sometimes meeting me halfway. I value its quiet, austere, calm take, and that it's able to produce great tension in the most silent of conversations. I especially value the core concepts it's working with, and I was sucked into the movie when it really knuckled down. But as someone who cared a lot less for the meandering bits about infidelity, or gender roles in parenting, or career aspirations, I drifted in this thing a lot more than I'd like. In short, a bit too long and a bit too all-encompassing for the energy I was willing to put in. Still, an impressive beast, and one I'll be thinking about -- in pieces, at least.

texto: Communication.  That was the main theme of this film.  While I liked the overall theme and plot points of this, I felt like there was a lot of filler that could have been cut out of it to make it a more tightly edited film.  After seeing Drive My Car a few months ago, I was interested to check out Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s work, as Drive My Car was a three hour long film, it didn’t feel that way.  I could definitely feel the running time on this as it felt like some of the conversations went on longer than they needed to.  Examples are: the communication exercise (which wouldn’t surprise me if it was an homage to Out 1 ) and the q&a also felt like it went on for too long. *Minor spoilers ahead* I did like the plot points revolving around the divorce court, underage pregnancy, and the dosing error that the nurse made, as it felt like all of these issues could have been prevented with better communication skills.  I also liked that the women began to question their respective relationships with both their significant others and with each other throughout the film. I still want to check out more of Ryusuke Hamaguchi as he seems to have his own style when making a film.  I personally feel that Drive My Car should be in the letterboxd top 250 over this.

texto: During the latter half of the expedition that is Happy Hour , there is a scene where a young author named Ms. Nose is criticized for having read her book to an audience in a monotone voice. She answers that since she knew the characters she wrote so well, and all of the emotions are on the page, no matter what vocal inflections she adds, the importance is found in the words. Happy Hour hinges on words and communication. For what's basically a five-hour-long monologue how could it not be about these things? The story follows four women who vocalize their anxieties to everyone except the people who these actual anxieties originate, mostly their husbands. The story becomes how communication gets lost in a marriage. Saying a couple of words as a husband and wife pass by each other around the breakfast table is not the kind of interaction that can sustain a marriage. Before long the important needs of these women go unaddressed and they realize they could do better. I like where Hamaguchi takes the story. In a very Bergman-esque fashion, he captures the female perspective with confidence. However, to draw on how Ms. Nose reads her book in a monotone way, the rest of the movie features the most unemotive acting I've ever seen. I believe this was done purposefully to show the true emptiness behind each woman's marriage. None of the cast are trained actors either for this reason. The scene I brought up basically literalizes the intent of emphasizing the dialogue. For my personal enjoyment of this film, I couldn't get compelled to care about any of these characters for the lack of them feeling like people I know or acting like actual people at all. A character would be told about how their partner wants a divorce and they would wear an awkward blank stare. Outside of the film's length showcasing an incremental decline of each character's relationship with their spouse, I did not see the need for a five-hour project. I would've settled for three. I think for anything dialogue-heavy, talented actors really go a long way to sell key emotional moments. A lot of the time I couldn't read what emotion a character was showing, rendering the point of the scene mute. Hamaguchi builds a believable world around its characters, but there was so much more to explore, things that were left unsaid, which makes me think that the five hour runtime could've been used more effectively.

texto: The story of four friends in Kobe and their disintegrating relationships amidst endless and varied attempts to communicate. Akari is divorced and outspoken, a strong nurse with an empathy deficit. Sakurako is a put-upon housewife with an ungenerous husband and a teenager (who in turn has a unexpectedly pregnant girlfriend). Fumi is a childless curator with a husband who's more a roommate than a romantic (or, at least, his romantic affections are directed elsewhere). And Jun is divorcing her spouse, a cold blooded scientist who hasn't harmed her but won't ever let her go, even if she has to fly into hiding with her unborn child. I've seen "Happy Hour" described as novelistic and that's true, but also a coded way of excusing its 317-minute run time. Just as much of a novel, however, the film reminds me of a workshop, and indeed two very long stretches of the movie are centered around performances of sorts at Fumi's arts space, PORTO (not to mention the extended, fractious discussions after both). Perhaps fitting as I understand that Ryusuke Hamaguchi developed the script through improvisational exercises with his non-professional actresses. Not entirely successful in its own right, as the dyads can feel a bit obvious and the pacing languorous, but I'm convinced that this work is a rehearsal for a compelling cinematic voice.

texto: An incredible cast, really making these characters feel real. Interesting ideas about love, when we need change in our lives. Unfortunately, this didn’t fully click with me on the same level as other Hamaguchi films I’ve seen. I just feel it was way too overlong for its own good, and the themes (while well done) were tackled even better (AND in half the runtime) in other films from him. The opening enticed me, but afterwards, I caught my attention starting to wander multiple times throughout (each time I would rewind to make sure I didn’t miss anything). It felt exceptionally raw and human, but was lacking the emotional punch I was looking for. Still, this further solidified to me that Hamaguchi is a one of a kind director in capturing the human condition. I wouldn’t recommend this to everyone I know like his other films, but by the end, I’m glad I checked this out. 6.5/10 Hamaguchi Ranked

texto: So, how do I represent the world, and not just myself? Happy Hour , more like Somber Five Hours . Hamaguchi, you madman. An over five hour movie that's more or less made up of conversation after conversation sounds like a death sentence for engagement. Instead, while I wasn't truly wowed by it like seemingly all of my mutuals on here were, I was at least impressed by it more often than not. It's conversational and almost scarily like watching genuine interactions between people that, despite how clearly so much effort is put into each exchange between its characters, the film with time starts to feel less like a narrative work and more like documentary. It's through these moments that the characters share, and what they talk about, that they are able to work through the woes of their lives. It is through talking that they will seemingly be taking a new path towards being better. Do I think Hamaguchi has portrayed that better in his other films at a much shorter length? Absolutely. I do also think that being able to make the ending to a film that's this long feel in some way cathartic, and it's not because you are in relief that it's finally over, that's still an achievement. I think also especially with intense family drama going on with myself currently, the moments reflecting on love and divorce had extra poignancy. I'll do my best to take from what Ryûsuke offers here and know that when darker feelings seem more fruitful, it's taking a breath and being able to communicate with others that's more valuable. 6/10

texto: The biggest scam of recent years in french cinemas: to cut a 5 hours film in five parts over three (increasingly short) showings, under the guise of some nonsensical theme (the five senses, with some cardboards forcefully inserted into the film). Nevermind, this is a very delicate portrait of modern Japan, especially its women, without big artifice. Some stand out sequences: the beginning, the workshop scene, the reading scene. But after an overall disappointing last fifth stretching an already quite stretched movie, the pretend ending seems tacked on a chronicle that was made without one in mind. Senses score: Part 1-2: 7/10, 3/5 Part 3-4: 7/10, 3/5 Part 5: 5/10, 2/5 Overall: Score: 6/10 Enjoyment: 2/5

texto: Communication.  That was the main theme of this film.  While I liked the overall theme and plot points of this, I felt like there was a lot of filler that could have been cut out of it to make it a more tightly edited film.  After seeing Drive My Car a few months ago, I was interested to check out Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s work, as Drive My Car was a three hour long film, it didn’t feel that way.  I could definitely feel the running time on this as it felt like some of the conversations went on longer than they needed to.  Examples are: the communication exercise (which wouldn’t surprise me if it was an homage to Out 1 ) and the q&a also felt like it went on for too long. *Minor spoilers ahead* I did like the plot points revolving around the divorce court, underage pregnancy, and the dosing error that the nurse made, as it felt like all of these issues could have been prevented with better communication skills.  I also liked that the women began to question their respective relationships with both their significant others and with each other throughout the film. I still want to check out more of Ryusuke Hamaguchi as he seems to have his own style when making a film.  I personally feel that Drive My Car should be in the letterboxd top 250 over this.

texto: A lot to like in Happy Hour but at over 5 hours in one sitting, I found it taxing on my attention span. It felt like it took a good two hours to even get going. The plot is quite compelling, a confrontation between Jun, Fumi, Akari, and Sakurako and the lives they have made for themselves. Most of the cast are non-actors from which Hamaguchi coaxes naturalistic performances. Especially given the long speeches the characters make, it’s impressive. But communication is the real key for these characters, and it’s the lack of communication between husbands and wives, parents and children, and dear friends which is the root of so much unhappiness. The film strips away structures and order, the detailed planners of the opening, to make room for the possibility of growth and fulfillment.

texto: Passei cinco horas do meu domingo imersa na vidinha de quatro amigas e que experiência confortante principalmente quando você não está com a menor vontade de viver a própria vida. O filme tem essa capacidade deliciosa de simplesmente deixar as coisas acontecerem, acompanhar o desenrolar espontâneo, coletivo e individual dessas mulheres, suas particularidades, relações, pequenos conflitos e a rotina, até que você sente que realmente passou aquele tempo convivendo com elas. E o melhor é como o melodrama vai surgindo aos poucos, em cada canto do filme. A amiga que está se divorciando da maneira mais dramática possível, a enfermeira despojada que quebra o pé, a mãe, esposa e dona de casa que passou a vida se reprimindo e a outra que assiste ao marido se apaixonar por outra sem poder fazer muita coisa. Tudo vai ganhando proporções cada vez mais dramáticas, mas sem que o filme abandone seu ritmo contemplativo. Narrativamente, ele trabalha muito com a duração, os silêncios e as conversas, deixando que os conflitos se desenvolvam organicamente das relações, em vez de conduzir a história por grandes viradas. É justamente essa estrutura paciente que faz tudo parecer tão espontâneo, quase como se estivéssemos apenas testemunhando pedaços da vida dessas mulheres. Cinco horas de filme que passam como cinco horas da vida de alguém. Filme lindo!

texto: - This is one of the movies I think about the most in my day to day life. It contains, I think, so much of the feeling(s) of being alive. - So effective and well paced and with such ridiculously great performances. And camerawork/editing (though they are so subtle)! - I was thinking about why its important that this is a 5 hour movie, and not, like, a 5 episode miniseries. Beyond the fact that its not paced in a way that would allow episodes, I think the length necessitates a unique kind of attention. In a similar way to what theater achieves with its literal presence in the room, when a movie is 4+ hours long, it compells you to enter a kind of lower frequency flow state where you just live in its world for a day. And I think that's awesome. 5 hour movies 4 life

texto: Happy Hour is a quiet marathon of raw emotions and subtle revelations. You sit with these women for over five hours and you get to know each of them in such depth that it compels you to reflect on your own life. The conversations linger, silences speak volumes, and relationships unravel so realistically, and yet the runtime sucks you in as opposed to feeling daunting or exhausting. The payoff is worth it as it feels like a portal into other people's lives, yet it shows how little we truly know about one another.

texto: Follows four female friends who are each at different crisis points in their relationships with their partners, each dealing with and understand them in different ways. I love how complex and deep each of these characters is and how we come to lean about each's perspective and ways of dealing with navigating life, relationships and themselves. Even the side characters feel like them contain multitudes, even the ones with limited screen time or ways of expressing themselves. It is good to have friends who are different, to have people to be vulnerable with, to communicate in ways you can't with others. There were many times when a character would express a unique and nuanced thought or idea about life that resonated with me. Watched as part of my 5 Directors X 5 Unseen Films: Part 5 Challenge. texto: The four main characters' lives form a parallel. If divorce is the mark that separates each character's own life, then Fumi and Sakurako are the before-divorce, Jun is the during-divorce, and Akari is the after-divorce. Neither Fumi and Sakurako legally divorced or even brought out divorce, yet they both experienced similar emotions and events that Jun and Akari went through that led to the end of their marriage. Between the last 1.25-1 hr, I was quite pissed to the fact that, so far, almost every character kept mingling in others' business, supported by what I understood as their sense of righteousness. It was only until later, after both Sakurako and Fumi couldn't stand their marriage anymore and fought back, that I realized they cared because they saw themselves in the couples they criticized. It's quite pessimistic that the writer of the movie decided for everyone to no longer stand their marriage. I don't have any data, nor am I familiar with Japanese culture or marriage life. So it could be a norm for most couple that, at some point, their love for each other diminishes infinitely to none, and all is left is the legal paper that binds them.

texto: This shift my views on women to even more realistic and humane dimensions. This movie might save my marriage with them in future and i realize relationship with them hold the same divinity that if left alone wither and may well ever be unrecoverable. Women who hold life together with their very thin threads of tenderness and softness is in fact breakable and this awareness of fragility beneath the strength of their sex is their superpower. The power that brings destruction and creation. Men have no choice but to surrender, yet as a man i understand that this surrender must come with balance and recognition and i wonder how women perceive the same balance from their prospective. Their perspective, for me, is the greatest mystery that shall forever be remaining insoluble. And this mystery compels me, almost forces me, to bring forward the love eternal.

To love is to lie sometimes. To love is to accept that you don't have to understand every desition that your friends make, but love them anyway. To love is to get angry on behalf of those who can't. To love, sometimes, it's just to be there.

texto: Follows four female friends who are each at different crisis points in their relationships with their partners, each dealing with and understand them in different ways. I love how complex and deep each of these characters is and how we come to lean about each's perspective and ways of dealing with navigating life, relationships and themselves. Even the side characters feel like them contain multitudes, even the ones with limited screen time or ways of expressing themselves. It is good to have friends who are different, to have people to be vulnerable with, to communicate in ways you can't with others. There were many times when a character would express a unique and nuanced thought or idea about life that resonated with me. Watched as part of my 5 Directors X 5 Unseen Films: Part 5 Challenge. texto: Clocking in at over five hours, Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Happy Hour (Happī Ā) is a quiet, monumental masterpiece of slow-cinema intimacy that feels less like watching a scripted movie and more like observing real lives unfold in unhurried, real time. Set in Kobe, the film follows a tight-knit circle of four women in their late 30s whose long-standing dynamics fracture when one of them suddenly reveals she is undergoing a messy divorce prompting the remaining three to re-examine their own stifled desires, marriages, and personal truths. What makes the film so uniquely captivating is Hamaguchi’s extraordinary process: developed through acting workshops with non-professional actors, the performances possess an astonishing, naturalistic grace (jointly earning all four lead actresses the Best Actress award at Locarno). Extended sequences like a fascinating body-listening workshop or a literary reading are allowed to breathe so fully that minor shifts in conversation carry the emotional impact of major plot twists. It’s an epic, exquisitely patient exploration of female friendship, emotional honesty, and the quiet compromises of adulthood.

texto: No one clocks the day you disappear. A facade- not even of happiness, just a numb sense of normalcy- masking the quiet agony of your soul dying its slow death. The quite simple attempt to touch the other. To feel the other. To explain the other to myself - is that futile? Is that love? It's not your place to say such things - you know nothing. Better the illusion, "knowing," leaving everything unsaid. I know already, a living hell awaits - but I'm okay with that. I know what makes me happy.

texto: Happy Hour is a quiet marathon of raw emotions and subtle revelations. You sit with these women for over five hours and you get to know each of them in such depth that it compels you to reflect on your own life. The conversations linger, silences speak volumes, and relationships unravel so realistically, and yet the runtime sucks you in as opposed to feeling daunting or exhausting. The payoff is worth it as it feels like a portal into other people's lives, yet it shows how little we truly know about one another.

texto: I ordered a region-free DVD player just so I could watch this intimate, five-hour-plus epic of domestic life from Ryusuke Hamaguchi, who’s quickly become one of my favorite working directors (and quite possibly my very favorite). Two discs, three viewing sessions, and one day of rumination later, I can say that Happy Hour is an essential part of Hamaguchi’s filmography, thoroughly imbued with the intelligence and humanity that mark his extraordinary recent work ( Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy , Drive My Car , Evil Does Not Exist ). I have a few hesitations about some recurring elements that, despite the massive runtime, feel less consequential than I’d like them to be (guy who runs the New Age workshop that we experience in full, I’m looking at you). But on the whole, I was happy to be immersed in a film that values the mundane but that, in its very form, departs so strikingly from ordinary moviegoing experience. A few areas of thought: * Loved how completely female friendship permeates the film, even through some long stretches in which Akari, Jun, Sakurako, and Fumi remain apart. I thought from time to time about Virginia Woolf’s The Waves , in which the friendship between six characters who meet as children and interact only intermittently as adults forms a vessel that gives life meaning, a structure of belonging that has no official sanction or force but remains a continuous source of identity. The slow pace of the film’s first two hours comes in part from how the women, preoccupied by and/or attempting to cover up unhappiness related to marriage, family life, and work, don’t communicate very openly with one another, but one senses how their bond might offer a framework for disruption or renewal. I found the middle hour, leading up to and immediately following the trip to the hot springs resort, most compelling for precisely this reason, as the women begin to prod each other—lovingly, but not always pleasantly—to speak beyond their learned inhibitions, to risk a more radical, unsettling kind of honesty with one another. * As for what the film has to say about gender, sex and sexuality, and Japan’s still conservative mores and laws around marriage and divorce: forceful stuff, appropriately stamped with the texture and complication of actual life. None of the heterosexual relationships in Happy Hour are satisfying in any way, and Jun’s refusal to submit herself to a marriage she’s come to experience as deadly—as she attests in court, he’s killed her by lack of conversation—acts as a catalyst for some of the other women to ask themselves questions about desire, need, and sacrifice that would otherwise remain encased in the “cotton wool” of the ordinary (I’m borrowing from Woolf again). Nevertheless, it’s not apparent that there are right or wrong choices for each of the women, merely that there are choices: whether one seeks a separation or a strategy for marital repair, one can do and say things beyond the routine and reassert a right to happiness, even when the path to happiness remains elusive. * On the related topic of expressivity: I understand that the stolid reserve of the women has a cultural element and that it makes key moments of breakdown or decisiveness all the more poignant. At times, though, the performances verge on illegibility, and in some of the more charged stretches of the last two hours, I couldn’t quite work out what the film was suggesting about self-possession under duress. It occurred to me that the restrained affect might be related to the film’s understanding of itself as a kind of literary text, too. The visiting writer who reads her short story aloud at the cultural institute where Fumi works is herself asked why she performs with so little emotion, and the answer is a fascinating one: she doesn’t want to pretend that she can inhabit all of her characters, and she thinks that a sort of presentational truth, one that simply delivers the words themselves, still carries all the requisite feeling. A version of this idea may apply to the film, too. In the relative absence of histrionics, perhaps we are better able to understand and internalize the accrued weight of what these women have carried in their lives, the unspectacular ways they have been subsumed into (but thankfully not consumed by) the everyday. * Lastly, about duration: yes, I do think this could be an hour or two shorter and it would work nearly as well. And yet, I think it’s important to say that this isn’t a miniseries in disguise. It’s a novelistic film, just as Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy is a filmic collection of short stories. Although I watched in installments, I felt the continuous logic of the film’s development, the way the friendship group’s warm, complex, fraught tangle shifted and reconstituted, and how it informed the dramas in the women’s individual lives. Though I found some parts of the film too languorous, a bit too repetitive or restrained, I also didn’t want to leave these characters in the end, with their understanding of themselves and the impact of some of their bolder, pattern-breaking choices still very much in progress. But that’s the truth in which I suspect Hamaguchi is most invested: whatever span of time one chooses for a story, markers like beginnings and endings are arbitrary impositions, creations dictated by narrative. Life doesn’t work that way, and neither does friendship. letterboxd.com/cinemapoodle/list/ryusuke-hamaguchi-ranked-so-far/
