texto: In The Cloud-Capped Star , director Ritwik Ghatak is interested in how larger social-economic backgrounds impact the daily personal lives and social intimacies of the average person. The life of the individual acts as the catalyst towards these large-scale industrial changes underlying society. The rapid motion of the train in one of the earliest sequences of the film, which travels in the direction of Neeta (the protagonist), mirrors the rapid advancements that industrialization (a catalyst from India’s newfound independence given the context this film was released in) act as a means of rapidly changing the dynamics of the characters’ lives (if only present in the background). The use of music and general sound design functions as an on-the-nose connection between how the characters feel, especially on the metaphorical or metaphysical level. Juxtaposing their personal familial struggles to that of the mythical lyrics of the songs creates the notion that musical numbers function in two contrasting, yet complimentary ways. On the one hand, they harm the overall sense of realism that the film exhibits, but at the same time also work to express the repressed emotional sentiments of the interpersonal relationships of the film's characters that could not otherwise be depicted without music. The aesthetic close-up shots are very prominent, especially in the melodrama which of course allows for the intrigue of personal depth and insight into the emotions of the characters in this film, especially in the scene where Neeta and her brother sing together. This reflects an earlier scene in which Neeta is asked if her and her brother will be singing together, prompting her to say that she gave it up. We later see in the scene where they sing together in the dark room that she is only able to sing in these moments of intimacy and overall personal time. The presence of her brother then, indicates a closeness that she only shares with him as opposed to the rest of her family. Melodrama also functions as a political critique as it focuses on these internal struggles of family that are exacerbated by the advent of rapid industrialization around them.  Melodrama seems to exist in these extreme opposites of who is good and who is bad, but there also exists the historical contradictions within the film. For instance, her father recognizes all the ways in which Neeta is being exploited, but is inevitably the one to kick her out.  This creates a contrast to her internal struggles and the context she exists in. In this way, the film also bears similarities to the Italian Neo-realism film movement, but also cranks the realism up to a heightened level that can only be found in melodrama. Given this understanding we can look back to the train and understand it as a creation with the propensity to bring about Sysiphian repercussions. The train may represent progress, but the fact that the people keep repeating or perpetuating their condition, whether it be asking for donation money or treating Neeta poorly demonstrates that progress must come from both the individuals and society.

texto: Beautiful cinematography, probably surpassing anything by Ray at this point. Ghatak really uses his compositions to their fullest potential, frequently with something going on the foreground, middleground, and background. Unfortunately, the story ended up being this typical endless suffering, female martyrdom that Indian cinema seemed to love so much. Genuinely don’t know what I am meant to come away with by the end. I’m sure there are cultural critiques embedded in this, but I think excessive suffering of one person is a very limiting premise that is used too much.

She is talked down to, belittled, insulted- even when they are being nice to her. This movie has a meditative pace, beautiful close ups, and a lot of good elements- unfortunately when all put together it felt lackluster. Not bad, but just nothing special.

texto: The Cloud-Capped Star is a Pakistani film about a timeless story where a woman lives in hell with a family that does not appreciate her. It is a tragedy and a depressive one at that. The production quality is somewhat low for coming out in the 60's, but it is a film that broke new ground for its film culture, so of course it needs some credit for that. Watching it today, it does not hold up fantastically, but perhaps in the right mood it becomes more watchable.

texto: Viewed for My Criterion Challenge 2021 Okay, I'm like really surprised that I didnt get more out of this; Considering how much I loved Subarnarekha I was really expecting to be blown away with his seminal work in the trilogy. The issue was I had a hard time getting invested in any of the characters beyond a surface level appreciation; I dont know if it's because of a certain avoidant trait of mine that's been surfacing lately or if the film just failed to personally resonate. The music contained within the film is as gorgeous as any other; Bengali is a splendid language to listen to, and the humor throughout this feature sets the tones oddly for strife and whimsical fare to be delivered through such songs. Regardless of how I may feel, this film definitely has a crisp finish to it, the film feels perfected to details, it's just the melodrama I failed to sink my teeth into.

texto: One of the great melodramas of dislocation and displacement. Neeta (Supriya Choudhury) is a young woman whose labour, patience and self-sacrifice form the only glue holding together a declassé Bengali family uprooted from East Bengal after Partition. But Ghatak continually expands her suffering beyond the private sphere. Rather than some naive victim, Neeta is at once a fully fleshed-out character, all the more believable in her pain for having the intelligence, wit and wherewithal to realise she is throwing her life away for people who don't deserve it, as well as a stand-in for countless other refugees of Partition. This is clear by the final shot, when the film suggests another young woman might be another Neeta. Melodrama as always with Ghatak thus becomes the vehicle through which a collective historical trauma can be emotionally expressed and reflected for the mass audience who have lived through it. But Ghatak also fractures melodrama conventions by adding a wide range of audiovisual influences and techniques: Bengali folk and devotional music, Tagore song, theatrical gesture, Soviet montage, expressionist lighting and camera angles, violently modernist sound (the famous cracks, whiplashes, and other non-diegetic noises on the soundtrack which seem almost to make the deep fissure of Bengal itself audible). Visually, trains, fences, lattices and makeshift structures cut across rivers, trees, hills and open landscapes, setting arbitrary man-made lines against images of organic rootedness and a lost homeland --- the latter having been divided by the former through Partition. When I first watched, Neeta's famous cry reminded me a bit of that ending in Tsai Ming-liang's Vive L'Amour, another moment of raw emotion which, taken out of context, might seem too much, but which through the accumulation of the film up to that point builds up into a devastating and universal expression of existential anguish. Now, on second viewing it feels so clear Neeta is carrying something more, the weight of the history of an entire people and nation.

texto: Everything about this movie is great. But if I had to single out what struck me the most, it would be the cinematic composition. Ritwik Ghatak makes use of a wide array of techniques, and each one serves to frame the scene in a meaningful way regarding the drama that is unfolding, the psychological state of a character, a mood… I found especially beautiful the wide-angle shots of landscapes and nature. There is one that happens more than once where two characters are sitting next to a river. They are filmed from the road and every now and then someone passes and stops to look at them. This switches the couple to the middle ground, and the observer becomes the foreground of the image. Then, suddenly, a train crosses the very background adding even more depth of field; everything is in focus. And this is just one example, almost every shot is a painting in Meghe Dhaka Tara . There is a lot of interesting symbolism in the film too. The trains that, whilst in Anna Karenina bring modernity and freedom, in here break the tranquillity and peace of the natural scenery. An intellectual father who can only quote English poets while his good-for-nothing son sings Tagore. A sound design full of effects like buzzing, high pitched notes or the crack of whips interspaced with bewitching traditional music. In several instances Nita is filmed through window shutters and bars conveying oppression, there are also angles that frame the head as if choking the character… This is definitely a film to be studied and, with my poor knowledge of Indian history, particularly the partition times, I can barely scratch the surface. Ritwik Ghatak is a brilliant director who needs to be talked about much more in the west, I hope I can continue watching his filmography and learning from his cinema.

texto: De meeste melodrama's lijken de kijker te willen behagen door emoties en gebeurtenissen nadrukkelijk voor te stellen. Deze Indische klassieker doet dat niet per se, en lijkt vooral ons deelgenoot te willen maken van de belevingswereld van de compleet onzelfzuchtige Neeta, die haar hele gezin (inclusief volwassen broers en zus) tracht te onderhouden. Het drama verloopt onvoorspelbaar maar wel traditioneel. Het lot van de protagoniste doet ons wel iets maar de weigering om hier een echte tragedie van te maken doet voorspellen dat haar perikelen nooit echt onoverkomelijk zullen zijn. De zwart-wit fotografie is om van te snoepen.

texto: 67 Neo-realist melodrama? Yes sir. Ghatak seems to both empathise with, and indict his protagonist for choosing the passive option always. Curious to read and hear more about the interpretation and the allegories, if any. Thematically connected to Garm Hawa, of course also as both are looking at post-partition India’s impact on families, this one keeping it in the background. But both lead characters show a reluctance to put their well-being over the trust in the system that leads to their travails. Didn’t expect GH to have the more hopeful of the two endings. Gorgeous music throughout.

texto: I watched this without subtitles, which didn't seriously impede my understanding but was not ideal for understanding every single word. (Something interesting about a movie in a language you don't quite have mastery over is that the dialogue seems quieter because your brain has a harder time recognizing words and separating them from the ambient noise.) What it did do, though, is prime me to pay especially close attention to the language. To varying extents, all the men in the movie mix English words into their Bengali, while the women do not except when explicitly echoing a man. The foreign viewer is inclined to think of English as the language of modernity and advancement and the native language as connected to the traditional past, but the associations are different here: English is the language of dreamers and intellectuals, of would-be gentlemen putting on airs and of second-class degrees in pure physics that lead to nothing, while Bengali is the language of people who have to work for a living. The one scene set in an anglophone environment is the one scene completely removed from the material concerns of life in Calcutta. The classic stereotype of the Bengali is as an ineffectual intellectual. This archetype is most obviously represented here by the invalid father who sits and quotes Wordsworth while his education does nothing to provide for his family. It's tempting to take this story of a family fallen on hard times as a metaphor for the decline of Bengal from the richest province in India to its present state, a process that would have already been evident in 1960.

texto: Did anyone show this to John Green yet? Lol. A good-ish movie but I felt the director's ideology was telegraphed throughout. The Sanat character was written to show the kind of men Ghatak hated --- ones who prefer physical appearance and give up on their quest of knowledge to become a capitalist bootlicker. The end was better than expected though. I preferred Subarnarekha to this. Exceptional acting by people playing Neeta and Shankar. Their father's character felt a bit caricaturish though, except that one dialogue where he says the way that the society exploits women has changed. Although a lot of the things portrayed in the movie seemed close to reality --- poverty, unemployment, the pressure on a sole breadwinner and men making decisions with pee pee --- I really did not find them convincing enough. As a Bengali used to the language from the western side of the border, it was a bit difficult to grasp at first. Kudos on not going with the sanitised language of Kolkata. He also brings in literature to drive home the point very well. Other than that, the music, the atmosphere of post-partition Bengal and the concept of a female lead (can I say titular character?) in the 1950s was very well done. I agree that Bengal is yet to recover from the horrors of partition and now the BJP government. I wish I liked it more.

texto: Ritwik Ghatak’s Indian cinema The Cloud-Capped Star (Meghe Dhaka Tara) delivers a harrowing portrait of displacement and human greed through the tragic unraveling of Nita, a self-sacrificing young woman supporting her refugee family in post-partition Bengal. Set against the backdrop of a fractured homeland where survival overrides morality, the film employs stark symbolism, such as Nita's fatal tuberculosis representing the parasitic consumption of her spirit by an ungrateful family, and a recurring whipping sound effect that echoes her emotional trauma. Ghatak masterfully contrasts the suffocating confines of the family's refugee tenement with the vast, indifferent majesty of nature, a motif that peaks in the film's most iconic scenes. From the ominous opening setup featuring Pandit Ravi Shankar’s piercing sitar score to the heartbreaking moment Nita is quietly abandoned by her fiancé Sanat for her own sister, the narrative builds toward one of cinema's most devastating climaxes. On a hillside facing the open horizon, Nita lets out a final, agonizing cry, "Brother, I want to live!", cementing her status as the ultimate emotional and financial anchor destroyed by the very people she sought to save.

texto: Samuel L Jackson and Walton Goggins deliver great performances, the scope cinematography is excellent and Ennio Morricone’s music from The Thing and others is used to great effect. But I didn’t like this any more than the last time I saw it, which was in the cinema on release. It doesn’t hold together like other Tarantino movies for me, and the stylistic choices (particularly the director’s deliberately intrusive voiceover after the intermission) often come across as smug rather than clever. The worst thing is the way it wears its misogyny on its sleeve, not helped by the presence of the Weinstein name and logo all over the credits. It’s inspired by classic westerns of the 60s and 70s that have clearly racist and misogynistic moments… but those films were made over 50 years ago. This is from 2015 (although that’s a lifetime away in some respects). The use of slur words is extreme, even for Tarantino, and the final scene so grotesque that it overshadows anything good that came before. I don’t know anymore if it’s okay to admire the craft of a film if you find so much of the content repulsive.

texto: Le risque de développer un style de mise en scène est à la longue de s'enfermer dedans et d'en être prisonnier. Peut être que certains esprits plus fermés et ayant une très grande confiance en eux sont moins propices à la remise en question et aux changements propres à la curiosité, ce qui en découle une certaine stagnation quel que soit ce que l'on fait. Ça fait 30 ans que Tarantino répète les mêmes schémas qu'ils narratifs ou dans sa mise en scène. Déjà très marqués dès Pulp fiction, j'ai l'impression que l'on atteint le plus haut dans Kill Bill. Depuis j'ai cette sensation de plus en plus présente dès Inglorious Bastard de revoir les mêmes mécaniques avec seul un décors en toile de fond qui changeait. Si dans ce dernier, cela passait encore, cette impression dérangeante s'est accentuée dans Jango. Ici avec Hateful Eight, cela en est presque une caricature de son propre style, tout devient trop un Déjà Vu et même les dialogues, souvent riches chez Tarantino sont un peu en deçà. Le film demeure agréable et sympathique mais je certaine lassitude l'emporte. Il a néanmoins rompu avec ce style avec Once upon a Time in Hollywood, ce que j'avais apprécié, même si il s'est rappelé à lui même dans les 15 dernieres minutes.

texto: QT’s There Will Be Blood, a violent, sadistic Western that amounts to something like an origin myth. It is easily his most alienating, least likable movie, and it competes with Django Unchained as his worst. It is baggy, self-indulgent, undisciplined filmmaking. You can sense the willful perversity behind it: It’s almost like a self-imposed challenge — how to make a 2-hour, 45-minute epic in the confines of a single location. (He fails his own challenge.) But despite my reservations, the go-for-broke, don’t-give-a-shit folly of it all earns respect, if not admiration. He knows exactly what he’s doing. I think he knows that there is not a single likable person here (see the title), that the violence is as over-the-top as it’s been in any of his movies, and that he’s pushing the limits of audience patience. He thinks his voice, his talent, his virtuosity, the power of his message, and his audience’s loyalty will carry him through. They don’t, not all the way at least.

texto: Tension boils in the shelter of a blizzard, a gaggle of mysterious western icons, two bounty hunters with contrasting ethics, many racists on varying degrees of the hatred spectrum, a suave British hangman with an iron grip on justice, all packed into one perfect thriller. As obtuse and aggressive as Tarantino can be, in spite of his repugnant attitude, he compensates his behaviour with the sublimeness of his character creations. The Hateful Eight is a later instalment of Quentin’s, and it shows with the challenging dynamic of this whodunnit style thriller. The Hateful Eight is like a heartfelt serenade of the entire western genre, every moment is smothered in history and every actor wears their character in the snug confines of this time period. The ensemble are the familiar faces of Tarantino’s career, with Jennifer Jason Leigh joining the ride in her fantastically devilish outlaw Daisy Domergue. The dialogue of this film is filled with fantastic nuances and character quirks, the film is very much a masterclass in characterisation, with every character introduction playing off unique and grandiose. For a near 3 hour film, The Hateful Eight wastes no time, plowing through the snow and the plot slowly bubbling up to a chemical explosion of Tarantino mayhem. It’s as if his films have a promise, to get as bloody as possible after a long, intense grind of cake cutting tension. This film is a flawless concept with so many intricacies to digest. Samuel L Jackson is as funny as ever, Walton Goggins even more so, Jennifer Jason Leigh displays all her talents, and Kurt Russell demands your attention every second. The final chapter of this film is one of the most joyous experiences I’ve ever had in the cinema. Everyone laughed and cringed at all the right moments. The final chapter is truly a spectacular piece of dark comedy that signs the movie out on a bleakly humorous and then rounds everything with a truly sweet palate cleanser of an ending. This movie is absolute perfection. It’s a modern classic with all the trimmings of a pure Tarantino quest, lead down a red stained path, all the way to a trigger happy stand off.

texto: This was my third to last Tarantino movie, and I was honestly surprised to still see him pulling out new tricks. It felt like Reservoir Dogs if I had dosed peyote before watching. The Hateful Eight was the complete opposite from the movie I was expecting, being the most cynical spaghetti western which revels in its simplicity and is a character piece through and through. I was pleased to find that, despite the runtime and despite the minimalistic approach, I was never bored. This is one of, if not Tarantino’s funniest movie, with some of his best dialogue. It has a really strong cast in general, but the three that shone the most for me was the master manipulator Major Warren, the oblivious Sheriff Mannix, and the feral opportunist Daisy Domergue. The catalyst of the conflict being a pot of coffee that sends a chain reaction of madness and killing is true Tarantino fashion. If I had to pull away one complaint, it would be that it’s a little too straightforward for its own good. While Reservoir Dogs actively had me pulling my hair out trying to connect the dots, here there was a mix of scenes I found predictable, and scenes that threw me for a loop. But then again, maybe that’s the point. Either way I found more enjoyment in the whacky characters and slapstick brutality than the whodunnit aspect.

texto: How can a film with this much acting talent be so poor? Alexander Skarsgard is in the lead, supported by Nicole Kidman, Ethan Hawke, Anya Taylor-Joy, Willem Defoe and Bjork yet parts of this film are pretty dreadful. It has one drawn-out plot (son seeks vengeance on uncle who killed his father and robbed him of his inheritance). There is no attempt at subtlety, no hint of sub plot and far, far too much semi-fantastical communing with the spirits. Skarsgard acts as if he’s been told to walk around like a grunting Neanderthal, arms splayed like a gorilla and while the action is lively and the setting probably as close to ninth century viking life as possible, the script is dire, the direction stolid and many of the performances lifeless. Alexander Skarsgard is in the lead, supported by Nicole Kidman, Ethan Hawke, Anya Taylor-Joy, Willem Defoe and Bjork yet parts of this film are pretty dreadful. It has one drawn-out plot (son seeks vengeance on uncle who killed his father and robbed him of his inheritance). Skarsgard acts as if he’s been told to walk around like a grunting Neanderthal, arms splayed like a gorilla and while the action is lively and the setting probably as close to ninth century viking life as possible, the script is dire, the direction stolid and many of the performances lifeless. texto: I'm starting to think that the people who praise Eggers for historical accuracy are the same kind of people who think that photos are better than paintings because they "capture" the "reality" more precisely; that is to say: there is some perceived virtue in "depicting" the "past" as "accurately" as possible. I am sorry for all the quotation marks, but that's the quickest way to underline that all these ideas are... kind of dumb. I honestly don't care whether Eggers' movies are accurate and well-researched or not. It does not matter. There is so little intention behind the images on the screen that I can't bring myself to care about them. Also, the mask of "historical accuracy" kind of absolves the director of responsibility for any artistic decisions he makes; because, you see, that's how things were back then: violent, grey, boring, miserable. He's just showing things as true as possible! The weirdest part about the whole Eggers oeuvre for me is that I don't believe that he has any real interest or love for the eras he's depicting. It is paradoxical; he has built a reputation as this geek who is obsessed with the past, and yet it feels like they are just different Instagram filters for him. Puritanical 17th century New England? 19th century Germany? 10th century Scandinavia? Somehow, Eggers manages to make all of these look and feel the same. Ugh. We should all go read some Icelandic sagas (which are really fun and colourful and even humorous at times, by the way) instead of watching this.

texto: More Art, with Less Splatter! So kann man, sich des Hamlets bedienend, diesen ebenfalls sich des Hamlets bedienenden Film wohl trefflich kommentieren, denn was Robert Eggers mit The Northman (2022) abliefert, ist im Grunde ein „Hamlet Light“, auch wenn es an schwergewichtigem Eisen und Blut keinesfalls mangelt. Wieder einmal gelingt es dem Regisseur, das Auge zu überwältigen, indem er die Kamera zahllose Bilder von dunkelumwölktem Unheil, nackter Brutalität, ungezähmter Kraft, aber auch betörender Schönheit zeichnen läßt, und auch sein Amlet könnte ein düsterer tragischer Held sein, denn er läßt sich unaufhaltsam von seinem Haß leiten, dem er Schuldige wie Unschuldige zum Opfer bringt. Ich sage hier bewußt: „Er könnte ein tragischer Held sein.“ In Wirklichkeit ist er es aber nicht, denn die Brutalität und Entschlossenheit, die er an den Tag legt, hat er mit allen Menschen, die um ihn herum leben, gemein, und mithin ist er eine gnadenlose Bestie unter vielen, und diese Gnadenlosigkeit ist es, die den Film letztendlich trotz all der Action, der Ausflüge in das Mystische und Übernatürliche, recht schnell langweilig werden läßt, gibt es doch nur einen einzigen Moment, in dem wir Amlet während eines inneren Kampfes erleben, nämlich dann, wenn er sich entscheiden muß, seinen Rachefeldzug abzubrechen, um mit der schwangeren Olga einer glücklicheren Zukunft entgegenzugehen, oder aber zurückzukehren, um seinen Onkel für sein Verbrechen zu töten. Dieser sehr kurze Moment wird jedoch schnell entschieden, wenn Amlet sich einredet, daß es für ihn und seine ungeborenen Kinder keine Ruhe geben würde, solange der Onkel noch lebt. Ungeachtet dessen, daß kaum ein Mann, der bei Trost ist und der mit Anya Taylor-Joy in einem Boot sitzt, ins Wasser springen würde, um jemanden anderen umzubringen, ist selbst dieser Augenblick einer, in dem Amlet keine eigene Entscheidung treffen muß. Schauen wir aber auf Shakespeares Hamlet, so sieht das schon anders aus: Eggers erzählt die Geschichte streng chronologisch und läßt den jungen Prinzen dabei auch zum Zeugen des Mords an seinem Vater werden. Mit eigenen Augen sieht er, daß sein Onkel die Meuchler anführt und danach den Befehl erteilt, den eigenen Neffen zu töten. Es gibt mithin keinen Zweifel daran, daß der Bastard-Bruder schuldig ist. Bei Shakespeare hingegen erhält Hamlet die Kunde, daß sein Vater keines natürlichen Todes gestorben, sondern ermordet worden sei, von einem Geist, der behauptet, der Geist seines Vaters zu sein, und ihm das Gelöbnis der Rache abnimmt. Im folgenden verwickelt sich Hamlet immer fester in ein Gewirr aus Zweifeln, denn er muß sich fragen, ob er tatsächlich dem Geist seines Vaters gegenüberstand oder einem bösen Geist, der ihn zu einem Mord verleiten will. Während Eggers‘ Amlet über weite Strecken des Filmes der Meinung ist, daß seine Mutter nur unter Zwang die Gattin des Onkels geworden ist, sieht Shakespeares Hamlet Gertrude freiwillig als Königin an der Seite des Claudius sitzen und sich so, nach dem 3. Buch Mose, des Inzests schuldig machen. Die solchermaßen komplizierte Situation läßt immer mehr den Zweifel an Hamlet nagen, der sich in einer aus den Fugen geratenen Welt wähnt, die er wieder ins Lot bringen muß, und diese Komplexität, sowohl die der Situation als auch die im Innenleben des Protagonisten, sucht man in Eggers‘ Verfilmung vergeblich. Selbst Amlets Liebesbeziehung zu Olga folgt dabei den 08/15-Regeln des Hollywood-Kinos, während der wahrhaft tragische Hamlet seine Ophelia, an der er auch zu zweifeln beginnt, mit seinem Verhalten zugrunde richtet. In The Northman mögen zwar die Landschaft und das Meer sehr oft nebelverhangen sein, aber eigentlich ist alles klar wie Kloßbrühe – und somit entsprechend langweilig und muß durch Sidequests wie den um das magische Schwert aufgepfeffert werden. Inszenatorisch und handlungsbezogen läßt sich The Northman mühelos in die Nähe von Wolfgang Petersons Hohl-Epos Troy (2004) rücken und ist für mich somit der, hoffentlich nicht nur bislang, schlechteste Film von Robert Eggers.

texto: If you asked me for my favorite revenge story, I'd have to give it to Berserk. I consider that manga to be a fantastic achievement and a shining example of what a revenge story could be. Berserk is a story that invites you to grow close to it's characters, to understand their desires, and to understand what they have to lose and what loss would mean to them. Upon the moment of betrayal, that seething hatred was something I felt on a visceral level. I was upset alongside the characters, and I was desperate (and still am) to see revenge take form. Comparing Berserk to The Northman is admittedly unfair. Comics, as a medium, can be much longer than movies. We're able to spend so much more time with the characters, and we're given a more intimate understanding of who they are. But what can I really say? I was ultimately disappointed with how little The Northman urged me to care about it's protagonist. It's a fairly familiar revenge plot (reminiscent of Hamlet) along the lines of "you killed my loved one; now I'll kill you". Protagonist vows to kill the man who "made his life hel", but you never get an understanding of what that misery looks or feels like to him. He is stoic, hyper-serious, and emotionally distant from the audience. None of this was aided by some non-sequitur side-questy sequences that were largely uninteresting. Don't get me wrong, the visuals are great. If all you want is brutality, it's in there. It's got a vibe of raw, primal hyper-masculinity through the filter of a psychedelic haze. It's actually pretty neat. Unfortunately the story is too unfocused and detached. Definitely my least favorite from Eggers. Pretty sure Willem Dafoe's character hangs dong, though, and that's cool.

texto: “I will avenge you, Father. I will save you, Mother. I will kill you, Fjoolnir’” Simple enough, from a plot standpoint at least. So then let’s drown it all in stylish atmospherics and unnecessarily heavy portent. Eggers’ penchant for period specificity is turned up to the max here. The budget is obvious, the production design sublime. Where it loses me is the unending discussions about faith and destiny. We’ve seen all this before, there’s no need to lay it on so thick. The boilerplate Bollywood revenge plot is hackneyed, everything involving Olga cumbersome, when all it really needed to do was shove a 90min display of the brutal savagery of revenge down our gaping throats. Speaking of gaping: Alexander Skarsgard.

texto: First act of the film introduced me to this testosterone driven culture of warriors (son and father running as a pack. Let’s fart and burp with daddy).  Ethan Hawke and Willem Dafoe set the stage for a young boy's story of revenge.  Except everything after feels so drawn out and eventually moot. Why, because we’re given the truth behind Amleth's vengeance.  We're told of the horrors his father committed, the freedom his mother was afforded from his death and still Amleth continues his rage.  It sucks the air out of his hero's journey and reframes his rage as childlike ignorance. Which to an extent is fine. We’ve seen stories of children continuing cycles of anger started from their forefathers. It just kind of made his mother and uncle a bit more sympathetic than I expected. A beautiful film, nonetheless.  Anya Taylor-Joy playing a witch in this film was a tongue-in-cheek nod to her previous work with Eggers. While I grasped the message of our fates predestined (nature v nurture), I had hoped Amleth would’ve broken that cycle on that boat. He doesn’t and instead gives us a sick battle below a volcano. Sick visuals! Not my favorite film entry from Eggers, but he gave me a vengeful Nicole Kidman. I take what I can get.

texto: 《北方人》由《女巫》、《燈塔》的導演羅柏·艾格斯所執導，並與冰島小說家松共同編劇。 故事講述一名年幼的維京王子阿姆雷特，因父王遭叔叔謀殺而立誓要為父報仇。離鄉多年後的阿姆雷特將展開他的復仇之路，同時也要拯救被擄走的母親… 雖然《北方人》的故事架構就是經典的「王子復仇記」，但本片那種極為冷冽的色調、景觀以及充滿視覺張力的場面，都讓這充滿泥濘、鐵與血的世界更加鮮活，另外本片也融入了許多北歐信仰、巫術、宿命論等要素，讓這趟復仇之旅有了更悲壯、更浪漫的史詩感！

texto: I am REALLY glad this did not turn out to be your average everyday viking oonga boonga brainless sword and shield clanging action movie, but rather a fated - prophecy foretold Gods supported revenge story of a royal blood that lived his life as a ghost. Dont get me wrong, it still has plenty of the previous things that I mentioned, but the film plays its cards really well, this is actually one of the better viking movies. Alexander Skarsgård as Amleth is amazing, dude built like a tank and because of it it takes me a while to actually find a decent review that doesn't just drool over his physique, but meh the other side just drools over Anya Taylor-Joy so I guess everything is balanced as it should be. They both put on a really great performance anyway. There are a good few brutal and action packed scenes, but it also had some awfully slow ones with barely anything happening and I feel like the two did not make up for each other:( Overall worked for me tho, not a 10/10, but not an average viking slop.

texto: Even after giving this another watch, while I do still like it overall, I would still consider this to be my least favorite of the four main SpongeBob movies. And I say that because, as a longtime fan of SpongeBob, it is noticeable that the story does reuse some elements from the previous films (such as SpongeBob wanting to prove that he's not just a kid, which was part of the first film's story, the climax happening on the surface like in the second film, and characters going after SpongeBob to save him, like in the third film). Additionally, the story can be a little predictable at times, since we know that SpongeBob is being tricked by the Flying Dutchman before he reveals it to him. And lastly, like I said in my first first review of this film, the film also repeats the main flaw the first film has, which is sidelining some of the main characters of the show and only focusing on a small number of them. But even with those, there are still things to like about the film. The animation is great, the voice actors give great performances, the fight scenes are good, it has a good amount of funny moments, and it is in general a good movie to watch overall. So even if I'd still say that this is one of the weaker SpongeBob movies, I still like it overall and would say it's worth watching.

texto: Ini film SpongeBob bioskop ke-4. Judulnya langsung to the point: SpongeBob mau buktiin dia udah "big guy" dan gak dianggap anak kecil lagi. SpongeBob pengen naik roller coaster "Shipwreck" tapi ketinggian belum cukup. Mr. Krabs cerita dulu dia bajak laut bareng Flying Dutchman. SpongeBob kegeeran, tiup terompet terkutuk, dan ke-summon lah Flying Dutchman versi Mark Hamill. Dutchman bilang: "Mau jadi swashbuckler beneran? Ikut aku ke Underworld, selesaikan tes kedewasaan." SpongeBob + Patrick pun masuk ke dunia monster, siren bergigi tajam, squid raksasa, dan benteng ala video game bernama Challenge Cove. Di sana tujuannya bukan cuma selamat, tapi buktiin kalau dia udah dewasa. Sementara itu Krabs, Squidward, dan Gary nyusul nyelametin dia dari Underworld. 1. Kembali ke silliness klasik Setelah beberapa film spin-off streaming, ini kerasa "SpongeBob banget" lagi. Humor slapstick, pun konyol, dan muka SpongeBob yang dibikin desperation pas kedip doang udah bisa ketawa. Rata-rata 1 joke pantat tiap 5 menit. Dumb, tapi niat. 2. Visual & dunia Underworld Animasi 3D CG nya colorful dan "squishy, gross" kayak series awal. Underworld nya kayak taman hiburan gila: campuran Odyssey, Jurassic Park, dan episode SpongeBob lama. Buat anak kecil ini pesta mata. Buat orang dewasa ini "light dip into an acid trip". 3. Pesan simpel tapi kena Di balik kekacauan, film ini ngomongin nerima diri sendiri: kelemahan kamu bisa jadi kekuatan di situasi yang tepat. Dan "keberanian itu soal hati, bukan tinggi badan". Gak berat, tapi pas buat target anak-anak. 4. Mark Hamill sebagai Flying Dutchman Dia beneran main karakter, bukan cuma cameo "eh liat nih aktor terkenal". Vibes bajak laut hantunya nambah epic ke petualangan ini. Kelemahannya 1. Gak ada yang baru Ini "just a SpongeBob movie". Strukturnya: SpongeBob kena masalah > masuk tempat aneh > belajar pelajaran > pulang. Kalau kamu cari plot twist, gak ada. 2. Terlalu overstimulating buat sebagian orang Enerjinya nonstop. Beberapa kritikus ngerasa lingkungan n worldbuildingnya "sparseness" dibanding film CG lain Thun lalu. texto: Ini film SpongeBob bioskop ke-4. Judulnya langsung to the point: SpongeBob mau buktiin dia udah "big guy" dan gak dianggap anak kecil lagi. SpongeBob pengen naik roller coaster "Shipwreck" tapi ketinggian belum cukup. Mr. Krabs cerita dulu dia bajak laut bareng Flying Dutchman. SpongeBob kegeeran, tiup terompet terkutuk, dan ke-summon lah Flying Dutchman versi Mark Hamill. Dutchman bilang: "Mau jadi swashbuckler beneran? Ikut aku ke Underworld, selesaikan tes kedewasaan." SpongeBob + Patrick pun masuk ke dunia monster, siren bergigi tajam, squid raksasa, dan benteng ala video game bernama Challenge Cove. Di sana tujuannya bukan cuma selamat, tapi buktiin kalau dia udah dewasa. Sementara itu Krabs, Squidward, dan Gary nyusul nyelametin dia dari Underworld. 1. Kembali ke silliness klasik Setelah beberapa film spin-off streaming, ini kerasa "SpongeBob banget" lagi. Humor slapstick, pun konyol, dan muka SpongeBob yang dibikin desperation pas kedip doang udah bisa ketawa. Rata-rata 1 joke pantat tiap 5 menit. Dumb, tapi niat. 2. Visual & dunia Underworld Animasi 3D CG nya colorful dan "squishy, gross" kayak series awal. Underworld nya kayak taman hiburan gila: campuran Odyssey, Jurassic Park, dan episode SpongeBob lama. Buat anak kecil ini pesta mata. Buat orang dewasa ini "light dip into an acid trip". 3. Pesan simpel tapi kena Di balik kekacauan, film ini ngomongin nerima diri sendiri: kelemahan kamu bisa jadi kekuatan di situasi yang tepat. Dan "keberanian itu soal hati, bukan tinggi badan". Gak berat, tapi pas buat target anak-anak. 4. Mark Hamill sebagai Flying Dutchman Dia beneran main karakter, bukan cuma cameo "eh liat nih aktor terkenal". Vibes bajak laut hantunya nambah epic ke petualangan ini. Kelemahannya 1. Gak ada yang baru Ini "just a SpongeBob movie". Strukturnya: SpongeBob kena masalah > masuk tempat aneh > belajar pelajaran > pulang. Kalau kamu cari plot twist, gak ada. 2. Terlalu overstimulating buat sebagian orang Enerjinya nonstop. Beberapa kritikus ngerasa lingkungan n worldbuildingnya "sparseness" dibanding film CG lain Thun lalu. This movie’s not as great as the first one (or even the second one - which I’m not even that keen on) but it’s still a fun ride. Don’t really have any problems with it, I kinda wish the animation was 2D but the CGI is still pretty good and cartoony, not really theatrical quality but there were plenty of funny faces and visual gags. Plus I don’t think any of the jokes sucked. The voice acting is definitely the star of the show here and Mark Hamill does a pretty good job as the Flying Dutchman, on par with the original voice actor IMO! Overall I probably wouldn’t rewatch it on my own volition (only with family or friends) but it’s a fun film. Unabashedly for kids but the whole family can enjoy it too!

texto: Random Movie #3 As a fan of Spongebob Square pants TV show.  I was wondering how this would be.  I definitely am too old to say I watched Spongebob as a kid, but I did watch it a bit when in college, and honestly never really had a bad thing to say about it.  Ok Sometimes he's annoying and I'm sure if people quoted him to me over and over I could learn to hate it, but overall not a bad show. Admitedly I haven't seen many of the movies, or much after my college years, but coming back to it... I enjoyed myself on this one.  Going to 3d Animation might upset some people, but it felt like a 2 hour "episode" and I don't meant that the way I might on many shows.  many shows stretch out an episode or slap 4 together to make a movie.  Here this definitely felt like a 2 hour episode but with the same humor and clever writing of the show. I will say I didn't laugh out loud but I got a couple chuckles and enjoy the jokes.  Nothing that bad, and if someone liked the show, they could do a lot worse watching this. On the other hand if someone doesn't like the show, or never seen it.  Easy pass.

Overall the movie is very inoffensive in terms of everything and even enjoyable for some parts, a good watch if you just wanna relax and have a good time.

texto: If I had a nickel for every time Derek Drymon directed a fourth installment of a movie franchise known for zany and wacky shenanigans of colorful characters that had scripts that took some story elements from the first installments, I would have two nickels! Which isn't a lot, but it's weird that it happened twice, right? I, like a grand majority of people, have had this childlike, whimsical, hilarious, optimistic, loving, and hardworking sponge as a major part of my childhood and have even implemented his way of going about the world into our daily lives. I have watched from the first seasons, all the way up to season 12, and have watched all of his movies up to this point. Sponge on the Run has its genuine moments but is severely lacking in other important areas. Sponge Out of Water was a blast and a half adventure, but the first movie is genuinely one of my favorites, and I don't believe anything could top its humor, animation, story, spectacle, and characterization of these characters we have come to love. I have noticed that every movie was helmed by someone heavily involved throughout the show and its run. The legendary creator, Stephen Hillenburg, for the first movie, the showrunner for the show when Hillenburg left after the first few seasons, Paul Tibbit for SOoW, and the co-developer of the show, Tim Hill, for SOTR. Now we have come to this movie, helmed by Derek Drymon, the creative director for the show in its earlier seasons. I was cautiously optimistic, as I liked Drymon’s direction in the things I've seen, but I was wondering how exactly funny it would be, how exactly the cast would be characterized, and whether the plot could carry a whole movie. They also really wanted to emphasize how this movie would bring back vibes of the first iconic seasons. So they intentionally were trying to raise expectations. How did I like it? I honestly had a blast, just as much as I had with Sponge Out of Water, if I am being totally honest. If I wasn’t laughing at how surprisingly funny and zany it could get with well-timed jokes and slapstick, I was always smiling from ear to ear. I even enjoyed the plot and the story, where the BOB wants to be seen as a BIG GUY and be respected as such by being brave, especially by Mr. Krabs, one of the biggest guys he knows, so he goes along with Patrick to help the Flying Dutchman to the Underworld to prove he is indeed a BIG GUY, who was surprisingly well-acted by Mark Hamill. Not only was the comedy on point for me, but also, I really enjoyed the relationships displayed in this movie, especially the father-son dynamic with Krabs and SpongeBob. Even has a nice enough message, though I do admit it is taking a lot from the first movie and is not as well executed as it was then. The animation, while not as detailed as SOTR, is stylised in a way where it is essentially how the show looks in 3D. While this is not a perfect movie, let alone a perfect SpongeBob movie, I still had a lot of fun and even felt as happy to see SpongeBob on the big screen through this movie as I was when I was a kid rewatching the first filam an the constant reruns of episodes. So in a sense, I do feel it somewhat captured the vibes of the early seasons, just a bit. Well done, Drymon!

texto: To be fair to this film, it fought a bit of an uphill battle since I just watched Fritz Lang's brilliant Destiny right before this, but I just gotta say I did not enjoy this at all. Maybe I actually just chose the wrong day to watch this because on the surface there's a lot about this film that I should love. The direction is pretty dynamic, camera movements are thoroughly planned out with some really impressive long takes, the performances are all good and the film is a classic European art house character drama. However, none of it really worked for me. The direction felt more showy than intentional most of the time. The performances were strong but I could barely tell the two male characters apart if I'm being honest. But this probably has more to do with the film's biggest weakness, which is of course its script. My god is it a drag to sit through endless scenes of these 4 boring-ass people doing mundane stuff for two hours. It all feels so inconsequential and weightless. Then there is of course the climactic moment at the titular swimming pool, which was the only genuinely pretty cool scene in the entire film, but I thought that meant the film would finally start to warp up but nope. We get to watch more paint dry for the rest of the runtime. I don't know what people see in this film. All I see in it is a failed attempt at creating one of these art house classics that were being made by the dozens at this time but this just felt fraudulent. Maybe I'll give it another shot at some point but I was really struggling to get through this.

texto: A classic of European cinema. Hugely influential as a long, languorous summer in the south of France takes a dramatic turn to the dark side when a friend arrives with his 18 year old daughter to upset the rhythms of Alain Delon and Romy Schneider. A film of it's time (1969 on the cusp of the 70's) with a film making style that hasn't aged well. Too many stilted 'conversations' and slow moving scenes and social mores that don't sit well with today's audiences. Still, it's got Alain Delon and Romy Schneider so it can be given some latitude. Still too long, though

texto: aka: La Piscine NS Alain Delon Romy Schneider Maurice Ronet Jane Birkin Paul Crauchet FRANCE Jean-Paul (Delon), a writer, and Marianne (Schneider), his girlfriend for just over two years, are holidaying at a friend's villa near Saint-Tropez. There is a tension in their relationship which excites Marianne: the film begins with a scene in which they are together beside the villa's swimming pool and she urges him to scratch her back. He does as she asks, but then throws her into the pool and jumps in after her. In a later scene he takes a branch and uses it to lash her bare buttocks, playfully but with a force that increases as the scene cuts away. Harry (Ronet), an old friend and record producer who was Marianne's lover before Jean-Paul, arrives for a visit, surprising the couple by bringing along his 18-year-old daughter Penelope (Birkin), whose existence they had not previously known about. Marianne, without asking Jean-Paul, invites Harry and Penelope to stay. The four stay together and Harry draws Marianne back towards him as the days go by. Taunting Jean-Paul for having given up serious writing to work in advertising, Harry drinks a great deal and throws a surprise party while Jean-Paul, a recovering alcoholic, stays sober. Meanwhile, it becomes clear that Penelope neither likes nor respects her father, whom she has barely known while growing up. She and Jean-Paul become close and spend a day alone together by the sea. That night, while the women are asleep, Harry drunkenly confronts Jean-Paul and accuses him of seducing Penelope to revenge his own shortcomings on his more successful friend. Trying to punch Jean-Paul, Harry falls into the pool and is too drunk to swim. Jean-Paul, who has also been drinking, at first stops him from climbing out of the water, then deliberately pushes Harry under and holds him down until he drowns. He covers up the crime by stripping Harry's clothes off and placing fresh trousers and a shirt at the poolside to make it look like an accident. After the funeral, a policeman, Inspector Lévêque (Crauchet), visits the house more than once. He confides to Marianne his reasons for doubting the story of an accident, that Harry had been wearing his watch, which was expensive and not waterproof, and that there is no trace of sweat on the clothes he was supposed to have been wearing. When she tells Jean-Paul, he confesses everything to her, and she goes to see Harry's clothes, hidden in the cellar, that would have given him away. But when she does not take this evidence to the police, the inspector reluctantly suspends the inquiry. Marianne takes Penelope to the airport and sees her off as she returns to her mother. When Penelope demands the truth about her father's death, Marianne assures her it really was an accident. She and Jean-Paul are then about to leave the villa when she tells him that they will not go together. She calls for a taxi but he places his hand on the telephone, cutting off her call and silencing her. In the end, neither leaves that day, and in the film's final shot they stand side by side looking out the window at the swimming pool, and then embrace.

texto: #30 of "26 Foreign Films in 2026" : France. There is a lot to like here. Beautiful French people in beautiful outfits in a beautiful château with a beautiful pool in the south of France in summer. A lot of romantic French drama and sexual intrigue occurs when an old friend/lover and his alluringly pouty 18-year-old daughter come to stay at a couples château. All four main characters are almost preternaturally attractive. The vibes are immaculate, and you can see the fashion model / advertising executive late 1960s design elements on every second of this film. When the drama is told quietly through longing looks and hateful glances, it works really well. When it finally becomes a thriller in the last 25 minutes, it pretty significantly loses its way. Interestingly, they shot every scene twice. Once in English and once in French. I watched the original French restored version. But it might be more accurate to say that both versions are the original.

texto: A classic of European cinema. Hugely influential as a long, languorous summer in the south of France takes a dramatic turn to the dark side when a friend arrives with his 18 year old daughter to upset the rhythms of Alain Delon and Romy Schneider. A film of it's time (1969 on the cusp of the 70's) with a film making style that hasn't aged well. Too many stilted 'conversations' and slow moving scenes and social mores that don't sit well with today's audiences. Still, it's got Alain Delon and Romy Schneider so it can be given some latitude. Still too long, though

texto: The untouchable hotness of Alain Delon, on an endless lazy summer by the pool. Is there shame in milking the days with sun, sex, and biding your time away? When change, temptation, and ultimately chaos upend your idyllic summer of wasteful days, you can’t help in hindsight to think maybe having all you needed was enough. Watching Delon shrug off the ex-lover, the seriousness of the situations, brings a sense of frustration, and you lose track of who it is you’re rooting for. Enjoyable enough film, but I think the end sort of faded into the sun. Interesting watching this after the Talented Mr. Ripley… the same “walls closing in” feel as the Investigator starts poking around the edges. The cast is gorgeous, the feel is there, but I can’t help think this one sorted floated along like a lazy summer day. Good enough in the moment, but not as memorable as you’d have liked.

texto: La Piscine é um daqueles filmes que vivem quase exclusivamente daquilo que fica por dizer, senti tensão no silêncio. A narrativa é simples, mas a forma como Jacques Deray manipula o espaço, o tempo e as relações entre as personagens faz com que exista uma tensão constante, mesmo quando aparentemente nada está a acontecer, e foi algo que eu adorei. É um filme que percebe que o desconforto nasce muito antes do conflito e constrói essa sensação com uma subtileza rara. O mais interessante é a maneira como o calor, a piscina e aquela casa isolada deixam de ser apenas cenário e passam a refletir o estado emocional das personagens, tudo parece demasiado confortável, demasiado perfeito, e é precisamente essa aparência de tranquilidade que torna inevitável a implosão. A mise-en-scène é extremamente rigorosa, sem nunca chamar demasiado a atenção para si própria, e isso faz com que cada olhar ou pausa tenha um peso desproporcional. Maurice Ronet introduz uma presença que desestabiliza toda a dinâmica do grupo, eu gosto que não exista propriamente heróis nem vilões, há egos, inseguranças e um desejo constante de validação que acaba por contaminar todas as relações. O filme evita julgamentos morais fáceis e acredito que prefira explorar as ambiguidades que surgem quando o desejo, o ciúme e o orgulho coexistem. Visualmente continua impressionante, a fotografia luminosa nunca contradiz a crescente sensação de inquietação, pelo contrário, parece intensificá-la, e também existe uma elegância quase hedonista na forma como Deray enquadra os corpos e os espaços, mas essa beleza nunca é gratuita, funciona como um contraste permanente com a deterioração psicológica das personagens. O meu interesse, e acho que o interesse geral, nunca esteve em descobrir o que vai acontecer, mas em observar como pequenas fissuras emocionais se transformam em algo irreversível. É um filme sofisticado e psicologicamente muito mais complexo do que eu pensei, mas gostei imenso.

texto: Estoy muy cachondo. Esta película es sensual, sutil, inquietante y perfecta para el verano. Desde la escena de apertura con Alain Delon al borde de la piscina, el erotismo está presente en pantalla en todo momento. De los tíos más guapos que he visto en mi vida. Es la primera película suya que veo y me dieron ganas de ver más, porque tiene una gran presencia en pantalla. Empieza como la fantasía de verano de cualquiera, y poco a poco va construyendo una tensión muy cargada, pero de forma muy natural. Hay que tener algo de paciencia, pero vale la pena porque el clima que crea es increíble, y lo más reseñable es precisamente esa tensión. Cada gesto y cada movimiento dice mucho y da pie a un sinfín de reacciones posibles del resto de personajes, todo presentado con una delicadeza y una estética impecable. La química sexual y esas micro reacciones son lo más importante a la hora de leer a los personajes, porque los principales acontecimientos ni siquiera aparecen en pantalla. No importa lo que haya ocurrido, solo lo que personajes (y tú) crean que ocurrió. Es cierto que cuando ocurre el asesinato y se descarga la tensión la película se hace un poco pesada, pero el final abierto es interesante.

texto: Um filme que captura bem a estética dos anos 1960. A sungueta estampada do Alain Delon, o vestido verde de estampa psicodélica da Romy Schneider, os quinhentos enlatados no jantar de comida oriental, a festa na casa com a cômica dança de rock n roll da época (que era o auge da modernidade)... E as cenas iniciais cheias de sol e piscina que vendem muito bem o filme até hoje. As atuações são meio engessadas, todo mundo meio duro, isso me incomoda um pouco, mas fica coerente com a proposta toda de ser um ensaio de dois homens competindo psicologicamente e simbolicamente para ver quem tem o "maio pau". Quando o cara aparece com aquele Maserati Ghibli deu para ver que, além de ter sido pedido da produção para geral poder dar um rolê em coupé esportivo durante as gravações, aquele personagem também seria o antagonista mor do filme. No mais é isso, um filme sobre a eterna temática fidelidade/traição para ver num fim de semana como uma viagem ensolarada com com hospedagem no sul da França.

texto: Alain Delon, Jane Birkin y Romy Schneider. Un buen reparto y una historia interesante, que tiene como epicentro una piscina de aguas cristalinas, la cual guarda un atroz secreto. En este filme francés cuatro personas se lanzan en amoríos más allá de sus propios lazos sentimentales y más allá del tiempo y de la edad. El padre de Penélope, Harry, quiere recuperar a su antigua novia, la cual mantiene una relación con su amigo, Jean-Paul (Alain Delon). Mientras que este va detrás de Penélope (Jane Birkin). En esta película todos pierden, pero algunos más que otros, y a través de un juego de miradas, que van del deseo hasta el terror y el arrepentimiento se plantea una cuestión, ¿Cuanto somos capaces de hacer por amor?

texto: The Swimming Pool turns a seemingly idyllic summer holiday into a tense study of desire, jealousy and guilt. Jean-Paul and Marianne appear to enjoy a carefree summer at their secluded villa until Marianne invites her former lover Harry and his daughter Penelope , whose arrival brings old feelings, insecurities, and unspoken resentments to the surface. What I liked most is how the film builds tension through small shifts in behavior rather than constant dramatic confrontation. Jean-Paul becomes increasingly jealous of Harry’s confidence and Marianne’s familiarity with him while Penelope’s presence adds another layer of attraction and uneasiness to the group. The beautiful Mediterranean setting and Alain Delon and Romy Schneider’s restrained performances create an atmosphere that feels both sensual and strangely suffocating. The slow pacing and emotionally distant characters kept me from fully investing but I liked how the film blurs desire, guilt and reality through Jean-Paul’s fears.

texto: GORGEOUS film Slow plot I appreciate it does a fantastic job at building and sustaining an eerie atmosphere, but I think the performances were perhaps underwhelming at the point of climax, making them fall flat — the pool scene (THE pool scene) could’ve just been a clip of my sister and I when we fell out rather than the climax to a film that’s worked so hard to establish the build up. The first hour and a half were really great, but the last 30 mins felt longer than the entire film. I didn’t like how the detective was purely suggestive, never assertive — I would’ve loved to have seen a more explosive performance from either Romy or Alain in response to this, it ended up being quite mundane. I liked the confined setting, though characters leave the house often, we never see clips of these places (except the supermarket), building a sense of distrust for the audience as we can’t confirm the answer when another character asks what they were doing. I think Jean-Luc and Penelope’s relationship diluted the dynamic between all other characters, it felt quite detached and I feel could’ve been utilised in a much more intense way to prompt the reactions of other characters. The sound of the pool water was delectable

texto: Estoy muy cachondo. Esta película es sensual, sutil, inquietante y perfecta para el verano. Desde la escena de apertura con Alain Delon al borde de la piscina, el erotismo está presente en pantalla en todo momento. De los tíos más guapos que he visto en mi vida. Es la primera película suya que veo y me dieron ganas de ver más, porque tiene una gran presencia en pantalla. Empieza como la fantasía de verano de cualquiera, y poco a poco va construyendo una tensión muy cargada, pero de forma muy natural. Hay que tener algo de paciencia, pero vale la pena porque el clima que crea es increíble, y lo más reseñable es precisamente esa tensión. Cada gesto y cada movimiento dice mucho y da pie a un sinfín de reacciones posibles del resto de personajes, todo presentado con una delicadeza y una estética impecable. La química sexual y esas micro reacciones son lo más importante a la hora de leer a los personajes, porque los principales acontecimientos ni siquiera aparecen en pantalla. No importa lo que haya ocurrido, solo lo que personajes (y tú) crean que ocurrió. Es cierto que cuando ocurre el asesinato y se descarga la tensión la película se hace un poco pesada, pero el final abierto es interesante.

texto: La Piscine é um daqueles filmes que vivem quase exclusivamente daquilo que fica por dizer, senti tensão no silêncio. A narrativa é simples, mas a forma como Jacques Deray manipula o espaço, o tempo e as relações entre as personagens faz com que exista uma tensão constante, mesmo quando aparentemente nada está a acontecer, e foi algo que eu adorei. É um filme que percebe que o desconforto nasce muito antes do conflito e constrói essa sensação com uma subtileza rara. O mais interessante é a maneira como o calor, a piscina e aquela casa isolada deixam de ser apenas cenário e passam a refletir o estado emocional das personagens, tudo parece demasiado confortável, demasiado perfeito, e é precisamente essa aparência de tranquilidade que torna inevitável a implosão. A mise-en-scène é extremamente rigorosa, sem nunca chamar demasiado a atenção para si própria, e isso faz com que cada olhar ou pausa tenha um peso desproporcional. Maurice Ronet introduz uma presença que desestabiliza toda a dinâmica do grupo, eu gosto que não exista propriamente heróis nem vilões, há egos, inseguranças e um desejo constante de validação que acaba por contaminar todas as relações. O filme evita julgamentos morais fáceis e acredito que prefira explorar as ambiguidades que surgem quando o desejo, o ciúme e o orgulho coexistem. Visualmente continua impressionante, a fotografia luminosa nunca contradiz a crescente sensação de inquietação, pelo contrário, parece intensificá-la, e também existe uma elegância quase hedonista na forma como Deray enquadra os corpos e os espaços, mas essa beleza nunca é gratuita, funciona como um contraste permanente com a deterioração psicológica das personagens. O meu interesse, e acho que o interesse geral, nunca esteve em descobrir o que vai acontecer, mas em observar como pequenas fissuras emocionais se transformam em algo irreversível. É um filme sofisticado e psicologicamente muito mais complexo do que eu pensei, mas gostei imenso.

texto: The premise is too horrific and too impracticable for me to buy into. A corporation acquires a baby, imprisons him for 30 years, deliberately traumatizes him by staging his father’s death, manipulates every intimate relationship he has, prevents him from leaving through phobias and coercion, and broadcasts his entire existence for profit. I get that it's a satire. But there’s a realism problem. This isn’t merely exploitative reality television. It’s a human-rights atrocity happening in public. Where are the protesters? Lawyers? Governments? Religious groups? Journalists? People trying to break into the dome? Sylvia is essentially the only person behaving the way you’d expect millions of people to behave. The movie wants the audience to make the comparison to celebrity/Hollywood/reality TV -- but for me that was asking too much. I don't think celebs or reality tv stars are victims. Truman is. The logistics also become ridiculous if you think about them for 30 seconds. The number of people required to sustain this conspiracy, the legal structure permitting it, airspace, utilities, medical care, education, sex and reproduction, emergency situations, Truman’s legal identity, outsiders getting in, employees never exposing it, governments allowing it—the movie simply says, essentially, don’t think about that. I get that people love this movie for its message and the satire. It just wasn't for me.

So why not share that with the world!

texto: דרמה, מתח, קומדיה, מסתורין. לפני שנים רבות, ארבעת הז'אנרים חיו בהרמוניה, אבל הכול השתנה כשהכניסו אותם לסרט של שעה וארבעים דקות. צחוק בצד, איזה קונספט מטורף לסרט. אפשר לעשות איתו כל כך הרבה וללכת אותו לכל כך הרבה כיוונים. הבעיה שלי היא שהרגשתי שכל פעם אני מקבל לגימה קטנה של משהו מעניין, רק בשביל שישר יעברו לדבר הבא. התחלנו בקומדיה סאטירית, ואז עברנו לבלשות ומסתורין, ואז דרמה על בן אדם שכל החיים שלו הם שקר, ואז לחרדה וקלסטרופוביה, ואז לאקשן עם הרבה הומור פיזי. ואז, טוב, די, אתם מבינים מה אני אומר. כל כך הרבה דברים, כל כך הרבה רעיונות, אבל הסרט פשוט לא נתן לי לשקוע בשום דבר. מה שגרם לסרט של שעה וארבעים להרגיש כמו שלוש שעות. בצורה מצחיקה, אולי אם הסרט היה קצת יותר ארוך או יותר ממוקד, הסרט היה עובר בצורה חלקה. ושלא תבינו אותי לא נכון, אני מבין למה כולם אוהבים את הסרט. יש כל כך הרבה מה לאהוב ולהעריך פה: המשחק נהדר, הקונספט מדהים, ויש סצנות נקודתיות שמבוצעות מעולה. אבל כמכלול, לא עבד לי. לסיכום, חפרתי.

texto: A fun and interesting delve into the human psyche influential enough to the point where we use it in everyday dialogue to describe any sorts of weird coincidences. Jimmy Carrey as always is a thrilling watch, even in a more serious role than he is usually given. It takes a brilliant actor to carry a film in which only one character experiences the plot and develops throughout it. The supporting cast does their work but i can't help but find them slightly underwhelming in comparison to Carrey's starpower, even if that fact comes with the nature of the role. Unfortunately, I believe this is one of those films where the concept and premise far surpasses how it is actually presented on screen. The whole plot feels like a rush to get Truman to discover the truth, rather than spending time with this pre-established world that could present a unique dynamic between characters. The execution picks up massively once the shift happens but I think the first half of the film suffers massively through it lack of eventfulness. Culturally influencial but not the masterpiece it is often told to be. 6/10

texto: Le film était très sympathique dans l’ensemble. Je me suis fait chier au début, déjà parce que je ne comprenais pas où voulait nous mener le film. Je n’avais aucune connaissance du plot, je ne savais pas de quoi il traitait. Puis j’ai commencé à comprendre où le réalisateur voulait en venir, et commençait à faire des blagues sur “une experience sociale”. Et là ça m’a fait beaucoup réfléchir. Parce que vivre ce que Truman a vécu ça doit être super difficile. Un pantin du divertissement, qui n’est même pas conscient que sa vie a été décidée de A à Z par un inconnu. Mais encore plus lorsque tu te rends compte que ta vie a été visionnée par des milliards de personnes à ton insu. Déjà j’espère pour leur production qu’ils n’avaient pas mis de caméras dans les toilettes et les salles de bains. Parce que le niveau d’intimité était déjà très bas. Honnêtement, le film aurait du être classé film d’horreur. Parce que ça c’est l’un de mes pires cauchemars, comme celui de beaucoup de personnes qui angoissent rien qu’à l’idée d’être filmées ou enregistrées. J’étais trop choquée qu’ils soient allés jusqu’à lui faire consciemment développer une phobie de l’eau juste pour divertir des gens. Ils sont complètement dingues. En plus les relations parasociales de dingues que tu dois développer. Déjà qu’ici, énormément de personnes sont parasociales avec des stars qui gardent énormément d’intimité… Alors avec un quelqu’un dont tu peux stalker la vie 24/7… Sinon, regardeyyyyy pour l’anniversaire de chacha <3

exemplo: As reviews elogiam a atuação de Jim Carrey, destacando sua energia cômica e momentos dramáticos, considerando um de seus melhores trabalhos.
texto: “In case I don’t see ya, good afternoon, good evening, and good night!” What would you do if you found out that your entire life was fake? Every person in your life an actor dedicated to keeping you from discovering the truth. Every waking moment of your life broadcast to an audience that you don’t even know exists. Every aspect of your existence, from your job, to your marriage, even your birth; all meticulously scripted by an unseen hand with the intention of garnering ratings and views. It’s a profoundly existential concept, fit for an equally existential film. Jim Carrey’s best roles are ones where he can be emotional, yet still have moments that allow him to go off the rails when its appropriate, and his performance in this is a toss up with Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind as a career best. Even though we the audience are privy to the fact that Truman’s life is an illusion from the very beginning, it still doesn’t make it any less devastating as Truman’s reality begins to unravel around him, thanks in no small part to Carrey’s fantastic performance. It’s no wonder he won over the hearts of so many viewers. Obviously everyone already knows about the brilliant commentary this film has on reality TV and celebrity culture, but this film is so rich with thematic depth that that’s only the tip of the iceberg. One could easily point out the film’s criticism of mass surveilance, which is more topical now than ever with Flock cameras popping up on every street corner. Coinciding with that, The Truman Show (the fictional show, not to be confused with the movie about said fictional show) is really an idealized vision of the long-outdated American Dream. As a child, Truman dreamt of exploring the world and taking in everything that life has to offer, but his dreams were shot down by the authority figures in his life. Now he lives in a copy-pasted suburban house, working a 9-5 cushy desk job day after day, returning home to a bland loveless marriage and a mortgage that will likely never be paid off; living in blissful ignorance of the world outside of his little pocket of suburbia. It’s a role that, as Americans, we’re expected to fill no matter what, and any deviation from that role is tantamount to heresy. Coupled with the constant bombardment of product placements and advertisements throughout his life, it’s clear that Truman’s false reality is a picture-perfect snapshot of life within a capitalist/consumerist system; a safe and comfortable existence, but one that is ultimately neither fulfilling nor sustainable. And yet, Truman still yearns to follow his heart and do what gives him joy and meaning, and so he must break free from the confines of the system, and in doing so find that meaning and fulfillment he’s been searching for his whole life. With Truman questioning his place in both society and the world at large, it’s no surprise that his breaking of the status quo incur wrath of both the systemic and divine variety. Christof, (whose name is emblematic of another certain religious figure) is not just the voice of the corporate backers of the show, but also the literal god of Truman’s reality. He’s also an enigmatic control freak with a god complex, and brought to life by a great performance from Ed Harris. Similarly to his presentation as a god-like figure, he also represents a concept not too dissimilar to 1984’s Big Brother; a controlling force dominating society with an all-seeing-eye (or in this case, moon) that eliminates any individual’s sense of privacy. Truman’s defiance against him is not only an act of rebellion against authority, but also metaphorically and literally standing in defiance of his god, Christof, whose divine edicts boom down from the heavens. Truman chooses not to follow the path chosen for him in Christof’s divine plan, but to carve out his own story and forge his own destiny, a concept that Christof, simply cannot fathom, and therein lies his folly. The scene in which these events take place has got to be one of my favorite endings to a film. I mean, you’ve all seen the shots by now, they’re just incredible. We may never know what happened to Truman. Maybe he reunited with Sylvia, and the two sailed off into the sunset, bound for Fiji. Maybe he lived a life constantly oppressed by paparazzi, as so many celebrities of his status are. Or maybe he just faded into obscurity after being cast out of the limelight. We’ll never know, but the point isn’t the story itself, it’s the concept of not following a story written for you, but to write one for yourself.

texto: “We accept the reality of the world with which we’re presented.” A more than fine movie, with good performances, great moments, and a perfect ending, that masks some of its dark implications, with some dramatic and social humor. A psychological and existential horror in a lot of ways, and a poignant, and sharp commentary in a lot of others — a nightmare that doesn’t end on the other side of the door. It’s a role that was made for Jim Carrey, and it is a movie that still feels relevant today. “In case I don’t see ya…”

Was nothing real?

texto: The Truman show. Dirigida por Peter Weir. (1998) La película sigue a Truman Burbank, un hombre que descubre que su vida es un programa muy popular de televisión, pero debajo de esa premisa hay una película bastante inquietante sobre la libertad, la identidad, el control y nuestra necesidad de sentir que nuestra vida nos pertenece. Seahaven es prácticamente perfecto; es una pequeña isla con calles limpias, vecinos amables y casas bonitas. Todo eso está diseñado para que Truman no tenga motivos para querer irse de Seahaven. Prácticamente está encerrado por una rutina, y la manipulación constante. Su miedo al agua, por ejemplo, fue creado deliberadamente para impedirle abandonar la isla. No necesitan poner una pared delante de él si consiguen que él mismo crea que no puede atravesarla. •Al igual que Christof no se considera un villano. Él cree que le está dando a Truman una vida segura y auténtica dentro de un mundo diseñado exclusivamente para él. Y ahí está una de las partes más interesantes: Christof confunde conocer completamente a una persona con tener derecho y control sobre ella. Decide quiénes son sus amigos, quién será su esposa, dónde vivirá, qué verá y qué temerá. Incluso controla las circunstancias de sus relaciones. Es una forma extrema de paternalismo: "Yo sé qué es mejor para ti, aunque tú no lo sepas." •Sylvia es fundamental porque ella le dice, de alguna manera, que aquello que considera normal no es normal. Ella se convierte en la primera grieta de su realidad. La segunda fue sin duda la repentina aparición de su padre, el cual, en su historia, estaba muerto. En resumen. The Truman Show no trata solamente sobre un hombre que descubre que vive dentro de un programa de televisión. Trata sobre atreverse a cuestionar la realidad que nos entregaron. Y o sea fuera del tono serio, que miedo. Él realmente pensaba que se estaba volviendo loco. ¿Cómo podrías comprobarte a ti mismo que no estás alucinando cuando todos te dicen que es la realidad? Tipo, su mejor amigo desde los 7 años seguía un guión. Ay no, literalmente podría ser un episodio de black mirror. "In case I don't see ya. Good afternoon, good evening and good night" -Truman.

texto: “In case I don’t see ya, good afternoon, good evening, and good night!” What would you do if you found out that your entire life was fake? Every person in your life an actor dedicated to keeping you from discovering the truth. Every waking moment of your life broadcast to an audience that you don’t even know exists. Every aspect of your existence, from your job, to your marriage, even your birth; all meticulously scripted by an unseen hand with the intention of garnering ratings and views. It’s a profoundly existential concept, fit for an equally existential film. Jim Carrey’s best roles are ones where he can be emotional, yet still have moments that allow him to go off the rails when its appropriate, and his performance in this is a toss up with Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind as a career best. Even though we the audience are privy to the fact that Truman’s life is an illusion from the very beginning, it still doesn’t make it any less devastating as Truman’s reality begins to unravel around him, thanks in no small part to Carrey’s fantastic performance. It’s no wonder he won over the hearts of so many viewers. Obviously everyone already knows about the brilliant commentary this film has on reality TV and celebrity culture, but this film is so rich with thematic depth that that’s only the tip of the iceberg. One could easily point out the film’s criticism of mass surveilance, which is more topical now than ever with Flock cameras popping up on every street corner. Coinciding with that, The Truman Show (the fictional show, not to be confused with the movie about said fictional show) is really an idealized vision of the long-outdated American Dream. As a child, Truman dreamt of exploring the world and taking in everything that life has to offer, but his dreams were shot down by the authority figures in his life. Now he lives in a copy-pasted suburban house, working a 9-5 cushy desk job day after day, returning home to a bland loveless marriage and a mortgage that will likely never be paid off; living in blissful ignorance of the world outside of his little pocket of suburbia. It’s a role that, as Americans, we’re expected to fill no matter what, and any deviation from that role is tantamount to heresy. Coupled with the constant bombardment of product placements and advertisements throughout his life, it’s clear that Truman’s false reality is a picture-perfect snapshot of life within a capitalist/consumerist system; a safe and comfortable existence, but one that is ultimately neither fulfilling nor sustainable. And yet, Truman still yearns to follow his heart and do what gives him joy and meaning, and so he must break free from the confines of the system, and in doing so find that meaning and fulfillment he’s been searching for his whole life. With Truman questioning his place in both society and the world at large, it’s no surprise that his breaking of the status quo incur wrath of both the systemic and divine variety. Christof, (whose name is emblematic of another certain religious figure) is not just the voice of the corporate backers of the show, but also the literal god of Truman’s reality. He’s also an enigmatic control freak with a god complex, and brought to life by a great performance from Ed Harris. Similarly to his presentation as a god-like figure, he also represents a concept not too dissimilar to 1984’s Big Brother; a controlling force dominating society with an all-seeing-eye (or in this case, moon) that eliminates any individual’s sense of privacy. Truman’s defiance against him is not only an act of rebellion against authority, but also metaphorically and literally standing in defiance of his god, Christof, whose divine edicts boom down from the heavens. Truman chooses not to follow the path chosen for him in Christof’s divine plan, but to carve out his own story and forge his own destiny, a concept that Christof, simply cannot fathom, and therein lies his folly. The scene in which these events take place has got to be one of my favorite endings to a film. I mean, you’ve all seen the shots by now, they’re just incredible. We may never know what happened to Truman. Maybe he reunited with Sylvia, and the two sailed off into the sunset, bound for Fiji. Maybe he lived a life constantly oppressed by paparazzi, as so many celebrities of his status are. Or maybe he just faded into obscurity after being cast out of the limelight. We’ll never know, but the point isn’t the story itself, it’s the concept of not following a story written for you, but to write one for yourself.
