texto: Mmmmmmm yes the atmosphere. The mc’s monotone and general lack of facial expressions aside from key moments really spoke to me deeply and I think greatly contributed to the dread of it all. I really love these kinds of performances that are so understated. As someone who has a similar demeanor, it just works. It feels tangibly real to me in ways other films don’t, despite the more fantastical elements. I can feel this happening and place myself in her shoes instead of being just an onlooker which I find a bit rarer these days. I wish more performances portrayed a range of demeanors instead of what we typically see. This performance was just so so excellent and will stick with me. Also, I must sing my nic cage praises too. Man he really hits it out of the park with the gonzo performances. I should have known after his performance in Mandy permanently altered my brain chemistry. Add this to the altar of cage brilliance. I’m glad I waited to watch this one. What an excellent sick-day movie to stay up way too late to finish.

texto: Great horror. One of the first in a very long time to actually unsettle me on a deep level. Sort of thing that has me looking over my shoulder when I walk home from the cinema. Love the new theme in horror where it makes you brutally uncomfortable rather than relying on cheap sound related jump-scares. Loved the theme of cat and mouse. First time I watched it, I thought the twist at the end was stupid. However, upon re-watch, its painfully obvious the whole time that this is not really about an FBI agent hunting a killer. It's about the devil being the devil for the sake of being the devil. Pure evil, good pacing, great sense of discovery as the movie moves throughout acts. Film really rewards you for noticing small details in scenes allowing you to piece the truth together before the protagonist does. Acting was top-notch, really has you on the edge of your seat. Everyone is a suspect, tension is so great throughout. Man that opening scene with the iconic longlegs intro makes me think this will be a cult classic in the future. Loved the constant lingering shots, the open doorways, the strange camera angles that left you not knowing what was round the corner. Appreciated the lack of shitty tropes and cliches. Would give it 5 starts if it didn't have such a significant twist that still feels abrupt in an otherwise nearly perfect film!

tema: Direção de fotografia e estilo visual
exemplo: A fotografia e o design de produção são frequentemente elogiados, com menções a planos abertos, ângulos incomuns e uso de cores para diferenciar passado e presente.
texto: GENRE ET CONSTRUCTION HISTOIRE Le film est un mélange entre enquête et un peu d'horreur par la suite, c'est étrange. L'histoire est dévoilée petit à petit, mystère après mystère. MISE EN SCÈNE On est souvent ramené de force dans l'histoire grâce à la façon dont le film est filmé. Dans la grande majorité les personages sont tes projets de la caméra. Le film partagera par moment 2 temporalités, on les reconnaît avec les couleurs : Le présent sera les couleurs grise. Pour le passé, les couleur seront plus orange chaleureuse et/ou changement de résolution de caméra (Polaroid). Lorsque le film utilisera les couleurs chaleureuse, IRONIQUEMENT l'endroit sera tous l'inverse. Le film partagera donc des couleurs diamétralement opposées, tantôt chaleureuses, tantôt glaciales, même si la grosse majorité sera plutôt grisâtre. Petit reproche tout de même pour les plans qui sont majoritairement trop sombres (normal pour un thriller MAIS lorsqu'on ne voit rien du tout, c'est un peu dommage). THRILLER Le film est angoissant et nous tient en haleine constamment (mention spéciale aux génériques de début et de fin qui ont des musiques plutôt joyeuses, étonnant pour le type de film que l'on vient de voir juste avant, j'aime bien😅). JEU D'ACTEUR Les acteurs sont vraiment bon (Maika Monroe et Nicolas Cage). CONCLUSION Bref, le film dégage une ambiance spéciale et surtout UNIQUE, je le trouve VRAIMENT TRES TRES BIEN !!!!

texto: Interesting movie, not what I was expecting at all. I don't really have much to say about the plot and story organization; a bit confusing but not such that I couldn't understand what was happening. Where I think the film shines is in its specific images and scenes and (especially) in its performances. Yet another movie to be added to the genre of "Nick Cage doing crazy things". In this viewers opinion, this time it works with the film rather than against it. Also some interesting meditations on innocence/childhood and its interaction with the "hell of living". Overall, an interesting, well-acted, and well-made, but far from perfect, film.

Petit reproche tout de même pour les plans qui sont majoritairement trop sombres (normal pour un thriller MAIS lorsqu'on ne voit rien du tout, c'est un peu dommage). THRILLER Le film est angoissant et nous tient en haleine constamment (mention spéciale aux génériques de début et de fin qui ont des musiques plutôt joyeuses, étonnant pour le type de film que l'on vient de voir juste avant, j'aime bien😅). JEU D'ACTEUR Les acteurs sont vraiment bon (Maika Monroe et Nicolas Cage). CONCLUSION Bref, le film dégage une ambiance spéciale et surtout UNIQUE, je le trouve VRAIMENT TRES TRES BIEN !!!!

texto: Dear Wim Wenders, I've tried, man. I really tried with this one. Your films, while esthetically pleasing, carry nothing in terms of substance, story, or attention. I'm not saying I need action packed, narrative expository, tiktok noise to keep me invested, but Jesus Christ, Wim, give me something to work with. Your films are flat. They engage with the lonely side of life and less about the slice of it - and that's something to be commended for. But not everyone is lonely. Not everyone feels that way. And sometimes a lonely day is not that engaging. If I wanted to see a lonely slice of life piece that's a little more engaging, I would rather just watch a documentary. I'm sorry Wim, but I feel you will never write anything that's neither engaging or worth my time. The closest you got to making a film that explores loneliness while keeping your audience somewhat entertained was 42 years ago and it definitely shows. Maybe you're a lonely man who wants everyone else to feel as lonely as you, and maybe that's the point of your films. But I don't to feel that way everytime I want to engage with your art. You'll never change and that's okay, but I don't think I'll invest in your talent ever again. Your fans are few but dedicated, and your quality speaks to them in ways that I will never comprehend. I'm sorry I can never be part of that dedicated community that sees the beauty of your world, and I'm sorry I can't see what you see. Maybe someday I might, but not banking on that anymore. But keep making your art anyway. Film as a whole needs voices like yours. Sincerely, A.F.X. Heller

exemplo: O filme falha em desenvolver o protagonista ou qualquer arco dramático, contentando-se com situações superficiais que não geram envolvimento.
texto: www.fastretailing.com/eng/about/company/profile_yanai-koji.html so the film gives some nod to the fact that there's discontent within this worker despite his happy veneer throughout everything else that had transpired until that point. but does it explain what this could be or how it could come to happen? there is some interpersonal drama and we witness some cheating, but there is little if any attention paid to the structure these things exist in. when his coworker disappears and a new person shows up the next day, this just happens. the higher ups have taken care of it. and no further questions are asked. in [this one interview] yakusho says that his character sees the homeless man in the intersection and is moved by that he's the only one to really do so; but does he? this is a caricature too! and the film dupes us because we're grafted onto him. we have no choice in the operation, and it's made sure of that every step of the way. the whole thing is choreographed form the very beginning. take the tic-tac-to game, for example; there you have yakusho initially thinking it's just trash. the audience at this point is like, no! what are you doing, don't you see there's greater value there!! but then he realizes his mistake and even plays along. and this becomes a subplot of the film, of him filling out the tic-tac-to game, playing against some yet unseen opponent. and then when the game is over, he gets a thank you note for his role as such. and we get satisfaction in this because he did what we wanted him to. the film shines light on his face when his coworker's (ex?)girlfriend suddenly kisses him, but don't worry, it's just the light of the car door suddenly opening, no secondary function here. (by which i mean to say that this is specifically queuing us to receive this scene in a certain way). we get led along the whole time and then at the end there this pretense that it was all worth it but that life's tough and you just have to keep on. but what the real final shot is, it need be understood, gives the actual game away. that is, the grand city scape and the shining sun. while i'm not anti-city or anything like this, it's necessary to understand the relation to city that this film has from the point of its very inception. this is literally a propaganda piece for The Tokyo Toilet initiative -- an "urban revitalization" (we can just say gentrification, you don't have to be so coy) program masterminded by Yanai Koji, son of Uniqlo's CEO Yanai Tadashi. we can get another glimpse of this in a chance scene that happens when Yakusho comes across an older man standing in front of a developing plot. The old man asks Yakusho if he remembers what used to be here. Yakusho doesn't answer and the old man concludes, that's what it means to get old (you forget what used to be). But this is literally not true! Or, it doesn't have to be. It is not an inevitability of life that high end toilets financed by plastic industry and fast fashion will displace the perfectly functioning ones that existed before. It's not the fault of the people for forgetting, it's that there's a literal ongoing violence that makes people forget. And then part of this too can be the whole system of atomization that this is all tied up in, where people just exist as individual subjects, maybe tending to their own idiosyncratic archive, but there is no collective knowledge share -- there is no means of coming together and producing a history of what things have been like so that this knowledge can be passed down to future generations. Instead you get family heirlooms and hand-me-downs. Everything is purely familial, the film wants us to believe. Which has problems because generational wealth doesn't exist! This shit is stolen goods. And then so what, it's just too bad for people that never got a foothold to begin with? There has to be a better way. (More to come; this as to be the start of a research project; permitting everything goes alright tonight).

texto: It’s beautiful and all, but c'mon... it’s the most boring movie. I feel so uncultured for writing this, because it has a distinct Joseph Beuys quality to it. Beuys famously said that “everyone is an artist”, and here we are, watching the everyday life of a “simple” toilet cleaner in Tokyo and perceiving it as art. Honestly, it almost inspires me to film my own mundane everyday life and screen it in a theater. It’s shot beautifully, but I just fell asleep and have zero urge to watch it again.

texto: ☹️ textureless, pre-digested cinema. i like wim wenders quite a bit, especially in this stripped-back, observational mode, but there's an air of desperation that slowly suffocates this film. it's so terrified of being even the slightest bit unlikeable that it can't help but conceive of its character being anyone but the nicest, gentlest lil guy on earth, with only a wrinkle of genuine humanity devoid of affect hinted at in its last ten minutes. i'm usually quite soft on twee, slice of life bullshit, so i truly don't understand why this didn't work on me. the more i watched it and the more i write about, the more i kind of loathe it? the late inflections of melancholy help restore a semblance of gravity to the film. its vague musings on ageing would work better if we didn't have younger characters saying shit like "what's this? a cassette tape?? do they have this 'van morrison' on spotify?????" or elderly characters flatly explaining what growing old means. this was a heckin' wholesome experience with the profundity of your average ted lasso episode, and maybe a slightly more delicate sense of humour. an inoffensive nicecore crowdpleaser elevated by some tasteful naturalism and an exotic japanese cityscape. this will probably be nominated for an oscar. update: i fucking called it lmao

texto: MVFF 2023 #2 Maybe I haven't seen enough Wim Wenders yet but this was unexpectedly modest and wholesome. Yet, dare I say, not in a particularly earned manner? Hirayama could be an interesting character but the film does not probe him nearly enough, rather mainly showcases his content quotidian existence. I do generally like plotless slice-of-life films, and this is not quite an exception with its pleasant vibes and eschewing of narrative clichés. But I strongly prefer the genre to showcase some amount of complexity through their characters in lieu of much of a plot to lean on. Here, while there are a few small hitches via hints of Hirayama's past and being subjected to classist behavior, the film largely skates over them and feels too simple for my tastes. Hirayama appears to me as just a simple man with a simple job and simple hobbies. The film does ask ourselves why he is so content with his profession and quietude but without presenting even much of a hint, the answer(s) will not keep me up at night.

exemplo: Houve críticas quanto à romantização do trabalho de limpeza e da vida solitária, com alguns apontando que a realidade dessas situações é bem mais difícil, o que tornou a abordagem do filme pouco realista ou problemática.
texto: Demorei quase uma semana pra começar a escrever sobre esse filme, isso porque as sensações eram bem mistas e ele realmente me fez refletir sobre diversos temas. Eu gosto de como o filme começa, gosto de como a rotina ritualística de Hirayama é, apesar de repetitiva, diferente todos os dias por meio do que é ignorado, gosto da cadência com que ele nos é apresentado: aos poucos, enquanto nós só observamos sem compromisso, acompanhando a vida do protagonista sem de fato saber quem ele é. Entendo a posição contemplativa que Wenders tenta nos colocar, a de olhar através dos olhos do protagonista ou da lente de sua câmera. Creio que esse seja o principal ponto onde o longa pode ou não funcionar, a depender da capacidade individual de um espectador de enxergar beleza nessas pequenas coisas (o que não é nem um pouco fácil) e é também onde, pelo menos pra mim, Wenders fracassa em transmitir esse valor, chegando a soar artificial em certos momentos, pois o filme no fim das contas ainda é uma encomenda publicitária, e porque extrai sua beleza do que já é belo, não do que é banal e visto como tal. Não acho que o filme seja fetichista ou romantize um trabalho como o de limpador de banheiros, tampouco ingênuo em afirmar que tudo são flores e que problemas não existem, eles existem. Acredito que a escolha de não mostrar o impacto do preconceito ou do cansaço no protagonista pode ser interpretada como parte justamente da filosofia dele, e a forma como ele vive, mas até que ponto? A partir da segunda metade do filme, o usso e abuso da principal característica e filosofia de vida do personagem (resiliência estoica, contemplação, serenidade e deslocamento/distância) como justificativa para a falta de dramatização e proximidade expulsa a trama dos próprios trilhos. Parece que o filme frequentemente nos carrega pra uma situação dramática com grande peso para ele, mas sempre que algo precisa de tempo para ser sentido, até mesmo tempo para que haja a dúvida de por que um limpador de banheiros escolheria deliberadamente a vida que tem, o filme foge e inicia um novo dia, com a mesma desculpa. Tenho fé que deve existir alguém que nem o Hirayama por aí, mas que esse alguém É ou em algum momento foi/será maluco, eu tenho é certeza.

texto: elegant. minimalist without ever feeling empty. this movie reminds you that life doesn’t have to be extraordinary to be meaningful. It finds poetry in repetition, in routine, in the tiny moments most of us rush past. Hirayama’s life is quiet, but never small. His worth is not measured by his job, but by the way he moves through the world. His music, his books, his plants, his photographs, the way he notices light through the trees... all of it becomes a portrait of someone fully present, even if not someone free from loneliness or regret. as an exhausted corporate girlie, this one hit a little too close to home.

texto: A beautiful film about solitude, routine, melancholy and enjoying the little things. Hirayama’s solitude is beautiful and meaningful, but it may also be a protective shell he has built around himself. Short, sometimes wordless human interactions can be deeply meaningful, yet he has effectively cut himself off from his family for reasons we never fully understand. There is joy in listening to music alone in your car, but also in sharing that music with someone else. He has built a tiny world for himself inside an enormous Tokyo: his apartment, small izakayas and bookshops, the park, the bath house. I loved the way such a vast and sometimes impersonal city becomes intimate through these small spaces, where you encounter the same regulars and gradually become part of one another’s lives. He follows almost exactly the same routine every day, yet every day is slightly different: the light hits the leaves differently and creates new patterns of shadow, the homeless man strikes another absurd pose, a salaryman or a group of children passes through one of the toilets he is cleaning. Routine becomes a way of noticing change rather than escaping from it. A good life can contain both happiness and sadness, tears and a smile at the same time, as in that beautiful final shot.

texto: Perfect Days is only my second Wim Wenders film after Paris, Texas , and somehow he’s already given me two incredible films. I honestly feel like I may have peaked way too early with his filmography, because I don’t know how he tops either of these for me. There’s just something so beautiful about the simplicity of this film. Hirayama’s life is incredibly routine and on the surface there isn’t a huge amount happening, but Wenders makes that routine feel meaningful without ever forcing it to be. The pacing is absolutely brilliant. The film is more than happy to sit with Hirayama as he goes about his day, and I never felt bored or impatient. If anything, I found myself becoming more immersed in the rhythm of his life. The sparse dialogue works perfectly with this too. So much of Hirayama’s character is communicated through his expressions, his routines, the people he interacts with, the books he reads and especially the music he listens to. There’s very little need for exposition because the film trusts you to simply observe him and gradually piece together who he is. I also loved the visual style. The colour palette is gorgeous, the editing is really neat, and the Tokyo cityscapes are beautiful throughout. There’s something about the contrast between the busy, overwhelming city and Hirayama’s incredibly simple existence within it that I really loved. Wenders somehow makes cleaning public toilets, eating lunch in a park and driving around Tokyo listening to music feel almost meditative. It’s also interesting comparing this to Paris, Texas. They’re very different films, but there’s definitely a similar fascination with loneliness, human connection and people who have seemingly withdrawn from a previous life. Paris, Texas is much more emotionally heavy and dramatic, whereas Perfect Days feels far more content with simply observing life. It almost feels like Wenders has arrived at a more peaceful understanding of some of the same ideas. And Koji Yakusho is incredible. He does so much with so little dialogue, and the final sequence in particular is such a beautiful example of that. His face says more than pages of dialogue ever could. I think what I loved most is that Perfect Days never feels like it’s trying to convince you that Hirayama’s life is perfect. It’s just showing you that there can be something beautiful in an ordinary life if you actually pay attention to it. The repetition, the routine, the little moments of connection, the music, the trees, the photographs - all of these tiny things gradually become meaningful. This is easily the best thing I’ve seen from Wenders so far, although I’ve only seen two films, so maybe I’ve just started with an unfairly strong pair. Either way, absolutely beautiful from start to finish. 10/10 Top100

texto: A beautiful film about solitude, routine, melancholy and enjoying the little things. Hirayama’s solitude is beautiful and meaningful, but it may also be a protective shell he has built around himself. Short, sometimes wordless human interactions can be deeply meaningful, yet he has effectively cut himself off from his family for reasons we never fully understand. There is joy in listening to music alone in your car, but also in sharing that music with someone else. He has built a tiny world for himself inside an enormous Tokyo: his apartment, small izakayas and bookshops, the park, the bath house. I loved the way such a vast and sometimes impersonal city becomes intimate through these small spaces, where you encounter the same regulars and gradually become part of one another’s lives. He follows almost exactly the same routine every day, yet every day is slightly different: the light hits the leaves differently and creates new patterns of shadow, the homeless man strikes another absurd pose, a salaryman or a group of children passes through one of the toilets he is cleaning. Routine becomes a way of noticing change rather than escaping from it. A good life can contain both happiness and sadness, tears and a smile at the same time, as in that beautiful final shot.

texto: 15-20 minutes into the film... what a heartwarming depiction of the joy found in the everyday moments of life. 20-40 minutes into the film... okay what the fuck is wrong with this guy? ~1 hour into the film... one of the most emotionally devastating scenes I can ever remember. Such is Perfect Days, which felt wholly unlike anything I've seen before. Watching this felt like dropping a pebble in a pond or holding a mirror up to a mirror, creating a nesting reflection that stretched to space. Can it be taken at face value? A one-sentence mission statement about the beauty all around us? Or Is there some kind of dark riptide that undermines that beauty? The unspeakable rift that separates a family or the confrontation with mortality; the black and white negatives of the otherwise sun-dappled trees? Or does the contrast of those fissures again underline all the light and goodness we wake up to every morning? Perfect Days is a meditation. Or, maybe It's a haiku - its simplicity and bareness allowing the audience to graft their own meaning upon it. If one test of a writer is to see how much they can communicate with few words, then what Koji Yakusho is doing as an actor in a near silent-film performance is unbelievable. While it must have been difficult to convince studios to greenlight a movie about a janitor in which nothing happens, it's not difficult to latch on to what made this film so moving. Watching it, I felt the same way I do whenever I travel. That when I step away from the interiority of my own life and consider it from a distance I feel as if I am swept up into a greater world around me where anything is possible.

texto: elegant. minimalist without ever feeling empty. this movie reminds you that life doesn’t have to be extraordinary to be meaningful. It finds poetry in repetition, in routine, in the tiny moments most of us rush past. Hirayama’s life is quiet, but never small. His worth is not measured by his job, but by the way he moves through the world. His music, his books, his plants, his photographs, the way he notices light through the trees... all of it becomes a portrait of someone fully present, even if not someone free from loneliness or regret. as an exhausted corporate girlie, this one hit a little too close to home.

texto: No es para todos y pienso que dentro de esta especie de subgénero de películas "no pasa nada" hay mejores, pero aún así Perfect Days es una película bellísima que cambia tu forma de ver la cotidianidad de la vida, es una historia realmente sencilla, sin grandes giros ni pretenciones solo la vida de un hombre que limpia baños. Una película muy necesaria, muy contraria a lo que lo acelerado de la vida actual nos tiene acostumbrados. Me gusto mucho lo relajante que es ver está película, si bien no es la película más estímulante en cuanto a trama de la historia pues es que eso no es lo que busca daré está obra, entre la excelente dirección, la fotografía que hace que cada momento del film sea bello e incluso el sonido ambiental te transmiten muchísimo esa paz de Hirayama, de apreciar los pequeños detalles. Eso mismo los detalles son un gran acierto de Perfect Days, ver está obra por encima es un gran error, por más que sea una película en la que no pase mucho el verla de fondo es no entender lo que te está tratando de decir, cosas pequeñas como la nota del gato (#) que Hirayama dejaba en el baño, sus fotos, en indígente que siempre veía son las cosas pequeñas y fugaces que hacen en conjunto a Perfect Days una película tan especial sobre ver el mundo sin toda la prisa con lo que lo solemos ver. Un tema que me gustó como fue plasmado fueron lo choque generaciónales entre Hirayama con su sobrina y el wey que lo ayudaba a limpiar, un contraste entre la forma calmada y serena de vivir de alguien que alguien con su experiencia formó contra la forma apresurada y caótica que la juventud y la sociedad actúal tenemos. También me gustaron estás escenas intermedias surrealistas y en blanco y negro entre cada día que la película tiene, como si fueran solo instante de los recuerdos que las rutinas largas nos dan. En fin, este tipo de películas que usan un ritmo lento para resaltar los momentos pequeños siempre son las que más terminan renonando conmigo con el pasar del tiempo y Perfect Days siento que va a ser una de las que más me voy a quedar.

texto: Shallow Depth of Field, Soft Focus and Anomorphic Blur. The actual Hollywood cultural zietgeist. The modern fad of movies today is new filmmakers and directors trying to inject their films with that enigmatic juice that makes something cinema, that unexplainable feeling of the movies, ironic as most of these new directors are doing everything but making their films feel like cinema. The biggest victim of this new ideology is the visual department, most films are entirley filmed in shallow depth of field, which to put it simply is enhancing a subject and basically leaving the entire background out of focus and blurry (anomorphic blur) this is also called soft focus, when only the subject is in focus. Before today where its now considered normal to shoot 80% of your film in soft focus, movies used alot more deep focus, where subjects are crisp but the backgrounds where enriched with detail, visible detail and not indescrible blurry backgrounds. Now there are positives to using soft focus, it's not like a new technique that suddenly has been founded, filmmakers have always used soft focus, but in moderation, restricting to key character moments when all that is important in a scene is the character. Nowdays soft focus is used to film every scene, it removes world building and the distinct personality of the film. And it's not always a filmmaker problem, this issue has stemmed from studios becoming too lazy to fund and budget set designs properly, and will encourage shallow focus to paste over the cracks of the image being built and spin it as a "cinematic" effect. It's one of the worst trends in todays industry. Sinners is far from the only movie that falls victim to this terrible trend, but it is by far one of the most notable and consequential. 16 academy award nominations were granted to this movie, that is the MOST ever, what does that tell studios and aspiring filmmakers? that movies should be like this? that is a very dangerous precedent to set. This is considered good cinemtography? this WON best cinematography? for what? is soft focus spam considered good cinematography now? no regard for the image as a whole anymore? and I realize that not every shot in Sinners uses soft focus, most of the establishing shots are deep focus (although those are far and few) this constrics world building to images and shots that do not involve the character, which is extremly restricting, the movie feels so trapped in its own misguided idea of visual mastery. Another issue I have with Sinners is Ryan Coogler, more specifically his direction, quite frankly it is pathetic here, characters stand in the middle of the screen speaking to eachother back and forth, clearly Coogler doesn't care about blocking or elevating his written material whatsoever, every scene is just the same regurgitated directing technique, besides the showstoppy "I Lied to You" scene which is really well crafted, which disappoints me in further, because you can do that? but then the rest of the movie is just empty character standing still back and forth dialogue sequences. Coogler seems more trying to copy Tarantino (the Dusk Till Dawn and Django influences are very very prevelant) than to add any real social commentary, his misguided use of the blues in which he completley disregards it's mythic attributes that have shaped its prevelant inimitability in american culture in favour of a hollywoodized cynical use of the blues to pander towards millenials. Michael B Jordans performance is acceptable but replaceable, supposedly the face of dual performance now that the academy have decided to award him with the prestiged best actor award, Peter Sellers must be rolling in his grave, and im sure when Jeremy Irons isn't trying to cancel himself on the internet by miscommunicating his opinions on gay marraige he's asking himself "how the fuck did I not win for Dead Ringers". Obviously Michael isn't to blame for this, it's this new stage academy which so ignorantley percieves any sort of social commentary however true or misguided as "progressive cinema" that they flourish it with every award under the sun, I mean Wumni Mosaku? seriously, but that's what the oscars is now, it's a marketing game who's willing to pay the most money for facadical confectionaries. And it's no surprise that Coogler is returning straight back to Marvel (post credit scene whaaaaa) to finish his Black Panther trilogy, after Warner Bros chucked a ludicrous amount of money at Sinners (ironically which is seemingly outing their own depravity) Marvel now are chucking even more money in Coogler's direction to film whatever softfocusmaxxing project he ends up doing.

texto: Under all kritik. Bedrövlig på alla vis. Förfärlig, pretentiös och trångsynt—allt på samma gång. Det här är dålig fringe indie konst at its finest, tondöv inför allt den försöker röra och göra, som för närmast utomjordliga orsaker upphöjs till något coolt eller bra eller edgy??—när det sista den borde förknippas med är priser och mainstream. Det här är en spegelbild på hur djupt vi låtit gräva oss ifrån vad som en gång kunde kallas kvalitet. Alla som jobbat med denna film på nåt vis borde skämmas, alla som belönat detta borde skämmas ännu mer. Inte ens coola musik/dans-nummer, som ju bör vara denna karnevals saving grace, klarar den av. Eftersom Ryan Coogler är så inkompetent på att viska symboltongue och sälja sin ormolja, kommer jag symboliskt skänka honom en halv stjärna. En halv stjärna som ingen förtjänar, men som man antagligen bär med heder i denna uppochnedvända cirkusvärld. Jag är ju de facto clownen som faktiskt satt och såg genom 138 minuter av detta brinnkära helvete. 🤡

texto: • This film was a major disappointment to me. There were three dimensions where I think it had to succeed. First, the period piece about African Americans in the Jim Crow south, second, the horror or monster movie, and third, the interplay between these two themes. Unfortunately I don’t think it did well enough on any of these dimensions. • The twins are not interesting characters to me, they are caricatured as exceptionally masculine, aggressive, and competent. • The action sequences were boring and the special effects relating to the vampires and violence were inconsistent, which was distracting. • The scene where Sammy performs in the clubhouse and brings forth music from all times, past and future, is quite powerful and well done. • In my opinion, there should have been more subtlety in the way race was handled in the film. The white people are the monsters, they have corny music, and they turn out to be Klan associates. Once converted, they offer the remaining black people the chance to live forever, as a single (race-blind) community, but they have to forfeit their souls to do so. • I didn’t like the writing, which further detracted from my experience

texto: This film did not know what it was doing. It had great music, cinematography, characters, and what looked to be a great plot. Unfortunately this great plot was never flourished out. 2 and a half hours should be more than enough time to make a great film with so many cool elements that Sinners tried to include, however the movie started off slow not knowing much of what it was actually getting at. Even after the vampires came into the plot, the film did not pick up, as the vibes immediately changed. It was very confusing what to focus at: vampires? Or past, present, and future musical connections? I personally was a big fan of the music, yet the film actually did nothing with it besides showing that the vampires sing. It felt like a must to have more music and they just skipped over that. On top of that there is no explanation for the vampires and their motives, making me not actually care for them as characters I could truly understand. I am happy though they had some vampire elements that are less common in modern media such as asking permission to come in. While I’m being negative here the film is saved by the performances of the actors, the musical scenes, and the film’s breathtaking cinematography. Stand out performance for Micheal B. Jordan. In summary, this film focuses too much on getting to know the main characters, just to immediately skip to a climax with little if not any build up. For a movie so hyped up and talked about I expected so much more. Don’t even get me started on the useless scene of killing those racist men at the end. Aye yi yi.

texto: Pecadores é aquele tipo de filme em que a música rouba a cena. A trilha sonora é incrível, cheia de blues de verdade, e não fica só de fundo, ela realmente puxa a história, mexe com as emoções dos personagens e cria todo o clima do filme. O jeito que o filme mostra como o blues foi visto como "música do diabo" é muito bem feito. A prova de que se pode fazer um filme de terror inteligente, com estilo e impacta a todos, não apenas monstros horríveis e violência gratuita. Uma nova e melhor forma de fazer um filme de terror com uma mensagem forte. Arrisco em dizer que só quem é racializado ou tem consciência racial sentiu o puro sentimento que Pecadores veio nos proporcionar. Tem filmes que não são feitos pra se ver em casa, e esse definitivamente é um deles. “Este mundo deixou vocês pra morrerem. Não permite que vocês construam. Que confraternizem. É isso que nós vamos fazer. Juntos. Pra sempre.” “Uma vez por semana, talvez, eu acordo paralisado, revivendo aquela noite. Mas, antes de o sol se pôr, acho que foi o melhor dia da minha vida.”

exemplo: O filme é visto como uma obra ousada e original, que combina gêneros e temas de maneira inovadora, sendo comparado a clássicos e elogiado por sua ambição cinematográfica.
texto: Ryan Coogler swinging for the fences and connecting almost every time. The first hour is pure hangout-movie pleasure — building this world, this juke joint, these characters — and then it just detonates once Remmick shows up and the vampire mythology kicks in. That music sequence where Sammie plays and the film bends time to show every era of Black music converging in one room is one of the most audacious, purely cinematic things I've seen in a theater in years. Ludwig Göransson's score is doing insane amounts of heavy lifting throughout. Michael B. Jordan pulling off two fully distinct performances as Smoke and Stack without it ever feeling like a gimmick, and the way the film uses vampirism as a metaphor for cultural theft never feels heavy-handed — it earns every beat. If anything holds it back from a full five it's that the back half's genre turn moves so fast some of the character work from the first hour doesn't fully pay off the way I wanted. Still, this is a filmmaker operating at the absolute top of his craft. Original, ambitious, and unlike anything else that came out last year.

C'est regardable et je le conseille, mais je ne vois pas là le grand chef-d'œuvre qu'on m'a vendu. On le survend un peu trop je trouve.

texto: Could Guy Ritchie be considered as a “one-movie wonder” director? This is the fourth film of his that I’ve watched, and it’s impressive how none of them come close to the originality, humor, energy and entertainment value of Snatch. This one is just another generic crime movie. The famous “dad movie”, the kind of movie that an older guy who only watches action and crime films will watch and say, “What a masterpiece.” It has a great cast and good performances, especially from Matthew McConaughey, Colin Farrell, and Hugh Grant, who manage to save the film at certain moments. But Guy Ritchie relies way too much on events without truly good writing and throws in countless twists at the end just to keep the audience interested. I think there are at least five twists in the final act alone, seemingly to mask the pathetic writing of the film and characters. Btw this movie has many failed attempts at humor also. Anyway, it has some entertainment value, a good pacing and in certain moments Guy Ritchie directs well and gives us flashes of his originality, but there are very few of them. At one point, you might even think the film is going to take a good direction, but then it goes right back to its mess. Overall, it’s just very generic. It’s a movie to watch to kill some time, because it manages to keep the audience entertained throughout its two-hour runtime, but its content is cheap, a premium generic action.

texto: I feel Guy Ritchie is the biggest victim of his own style. It's clear he grew (grew?!) out of it eventually moving on to action setpieces altogether. And the worse part of it all is that Ritchie used to be great at dialogs - the main detail required for a movie that is 95% people talking to each other how smart they are to out-smart the other one. I do wonder if he thinks throwing so many irrelevant character (played by great actors) into unmemorable roles and with VERY stupid and obvious twists (that play more like "oh, yeah. I forgot about that because I was so uniterested in the story" than "wow, I did not see that coming!") would be the best way to tell yet another cockney underground crime story. Take Hugh Grant's crime paparazzi, for example. He is there for pure exposition (in a fun, cool way, right? Not really. He is annoying as f%$k) but his plan of blackmail makes less sense as he moves the story along.  Did he stop to think before acting (or start talking)? - I'm sure he did since one of the blackmail itens is... (drums please) a screenplay of a movie detailing every bit of the story. You see? It's this movie! For f%$ks sakes. This is so nonsensecle that by the end of it I was wondering if people noticed the story doesn't end at all. It just stops with many plotlines to lead somewhere. I'm actually glad, Ritchie moved on!

texto: Cool premise but the movie is way too in love with its own style. By the halfway mark, I could already see the formula: banter, cool quote, narrator interruption and repeat. Every time I got invested in Mickey and Raymond, the film cut away to Fletcher and completely killed the momentum. The dialogue tries so hard to sound witty that it ends up feeling forced. Same with the edgy humor. I don’t mind offensive jokes, but they have to be clever enough to earn it. Too many characters, too many subplots not enough reasons to care about any of them. By the end, I wasn’t watching the story anymore. I was watching Guy Ritchie trying really hard to make a Guy Ritchie movie

texto: i’m watching the exponential decay of guy ritchie movies in real time and it’s breaking my heart. i should’ve known when in the intro, the actors were being introduced by their actual names instead of their characters nickname!! speaking of, only one character had a nickname!!!!!! i’m from a guy ritchie time where only one dude in the whole cast had a normal name. additionally, we know guy ritchie has never been scared of a little homoeroticism. like, it’s REALLY obvious. he did better on In the Grey (though not by much if i’m being honest) but in this movie it’s treated as more of a gag than anything. the gay guy in this movie happens to be the guy that’s the hardest to like. I remember back in the day, the gay guy was the coolest one!!! and his feelings were actually treated seriously BEFORE the joke came. handsome bob, come back to us. Finally, and probably my biggest grievance, is how ritchie treated Rosalind. He set her up in the beginning to have this cool demeanor and major role, only for the most important thing she does is almost get raped. People have already mentioned this a lot but it’s worth mentioning. Why is the only female character in the movie degraded to a plot device for the male lead in the most despicable way possible?? There was so much potential for Rosalind the whole movie, and at the very end, we see that this experience has miraculously left her unaffected in any way and she pleases the male lead. like???? overall, an experience of me and sam pausing the movie every 15 minutes because of the sheer displeasure of watching it, and repeated “there’s still so much movie left”. this review isn’t even including the fact that the mediocre plot was difficult to follow. it gets 1 1/2 stars because of the toddlers, they were cool. 2000s guy ritchie, come back to me.

texto: I feel Guy Ritchie is the biggest victim of his own style. It's clear he grew (grew?!) out of it eventually moving on to action setpieces altogether. And the worse part of it all is that Ritchie used to be great at dialogs - the main detail required for a movie that is 95% people talking to each other how smart they are to out-smart the other one. I do wonder if he thinks throwing so many irrelevant character (played by great actors) into unmemorable roles and with VERY stupid and obvious twists (that play more like "oh, yeah. I forgot about that because I was so uniterested in the story" than "wow, I did not see that coming!") would be the best way to tell yet another cockney underground crime story. Take Hugh Grant's crime paparazzi, for example. He is there for pure exposition (in a fun, cool way, right? Not really. He is annoying as f%$k) but his plan of blackmail makes less sense as he moves the story along.  Did he stop to think before acting (or start talking)? - I'm sure he did since one of the blackmail itens is... (drums please) a screenplay of a movie detailing every bit of the story. You see? It's this movie! For f%$ks sakes. This is so nonsensecle that by the end of it I was wondering if people noticed the story doesn't end at all. It just stops with many plotlines to lead somewhere. I'm actually glad, Ritchie moved on!

texto: I watched this in cinemas when it came out, and all I remembered about it is that Hugh Grant is really sensational it in. I rewatched this because the second season of the spinoff show the Gentleman has just dropped and my confusion about the plot is getting in the way of my enjoyment of how hot and lovely Theo James is. I don’t feel like rewatching all of season one, so I thought watching the movie might jog my memory. It hasn’t. If anything I’m more lost. I did GREATLY enjoy this however. I couldn’t really FOLLOW what was happening, perhaps because I had three champagnes and was running on two hours of sleep. I have come to the conclusion that Guy Ritchie doesn’t make things that need to be understood , he throws out pithy dialogue and flashy action which is so fast paced that the viewer is completely swept away. I’m sure if you broke down the plot and characters point by point it would reveal logical sense, but this is not a film that requires any deeper thought beyond enjoyment, and that’s kind of amazing. Hugh Grant is still fantastic in this. Fabulously camp but not really at all in a gay way. Mathew McConaughey is being Mathew McConaughey.  Colin Farrell is cartoonish but like on purpose and it’s a delight. Jeremy strong is cartoonish and maybe it’s also on purpose, but it’s bad and annoying. Other actors do other performances as well.

texto: J’ai beaucoup apprécié le style de Guy Ritchie dans Snatch et on retrouve énormément d’éléments similaires dans le montage de The Gentlemen. Malheureusement c’est quitte ou double. Ici, je n’ai pas été pris dans l’histoire et j’ai trouvé le film très long. Si dans Snatch j’ai le sentiment que le style de Guy Ritchie sert vraiment l’histoire, que ce soit avec le montage nerveux, les changements de rythme ou les dialogues qui contribuent à rendre le film dynamique et à maintenir l’intérêt, à l’inverse, dans The Gentlemen j’ai plutôt eu l’impression que le style prenait toute la place au détriment de l’histoire. Le montage et les effets de mise en scène sont toujours très travaillés mais comme je n’ai pas accroché à l’intrigue, ils ont plutôt renforcé cette sensation de longueur. C’est dommage parce que le casting joue très bien et que le film en lui-même est assez élégant.

texto: Franchement, grosse déception. Je m'attendais vraiment à une masterclass vu tout ce que j'avais entendu sur ce film, mais je me suis ennuyé comme rarement. Trois heures de film avec énormément de blabla et très peu d'action, j'ai vraiment eu du mal à rester dedans. Je comprends le délire autour de la mafia et je peux comprendre pourquoi le film a autant marqué à sa sortie, mais aujourd'hui, je trouve ça vraiment difficile à suivre. Le film a clairement vieilli et ça se ressent énormément. Il y a sûrement beaucoup de choses à apprécier dans l'histoire et les personnages, mais personnellement, je n'ai jamais vraiment accroché. Peut-être que les deux suivants sont meilleurs, je les regarderai quand même pour me faire mon avis. Mais pour celui-là, je suis vraiment déçu. Trois heures pour avoir l'impression qu'il ne s'est finalement pas passé grand-chose… Pour moi, le principal problème reste le même du début à la fin : c'est beaucoup trop ennuyant.

exemplo: Alguns espectadores afirmaram que a temática de máfia não é atraente para eles, ou que preferem obras de outros diretores ou mesmo de outros gêneros, o que fez com que o filme não os agradasse.
texto: El Padrino no es una película: es un tratado audiovisual sobre la inevitabilidad del poder, la herencia y la corrupción moral disfrazado de cine de gánsteres. Coppola toma el sueño americano, lo estrangula con una corbata italiana y lo convierte en una tragedia shakespeariana donde la familia funciona simultáneamente como refugio y condena. Lo verdaderamente fascinante no es la violencia, sino la burocracia con la que se ejerce. Michael Corleone no desciende al crimen por ambición, sino por la lógica casi determinista de un sistema donde la ética termina subordinada a la sangre. Cada decisión parece una tesis sobre cómo el poder deja de ser una herramienta para convertirse en una identidad. La fotografía de Gordon Willis, conocida con toda justicia como "el Príncipe de las Tinieblas", no ilumina a los personajes: los juzga. Las sombras no son una elección estética, sino una declaración filosófica de que toda autoridad nace parcialmente oculta. Y Nino Rota compone una partitura que suena menos a música y más a un lamento histórico por una familia condenada desde el primer brindis. Decir que El Padrino es "una película de mafiosos" es como decir que La Odisea trata sobre un hombre que vuelve a casa. Es una reducción casi ofensiva. Lo que Coppola construye es un mito moderno donde el capitalismo, el honor y la violencia dialogan hasta volverse indistinguibles. Obra maestra. No porque sea perfecta, sino porque redefine el lenguaje con el que el cine habla sobre el poder.

texto: Man sollte keine Angst davor haben, Klassiker der Filmgeschichte zu kritisieren, bloß, weil dieser von der Masse gefeiert wird. The Godfather ist so ein Beispiel. Man kann nachvollziehen, wieso er ein großes Publikum erreicht: Der Plot ist gefällig erzählt , die Figuren sind schlicht und die Bildsprache eingängig. Wir verstehen sofort, was Sache ist. Copolla lässt kaum Raum für Ambivalentes, auch Politisches hält er hier vollkommen raus. Dabei kann gerade das Mafia-Genre rasant über die Entstehung von Kapital erzählen, doch das geschieht hier nur randständig. Stattdessen verschafft man dem Publikum Zugang zum Film durch die nervende Betonung von Familienwerten – ja, The Godfather ist ein durch und durch konservativer Film. Die Schwermütigkeit und die Länge des Films ist dabei nicht mit einer anspruchsvollen Kost zu verwechseln. Im Gegenteil kann man es sich immer ganz warm und gemütlich machen, wenn Don Vito Corleone vor dem Bildschirm läuft: Hier wird zwar geschossen und gemordet, aber immerhin ist hier das patriarchale Familienmodell noch intakt. An einem Scoresese-Gangster-Film, geschweige denn an einem Coppola, kommt dieser nicht ran.

texto: Overall good movie that I enjoyed watching. Most of the negative things I have to say about the film are a product of the era it was made. A lot of the acting seemed disingenuous, none of the female actors were very convincing in their roles. The foley work was very bad at times, and there were scenes with noticeable dubbing. Finally, I think many of the scene setting drew on too long (notably the wedding scene in the beginning, and the scenes of Micheal in Sicily). All that being said, it was a very enjoyable story. I can see how this movie clearly inspired a lot of media later on. There really aren’t many movies prior to 1990 that I have liked, but this was an enjoyable watch. The critical acclimation this film has received is - in my opinion - probably based a lot on how it compared to the other films of the period, and not based on all media from all time. This movie is ranked #2 movie of all time on IMDb. Without the nostalgia/bias I don’t think this movie could hold its own against many modern pictures

texto: - LEAVE THE GUN, TAKE THE CANNOLI - In a strange turn of events I ended up reading the book before watching the film. How I went so long without watching this I’ll never know, but wow it truly does earn every ounce of reverence it gets. Might just be one of the best book adaptations I’ve seen as well? If not the best? Shot for shot what I imagined from the pages. Michael’s transformation hit different for me tho. Seeing it visually, you can feel more of the weight he throws around. Might be the Al Pacino stan in me, but no one else could play that character. Can obviously say the same for Marlon Brando. Top to bottom a great, great film. I will say, having so much more context from the book helped immensely. I can see where someone going into the story completely fresh might find a few scene/shot inclusions a bit random or confusing. However, the story was still told wonderfully in the visual format. Felt a lot like reading the book again, which is a fun feeling.

If not the best? Shot for shot what I imagined from the pages. Michael’s transformation hit different for me tho. Seeing it visually, you can feel more of the weight he throws around. Might be the Al Pacino stan in me, but no one else could play that character. Can obviously say the same for Marlon Brando. Top to bottom a great, great film. I will say, having so much more context from the book helped immensely. I can see where someone going into the story completely fresh might find a few scene/shot inclusions a bit random or confusing. However, the story was still told wonderfully in the visual format. Felt a lot like reading the book again, which is a fun feeling.

texto: A depressingly lackluster watch for me. I found it near impossible to follow or care about the protagonist in the slightest… In fact I found myself just increasingly annoyed at him. It’s the first Lucrecia Martel movie that has not engaged me. But it’s not just because there wasn’t a lot happening. La ciénaga & La mujer sin cabeza were also slow & tense & subtle. But Zama just offered no grips to hang on to and as it went on I cared less and less to look for any. I certainly see how Martel was weaving some things together throughout, most significantly in the final declaration of refusing to offer false hope after learning what pain it can bring. But gosh I was so unhappy during the journey getting there that I could barely appreciate what probably did make it a decently good period piece and examination of masculinity, colonialism, rejection, etc. I just feel so bleh thinking about this movie, and I’m bummed about it.

texto: Making art about colonialism is a fool's errand, a necessary one, but still a fool's errand. The problem being that as a historical phenomenon, once you understand colonialism on a functional level, it’s appalling nature is self-evident. I mean, we quite literally still live in its aftermath, it’s pretty much impossible to go a day without some reminder of its legacy being present in your life. That makes it pretty damn challenging for a piece of art to really serve a constructive or insightful purpose, and Zama is no exception. It’s a very deliberate slog, one with cramped shots, bug-infested soundscapes, and long, monotonous conversations between colonial elites about mind-numbing nothingness. So yeah, it’s a film that practically dares its viewers to tune out, a film that works much better as something to think about with regard to how well-crafted it is, rather than something to watch. I really don’t wanna call it boring, because at the end of the day, it’s fairly well-made, but it’s quite honestly excruciating to watch. I’m far from opposed to a movie having a slow pace, or a deliberately unconventional style, but that can’t be its defining aspect. I watch movies to feel, to think, not be subjected to an artist's self-satisfied conveyor belt of irksome quirks.

texto: Zama (2017) es una película de cine nacional dirigida por la siempre interesante Lucrecia Martel. En este caso nos presenta un drama de época sobre un corregidor español en la "Argentina" colonial del Siglo XVIII que atraviesa una travesía de burocracia para lograr su deseo de que lo trasladen de lugar. Primero que nada, hay que destacar la enorme creatividad de Lucrecia Martel para hacer una película tan poco convencional como esta, porque es una película que no se ve todos los días y la directora se mete en el barro para contar esta historia tomándose todo el tiempo del mundo, con una narrativa muy interesante y los recursos que solamente Lucrecia nos puede entregar. En este sentido, la narrativa sería una mezcla entre una pesadilla de David Lynch con una historia de la Argentina Colonial. Pesadilla Lyncheana básicamente porque vamos a ver la historia de este protagonista en relación a su ahogo y frustración con respecto al lugar y la posición que ocupa. Para realizar esta trama, Lucrecia Martel hace un laburo estupendo, en especial con el uso de sonidos, para demostrar la claustrofobia del protagonista, unido a una serie de planos cortos que encierra al protagonista en este lugar que detesta tanto y no consigue salir. La sofocación, los impulsos sexuales, el ambiente húmedo y tenso, todo se responde a partir de los recursos de la cámara y el sonido. En especial, Lucrecia va a utilizar el agua como recurso y vehículo de la tragedia que va sufriendo el protagonista. Así, el agua viene a explicar el "ahogo" de Zama. Sin embargo, el mayor problema que tengo con este film es que me aburrió sobremanera, toda la historia que expliqué anteriormente no logra enganchar en ningún momento, haciendo que no te interese lo que le pase al protagonista ni a ninguno de los personajes que aparece en este film. Si bien en los últimos 10 minutos repunta un montón, haciendo un final más que decente donde podemos ver la calidad que tiene Lucrecia para filmar, no es suficiente para lograr que sea una película recordable. Quizás sea por el guión que hace que la película durante muchos tramos se torne muy pesada y lenta de seguir. Hay películas que son lentas y aun así logran ser una obra maestra, aca pasa poco y nada y no logra conectar con el espectador. También creo que el guión falla con el desarrollo de los personajes, que tampoco transmiten nada, ni para bien ni para mal. Los protagonistas o personajes no logran un sentimiento de empatía (ni siquiera de odio) por parte del espectador. Es como si los mismos personajes fueran los espectadores. En conclusión, Zama está lejos de ser una mala película, ya que se ve lo increíble que es Lucrecia Martel para entregarnos recursos cinematográficos para contar una historia a partir del juego de planos, sonidos y el agua. Sin embargo, mal uso de personajes, de escenas y de momentos, hace que la película se torne densa y, durante gran parte, aburrida. 50 de 100 Gasparcitos.

texto: Even with the Indios Tabajaras in the background, the movie managed to disappoint me and get me uncomfortable as much as the good baroque artists' enterprise managed to do, breaking the comfortable logic of imperialism. What was exactly what the Spaniards came to do? What is the purpose of the lawyers, the leguleyos, the scribes? So yes, there is this very XXth-century ambition to estrange and attack the logic of the intellectuals coming to confirm something that, in its very bottom, is inconfirmable and relies more on the reconquest for the reconquest for the sole adaption and expansion of syncretism. The traps of the signs, the labyrinths of meaning in a colony that has turned into an absurd place, with not many things to do, not many opportunities, catered towards either the sadism or the hedonism of its peninsular inhabitants. The criollos, as second-order Spaniards in a sense, become disposable populations; there is an outsiderness that comes with existential angst, an out-of-placeness that will be enforced upon the land and the societal. Perhaps more familiar with the US experience of the destruction of any indigeneity or correlation with the ground, the peculiarity here is that the hidalguia and the abstractive nature of the writers will cut that window of release that labor could have brought. When the writer tries to make some fiction, it is forbidden, as in a sense there isn’t even an allowance for the recreation of consciousness or of intelligence. Rather than living, the colonialists are walking symbols, vulnerable to their careerism. The body of the Vicuña Porto means the opportunity to break from the monotonous, to think of the land as something fully captured, fully dominated, and that can be transited. That will be more of the XIXth-century pact, but for the moment any person who wants to dismantle the assuredness of the powers in place will partake in its performativity of otherness. The hands are cut off to remind the loss of agency, the loss of action, the loss of participation in the land, the horrible castaway place of the intellectual. All of this is intriguing and exciting, but I have to subscribe to the critics of Latinamericanism: they are still intellectual feuds, repositioning the intellectual as the main subject of the story, as the most interesting or important piece of the empire, losing a whole broader picture. I get that there is a natural inclination for the writers or scholars to think of Angel Rama's legacy of where to position the empire of the letter beside that of the sword and call for its miseries, but still… it comes off as unnecessary, dull, reiterative, too allegorical, too tryhard. Way too easy to point out the servants as mute figures, the indigenous as second-order existences not captured or grasped by Zama, lived realities which amplify his isolation to reinforce the theme of impotence. Why is the drama always his? Why reinforce the subalternism who cannot speak? The decadence of the promiscuous Spanish woman is already a common trope of the false performativity of the colonial elites, always yearning for somewhere else. As much as the family he cannot access, the alienation of his agency, his lost home—we all feel that despair—but still, aren't we falling into the trap of feeling worse for the criollo than for the others, always reading the colonialism in his own terms? We already knew the illegitimacy of the crown and its absurdity, that has to come with stupid social norms skipped with the necessity for action. Feel sorry for the leguleyos not to be able to listen to the natural rhythm of the Indios Tabajaras?

texto: Even with the Indios Tabajaras in the background, the movie managed to disappoint me and get me uncomfortable as much as the good baroque artists' enterprise managed to do, breaking the comfortable logic of imperialism. What was exactly what the Spaniards came to do? What is the purpose of the lawyers, the leguleyos, the scribes? So yes, there is this very XXth-century ambition to estrange and attack the logic of the intellectuals coming to confirm something that, in its very bottom, is inconfirmable and relies more on the reconquest for the reconquest for the sole adaption and expansion of syncretism. The traps of the signs, the labyrinths of meaning in a colony that has turned into an absurd place, with not many things to do, not many opportunities, catered towards either the sadism or the hedonism of its peninsular inhabitants. The criollos, as second-order Spaniards in a sense, become disposable populations; there is an outsiderness that comes with existential angst, an out-of-placeness that will be enforced upon the land and the societal. Perhaps more familiar with the US experience of the destruction of any indigeneity or correlation with the ground, the peculiarity here is that the hidalguia and the abstractive nature of the writers will cut that window of release that labor could have brought. When the writer tries to make some fiction, it is forbidden, as in a sense there isn’t even an allowance for the recreation of consciousness or of intelligence. Rather than living, the colonialists are walking symbols, vulnerable to their careerism. The body of the Vicuña Porto means the opportunity to break from the monotonous, to think of the land as something fully captured, fully dominated, and that can be transited. That will be more of the XIXth-century pact, but for the moment any person who wants to dismantle the assuredness of the powers in place will partake in its performativity of otherness. The hands are cut off to remind the loss of agency, the loss of action, the loss of participation in the land, the horrible castaway place of the intellectual. All of this is intriguing and exciting, but I have to subscribe to the critics of Latinamericanism: they are still intellectual feuds, repositioning the intellectual as the main subject of the story, as the most interesting or important piece of the empire, losing a whole broader picture. I get that there is a natural inclination for the writers or scholars to think of Angel Rama's legacy of where to position the empire of the letter beside that of the sword and call for its miseries, but still… it comes off as unnecessary, dull, reiterative, too allegorical, too tryhard. Way too easy to point out the servants as mute figures, the indigenous as second-order existences not captured or grasped by Zama, lived realities which amplify his isolation to reinforce the theme of impotence. Why is the drama always his? Why reinforce the subalternism who cannot speak? The decadence of the promiscuous Spanish woman is already a common trope of the false performativity of the colonial elites, always yearning for somewhere else. As much as the family he cannot access, the alienation of his agency, his lost home—we all feel that despair—but still, aren't we falling into the trap of feeling worse for the criollo than for the others, always reading the colonialism in his own terms? We already knew the illegitimacy of the crown and its absurdity, that has to come with stupid social norms skipped with the necessity for action. Feel sorry for the leguleyos not to be able to listen to the natural rhythm of the Indios Tabajaras?

texto: A depressingly lackluster watch for me. I found it near impossible to follow or care about the protagonist in the slightest… In fact I found myself just increasingly annoyed at him. It’s the first Lucrecia Martel movie that has not engaged me. But it’s not just because there wasn’t a lot happening. La ciénaga & La mujer sin cabeza were also slow & tense & subtle. But Zama just offered no grips to hang on to and as it went on I cared less and less to look for any. I certainly see how Martel was weaving some things together throughout, most significantly in the final declaration of refusing to offer false hope after learning what pain it can bring. But gosh I was so unhappy during the journey getting there that I could barely appreciate what probably did make it a decently good period piece and examination of masculinity, colonialism, rejection, etc. I just feel so bleh thinking about this movie, and I’m bummed about it.

texto: *Reseña sin spoilers* Esta es mi 2da película de Lucrecia Martel, esta obra es totalmente desconocida aun con la cantidad de  premios que gano, hasta fue seleccionada para representar a Argentina en los oscares Quiero aclarar que no la termine a la película, pero siento haber visto suficiente para saber que no hay mucho mas allá de la mitad de la película. Las reseñas alrededor de esta película son muy dispares, de un lado la ven como una obra maestra (como en el caso de rotten tomatoes con una calificación de 96%), del otro lado la ven como una obra mediocre, me pongo mas del lado que dice que esta película es mediocre, cosa que me parece muy triste, ya que la fotografía y escenografía de esta película me  parece hermosa, una fotografía mucho mas profesional que la película anterior de la misma directora (La Mujer sin Cabeza), y como ya viene siendo tradición en las películas de esta mujer, el audio esta muy bien hecho, pero por mi parte siento que para mi no bastan una buena fotografía y un excelente audio para hacer una buena obra, la historia me pareció desesperante de verla, intento pensar que la autora hizo esto a propósito para que el espectador pueda sentir la misma desesperación que el protagonista, pero eso no quita que a mitad de la película me importaba mas pensar en la lista de cosas que tengo que comprar mañana que en la historia de la película. Con la película anterior, La Mujer Sin Cabeza, no llegue a dilucidar si había o no una critica social a la clase alta, y en esta siento lo mismo, no se si pecó de tibia o simplemente no le interesaba ahondar en el tema, pero queda todo tan al aire que simplemente desinfla mas un argumento que ya estaba desinflado. Quiero intentar decir cosas buenas de la película ya que siento que la estoy atacando demasiado: el inicio de la película y los primeros minutos me parecieron geniales, es una gran película si tomamos sus elementos por separado, pero falla desde el guion lento y sin mensaje. Me gustaría dejar como conclusión un comentario dejado  por alguien en uno de los tráiler de la película: "no tiene absolutamente nada que decir y aun así se empecina en hacerlo ¡maravilloso!" P.D: O la amas o la odias P.D. 2: No me gusta poner calificaciones numéricas, pero esta película se merece un 2

texto: pacifiction, l’aura et le fun en moins Je dois reconnaître qu’un certain ennui m’a saisi devant ce film, ennui pourtant travaillé de l’intérieur par une forme d’intérêt. Il s’agit de l’histoire d’un colon espagnol en Argentine à la fin du XVIIIe siècle qui désire revenir en Espagne auprès de sa femme et de ses enfants, mais dont le sort demeure suspendu à l’arbitraire de la monarchie et de ses relais administratifs. Ce récit apparent recouvre en réalité un processus plus profond : la lente désagrégation d’une figure de domination qui découvre, dans le décalage entre sa position imaginaire et sa condition réelle, qu’il n’est rien. Le film travaille alors cette chute non comme un événement spectaculaire mais comme une expérience sensible. Le son notamment se resserre, s’étouffe, jusqu’à laisser place à une sorte de rumeur sourde au moment précis où le personnage perd prise sur le réel et voit s’effondrer les signes de son prestige. La réalisatrice met également en scène les dispositifs de domination. L’homme est pris dans un réseau de rapports qui excèdent sa propre conscience : une épouse l’attend en Espagne, il a engrossé une femme "indigène", il drague l’une des jeunes filles du blanchisseur, il tente en vain de séduire l’épouse d’un représentant de la couronne, laquelle lui échappe précisément parce qu’elle ne se laisse pas assigner à la place qu’il lui destine. Ce faisceau de relations laisse entrevoir une articulation des rapports de domination, à la fois coloniaux et sexués. Aussi le travail du regard participe de ce dispositif. Souvent la scène se dérobe en tant que telle et ce sont les visages de ceux qui regardent qui nous sont donnés, comme si le film déplaçait le centre de gravité de l’action vers ses effets et ses répercussions subjectives. Ce choix produit une forme de décentrement qui redouble la perte de maîtrise du personnage. Enfin, la couleur, avec ces verts persistants et ces oranges poussés jusqu’à une sorte d’intensité terminale dans les dernières séquences, compose une matière visuelle d’une grande beauté comme si l’image elle-même portait, à son niveau, la trace de cette montée vers une limite. Malheureusement, tout cela ne m’a pas suffit pour faire en sorte de ne pas être profondément ennuyé.

texto: The premise is intriguing: a European colonial official stranded in South America, desperately waiting for a transfer that never seems to come. It's a fascinating setup that promises a slow descent into frustration and absurdity. Visually, the film is excellent. The cinematography, the period settings, and the use of color are all beautifully realized, creating a world that feels both authentic and strangely dreamlike. Unfortunately, the story never really goes anywhere. Despite its compelling premise, the narrative drifts for much of the runtime, and I found myself growing bored rather quickly. The final act injects some much-needed tension and is easily the strongest part of the film, but by then it was too little, too late. In the end, Zama left me with mixed feelings. I admired its craftsmanship and visual style, but emotionally I remained detached. What lingered most wasn't the story itself, but a sense of boredom and occasional confusion.

texto: Lucrecia Martel’s Zama is one of those films where I can recognize and even respect the craft behind it without necessarily understanding the acclaim surrounding it. Martel is clearly in complete control of her direction, creating a visually striking film that feels deliberately composed and full of strange, unsettling details, while the unusual use of sound adds another layer to its atmosphere. The performances are also strong, particularly Daniel Giménez Cacho in the lead, whose restrained portrayal gives Don Diego de Zama an appropriately weary and increasingly pathetic presence. There is certainly something fascinating about the way the film captures colonial stagnation, isolation, and the absurdity of a man desperately waiting for a transfer that may never come, but for me, that fascination rarely translated into an engaging viewing experience. The narrative felt extremely uneven, with long stretches where there seemed to be very little conventional plot momentum, making the film’s nearly two-hour runtime feel considerably longer than it actually is. More importantly, I found myself emotionally distant from de Zama throughout most of the film; despite what he goes through, I simply never became invested enough in his fate for the story’s increasingly surreal developments to have much impact. I can appreciate that the sluggish pacing, ambiguity, and fragmented storytelling are intentional choices, and Martel’s filmmaking is undeniably distinctive, but intention alone didn’t make the experience particularly satisfying for me. Zama is certainly an unusual and technically accomplished film, and I understand why its visual language and unconventional approach have earned it so much praise, but I ultimately found it more interesting to admire from a distance than genuinely enjoyable or compelling to watch.

texto: let's start off with the sound, which many of our finest critics and cinephiles have lauded. the one-and-a-half minute list of production companies at the start promises craftsmanship of the highest quality. it's not good. it is ordinary at best, ordinarily immoral at worst. it seems that people simply love when things are emphasized for them: here is a surge of creativity, intended for a purpose that does not seem incongruous with the overall subject matter, and thus we are in the hands of an auteur who startles, who controls her spectators with mastery. we are no longer content to see or hear what is only humbly in front of us. like the spaniards, we are too good for humility. now, i am unsure about something, and somebody please clarify it for me, but does martel think that cutting the frame just below the hairline achieves some sort of effect, or does she just not know where to place a camera? this is very astonishing, coming from someone who, for example, allows herself to use the mbayá as a tool for her formal allegory - the settlers have wandered off into atemporality. what spatial awareness, everything is so attentively cut, the atmospheric sounds are so immersive. so painstaking is the delineation of each sequence’s margins that martel denies characters the time that their gestures and actions require. even worse - she denies animals and the others their neutrality. the only shots that escape this deriding academicism are precisely the ones that, by some miracle (aha, martel creates miracles!), have rebelled through their own strength from the misleading disorder of a film made to be seen, and presented us with a well down to a chasm where the unknown may gaze back at us.

texto: It's been a minute since Argentinian director Martel's last feature, and she makes the wait worth it with an intimate adaptation of a novel about a colonial administrator who's trying to get out of his royal commission, a steamy backwater in the 18th century South America. The lead actor Cacho is absolutely perfect, doing everything you want a person with a sea of emotion and thwarted hopes to do. My only complaint is the languorous pacing, bordering on glacial. It kept me at arms length from some of the proceedings.

texto: This film has the weirdest fucking energy. Like a series of mad sketches, shifting in tonality, consisting of every bad thing that can happen to a single dude happening in the most bizarre way possible. I'm pretty sure every single shot has some weird shit going on. But don't mistake this as an endorsement. It's an exhausting and frustrating film; wholly stubborn in it's ways. Sometimes amusing or interesting, but mostly tedious and inaccessible. Gotta give major props to Daniel Jiménez for portraying the most miserable and pathetic little man to ever walk the earth. Playing the titular Zama with such dead eyes, like a walking corpse forced to endure purgatory for the rest of time. --- Esta película tiene de verdad la energía más extraña. Como una serie de bocetos dementes, cambiando de tonalidad, consistentes en todo lo malo que le puede pasar a un solo tipo sucediéndole de la manera más bizarra posible. Estoy bastante seguro de que cada toma de la peli tiene alguna mierda extraña ocurriendo en ellas. Pero no confundas esto con una aprobación o respaldo. Es una película agotadora y frustrante; totalmente terca con sus métodos. A veces divertida o interesante, pero por sobre todo tediosa e inaccesible. Tengo que cederle un gran reconocimiento a Daniel Jiménez por interpretar al hombrecito más miserable y patético que jamás haya caminado sobre la tierra. Interpretando al titular Zama con unos ojos tan muertos, como un cadáver caminante obligado a soportar el purgatorio por el resto de la eternidad. [FESTIVAL DE VENECIA Y TORONTO]
